title: Life Science Research Handbook
text: This handbook gives advice on scientific reasoning and professional practice in life science research. For humans it might still be unbearable to read, due to slop prose! But maybe it can inspire a more complete handbook in the future.

title: Choosing a scientific problem
text:
What would you learn?
Choose a question you want to spend time answering. Consider what you could learn and whether you can do the work with the time and support available. Comparing a few possible projects can help you decide [1, pp. 726–727].
Describe what you want to find out. “Single-cell analysis of regeneration” names a method and a topic, but leaves the question open. A more specific question would be: “Why does injured tissue recover more slowly in older animals? Are fewer repair cells present, or do those cells divide less?” You can then decide which measurements would help answer it.
Read the literature. What is already established, in which systems and under what conditions? What is being assumed? Which observation remains unexplained?
A gap in the literature can suggest a project, but explain what answering the question would add to our understanding [2, Rules 15–18]. For example, a treatment that works in cultured cells may fail in intact tissue. Testing it in tissue would establish whether the effect occurs there too. A project can also be valuable without testing an explanation: describing which cells appear during recovery may be a useful first step when little is known about the process.
Your own interest matters too. Notice the questions you keep returning to and the work you enjoy doing. You will spend time on routine tasks as well as discoveries, so consider whether the day-to-day work appeals to you [1, pp. 726–727].

title: Choosing a scientific problem
text:
Compare realistic alternatives
Compare projects you could undertake within the available time. For each one, describe the question and how you would begin answering it. Identify anything you would need to obtain or establish first, such as access to samples or a reliable assay. This makes it easier to compare the work involved as well as the scientific interest.
Alon proposes comparing interest with feasibility. A question that interests you more and is easier to investigate is usually the better choice. The harder decision is between an ambitious question that may take years to answer and a smaller project you could complete sooner. Consider how much time and support you have. If you need to develop a new method first, will enough time remain to investigate the question? [1, p. 726].
Check the assumptions that could change your choice. If a project depends on a collaborator’s samples, ask whether they can provide them, when they would arrive and whether you can use them for the proposed study. Until you have an agreement, sample access remains uncertain.
Consider the work needed to establish the method. If it is new to you or your laboratory, find out who can help and allow time to learn it. You may need a pilot experiment to check that the assay measures what you need before you can use it to answer the biological question.
In this fictional example, a researcher trained in live-cell imaging has eighteen months of funded work and a persistent interest in how living systems recover after stress. Two projects appeal to them.



Comparison: two recovery problems

A: Why do cultured cells resume growth at different times after nutrient restoration?

The first task is to distinguish cells that resume division from those that remain arrested or die. Explaining these different responses would require follow-up experiments. The laboratory already has the culture and imaging methods. The researcher still needs to check whether they can change the medium repeatedly, follow cell divisions and assess viability in the same experiment.


B: What explains differences in recovery after injury across species?

The researcher would need access to new cultures and a way to compare injury and recovery across species. They do not yet know how long this would take to set up.


Before choosing, the researcher needs to check whether A’s imaging assay can distinguish division, arrest and cell loss. For B, they need to establish which cultures are available and how recovery could be compared across species. These checks could show that one project is much harder to carry out than it first appeared.

title: Choosing a scientific problem
text:
Time, experience and support
For a first project, it can help to choose a question you can begin investigating with established methods and regular guidance. That gives you time to learn how to do research without also having to develop every method. A less predictable project may be reasonable when you have more experience, longer funding or colleagues who can share the work [1, p. 726].
When you feel out of your depth, ask what you need to learn. You may be missing background knowledge or a technique that someone can teach you. But you may also have reached a question that nobody knows how to answer yet. Schwartz describes this difference between learning established knowledge and doing research [3]. Reading and discussion can help you distinguish the two; an unknown answer alone is no reason to abandon a question.
Set aside time to read, discuss possible questions and check feasibility before committing. Alon’s laboratory gives new researchers three months for this, though he acknowledges that funding and deadlines can limit the time available [1, pp. 726–727]. Agree with your supervisor how much time you can spend exploring and when you need to choose.
If your broad topic is assigned, ask your supervisor which decisions are still open. You may be able to choose the specific question or the system in which to study it, even when the overall aim is fixed.

title: Choosing a scientific problem
text:
Making the choice
Write down why you chose the project and what you learned about its feasibility. Note the main risk and what would make you reconsider. As Alon describes, research may lead to a more interesting question than the one you started with [1, p. 728].
The fictional researcher contacts the imaging facility and the potential collaborator. The facility can support repeated imaging and medium changes for A. For B, the collaborator can provide two species, but an additional species is not expected for at least six months. The teams have not yet agreed how to measure recovery across species.



Decision record: choose a defined recovery problem
Chosen question: Why do cultured cells resume growth at different times after nutrient restoration?

Reason to pursue it: I want to understand why some cells recover while others remain arrested. I have the imaging experience and local support to begin studying this.
Information checked: The facility can support repeated imaging and medium changes. I still need to test whether the assay can distinguish resumed division, continued arrest and cell loss.
Alternative set aside: The cross-species comparison interests me, but I cannot yet obtain all the cultures or compare their recovery reliably. I judge that setting this up would leave too little of my eighteen months to investigate the question. I will discuss a longer-term project with the collaborator.
Risk accepted: Developing the assay may take longer than expected. I need a way to assess viability, because a cell that does not divide may be arrested or dead.
Condition for reconsideration: If the assay cannot distinguish division, arrest and cell loss, I will need to change the measurement or narrow the question. If cultures and a suitable comparative assay become available for B, I will reconsider that project.

title: Developing ideas
text:
Start with an observation
An observation you cannot explain can give you the beginning of a research idea. Explore possible explanations and look for a way to test them. The question may change as you learn more.
Yanai and Lercher call exploratory thinking night science and systematic testing day science, following François Jacob’s distinction. You can move between the two as an experiment suggests a new idea or an idea becomes ready to test [3].
Write down what drew your attention and why it is surprising. Keep the observation separate from the explanation. “The processed images look brighter near the colony edge” reports something you can inspect. “Cells at the edge activate the pathway” adds claims about cells, measurement and mechanism. Those claims may become ideas to investigate, but they should not replace the starting observation.
You can explore data before choosing a hypothesis to test. You still need to understand what the assay measures and how the data were produced. Familiarity with the biology helps you recognize an unexpected observation; familiarity with the method helps you judge whether the procedure could have produced it [7, p. 2].
Try different views of the data. A distribution can reveal variation hidden by an average; individual trajectories can show whether samples change in the same way over time. Check whether a pattern coincides with how or when samples were prepared and measured. If the pattern appears in processed data, compare them with the raw observations to see whether processing created it. Shoresh and Wong distinguish plots used to explore data from plots used to explain a finding already identified [2]. Choosing a figure or table explains what different displays can reveal.
A specific hypothesis can focus attention so narrowly that other features go unnoticed. But searching many views of a dataset can also turn up patterns by chance. Keep a record of the plots and analysis choices that led to an idea, including any observations you excluded. Identify it as an idea developed from those data: the pattern that suggested it does not also provide an independent test of it [4, pp. 1–4].

title: Developing ideas
text:
Connections with other fields
An idea from another field may help explain an unfamiliar pattern. If a signal changes with distance from a colony’s edge, for example, you might ask whether a substance reaches the center less readily. Transport theory could help you develop that possibility [5, pp. 2–4].
Check the assumptions before applying a model from another system. In the colony example, ask which substance the model could describe and whether differences in its availability could change the reporter signal. A model might assume that concentrations have reached equilibrium, whereas your experiment observes a changing supply. Read how the model was derived, and ask someone familiar with it to help assess whether its assumptions fit your system.
An informal phrase such as “the colony’s center is being starved” can suggest an idea before you know which substance might be scarce. Before designing a test, spell out the proposed explanation: “Perhaps a substance supplied from outside the colony reaches the center at a lower concentration, causing the reporter to be dimmer there.” You would then need to find out which substance could do this and how it would affect the reporter. Yanai and Lercher describe how metaphors can help generate ideas that later need more precise wording [6, pp. 4–8].
Several other explanations remain possible. Lower fluorescence could mean less reporter per cell, different reporter chemistry or fewer cells in the imaged region. It could also arise from how the microscope records light. The nutrient explanation needs to be considered alongside these alternatives.

title: Developing ideas
text:
Discussing unfinished ideas
Discuss the unfinished idea with someone who can help you develop it. A colleague familiar with the assay may notice a measurement problem; someone from another field may suggest an explanation you had not considered. Choose a person or group with whom you can think aloud before you have a defensible answer [9, pp. 2–8]; [11].
Give a tentative idea time to develop before rejecting it. Ask what would have to be true for it to work, or whether a narrower version could explain the observation. Then examine it critically: does it conflict with known evidence, and what alternatives have you overlooked? Yanai and Lercher recommend this constructive exchange without requiring colleagues to agree that an idea is true [9, pp. 3–4].

Developing a spatial question

The following fictional conversation concerns processed fluorescence images of bacterial colonies that appear brighter near their edges. No mechanism or quantitative difference has been established.



Conversation: from a plausible story to alternatives

Researcher: Perhaps cells near the edge get more nutrients, so the reporter is brighter there.
Colleague: Then we should look at how brightness changes with distance from the edge. Do we see the same pattern in different colonies?
Researcher: We could look for that. But the reporter might also behave differently where oxygen is more available. We have not checked its chemistry under these conditions.
Colleague: And are we sure the pattern follows the colony? If illumination is uneven, its position in the image could matter. Colony thickness might change the recorded signal too.
Researcher: Let’s first check the raw images. Are the bright regions near colony edges, or do they occur in the same part of the microscope’s field of view? If the pattern follows the colonies and remains after checking acquisition and processing, we can investigate nutrient access and reporter chemistry.


After a discussion, note how the question changed, what you still disagree about and who contributed each suggestion. Include alternatives you do not favor, so that your notes do not preserve only your preferred explanation.

title: Developing ideas
text:
Questioning assumptions
When an observation does not fit, examine the observation and the expectation together. An apparent contradiction may reflect a technical problem, a difference in conditions or a hidden assumption about the biology. Apply the same scrutiny to an attractive finding. Gosling and Noordam warn both against dismissing data that disagree with a hypothesis and against mistaking systematic error or ordinary variation for a discovery [1, pp. 24–25].
State the assumption you need to check. In the colony case, you might have assumed that a brighter region contains more reporter per cell. But a thicker region may contain more cells along the imaging path. Before interpreting brightness as a difference between cells, you would need to account for how many cells contribute to the signal.
When you are stuck, ask whether the facts you already have can explain the observation or whether you need to look elsewhere. You may need to learn about a process outside your field, as in the transport example. Or you may have imposed a restriction without noticing it, such as assuming that brightness must reflect a change inside individual cells. Yanai and Lercher’s puzzle framework offers these as different ways to reconsider a problem; you may not know in advance which one will help [10, pp. 3–7].
Try developing the strongest contrary account of your preferred idea. What would a careful critic say you had overlooked? Which observation would be difficult to explain under your account? Yanai and Lercher suggest imagining a future paper that challenges the project as a way to expose assumptions. Use that exercise to generate alternatives, then assess whether they actually fit the evidence [8, pp. 5–6].

title: Developing ideas
text:
What to check next
Choose the next step by asking what you need to learn before designing an experiment. If you do not yet understand the reporter, read about its chemistry and check how it behaves under your conditions. If the observation is reliable but several explanations fit, work out what each would predict. You do not need a complete explanation before beginning, but you should be able to say what the next check would tell you.
For the colony example, the discussion produces the following note.



Idea note: does the spatial pattern belong to the sample?

Starting observation: Processed fluorescence images appear brighter near colony edges. This is an impression from images, not a validated estimate of reporter abundance per cell.
Developed idea: A substance supplied from outside the colony might reach the center at a lower concentration and affect the reporter signal. We could examine how brightness changes with distance from the edge.
Alternatives to retain: Reporter chemistry may vary with local conditions; colony thickness may alter the recorded signal; illumination or background subtraction may create a pattern. We have not established which explanation applies.
Next check: Inspect raw images, acquisition metadata and processing settings. Establish whether the pattern exists before processing and follows colony position rather than position in the field of view. Check what the reporter can indicate under these conditions.
Decision after that check: If acquisition or processing creates the pattern, investigate that cause before interpreting it biologically. If those checks leave a pattern that follows the colony, compare the predictions of the remaining explanations. We still need to determine what the reporter measures before choosing a biological test.


For the next experiment, compare the predictions of the remaining explanations.

title: Connecting questions, models and experiments
text:
Defining the question
You may need to describe a pattern before trying to explain it: when does the response appear, how much does it vary, and does it recur? Once you have possible explanations, choose a comparison for which they predict different results. Then check whether your measurement can detect that difference.
The question states what you want to learn. A hypothesis offers a possible answer; a model describes how the proposed explanation works and what it assumes. A prediction states what you would expect to observe if the explanation and its assumptions hold. A statistical test can assess a difference between conditions, but that difference may have several biological explanations. [5, pp. 723–724]; [4].
Describing a response over time can be worthwhile before you have a mechanism to test. Decide which population you want to describe, what you will measure and how you will sample it. To investigate an unexpected pattern, you also need to understand how the method could produce it. Yanai and Lercher argue for moving between exploration and hypothesis testing as the work develops. Neither must always come first, and both depend on assumptions about the system and its measurements. [7, pp. 2–4].
Separate the observation from the explanation. Higher reporter fluorescence in dense cultures is an observation; communication between cells is one possible explanation. A question such as “Do these cells communicate?” leaves many choices hidden. Which cells, which response, under which conditions, and what would count as communication? A narrower question might ask whether something in medium conditioned by dense cultures increases a recipient population’s reporter response after a depleted nutrient has been restored.
“The cells warn their neighbors” may help you imagine a mechanism. To test it, ask whether a factor released by one population changes the response of another. You then need conditions that distinguish the factor’s action from other changes in the medium [6, pp. 3–6].
Keep the biological model and the measurement assumptions distinct. The biological model describes what produces the response. The measurement assumptions explain why your readout represents that response: whether fluorescence reflects promoter activity, whether a tag changes protein behavior, or whether a sample represents the population you intend to study. A precise measurement of the wrong proxy can produce a reproducible result without answering the biological question [2, pp. 2–4].

title: Connecting questions, models and experiments
text:
Comparing predictions
Write a small set of plausible models, including an explanation that challenges your preferred one. For each, ask what should happen under the proposed intervention and why. A statement such as “expression will change” is rarely enough. Direction, timing, dependence on another factor, or the shape of a response may distinguish models that agree about an endpoint. If their predictions overlap, change the conditions or measure a different feature before treating the experiment as a test between them [8, pp. 4–6].
A model can start as a verbal mechanism or a sketch. Mathematics becomes useful when it exposes an assumption or yields a prediction that the verbal account leaves vague. For example, two mechanisms may both predict an increase but differ in how the response depends on concentration. Check whether those predicted differences exceed the variation and resolution of the proposed assay. Adding equations does not help if the competing models remain indistinguishable at the conditions you can measure [5, pp. 723–724 and 728].
Explaining existing data is useful work. It can expose missing mechanisms and suggest the next comparison. However, a model adjusted to reproduce a dataset has not thereby passed an independent predictive test. Mark which observations shaped it and identify a prediction to examine with new data or data kept separate from model development. Theory can guide an experiment, and an unexpected observation can prompt a better theory; neither must come first in every project [5, p. 728]; [7, pp. 1–6].



Example: a proposed test of conditioned medium
This fictional bacterial strain carries a promoter reporter. At a fixed sampling time, background-corrected fluorescence per viable cell is higher after exposure to cell-free medium conditioned by dense cultures than after fresh medium. A nutrient, N, is measured to be lower in the conditioned medium. These observations establish neither a signal nor its mechanism.

Consider two simple models. In A, N depletion alone causes the increase. In B, an extracellular factor released by the donor cells causes it, N depletion has no effect on its own, and the factor acts independently of N over the tested range. Compare the following conditions in recipient cultures started at the same density. “Baseline” means no increase relative to fresh medium; these are predictions, not results.









Proposed condition
Model A: N depletion
Model B: N-independent factor




Fresh medium
Baseline
Baseline


Untreated conditioned medium
Increased response
Increased response


Fresh medium with N lowered to the measured conditioned-medium level
Increased response
Baseline


Conditioned medium with N restored to the fresh-medium level
Baseline
Increased response




Both models predict an increase in untreated conditioned medium, so that comparison cannot distinguish them. They disagree about the two conditions in which N is changed. These test only the two explanations specified here. If the response increases in both, neither simple model accounts for the full pattern. Multiple causes or an interaction could be involved, but the result alone would not establish that two mechanisms coexist.

title: Connecting questions, models and experiments
text:
Assumptions and controls
Ask what else your intervention changes. Deleting a gene may induce compensation; adding a compound may affect growth, uptake or the reporter itself. A loss-of-function phenotype can support a role for the gene in the response, without showing how it acts. Likewise, reproducing a behavior with selected components shows what they can do together under those conditions. It does not establish that the intact organism uses the same mechanism [2, pp. 2–5].
In the medium example, restoring N must leave the proposed extracellular factor available and active for the table’s B prediction to hold. If N changes the factor’s stability or uptake, loss of the response after restoration could fit either explanation. Conversely, nutrient depletion can alter recipient physiology and reporter production. Dividing fluorescence by cell count addresses cell number, but does not automatically correct those effects. Keep the fluorescence, viable-cell counts and growth measurements available alongside the ratio.
Choose controls that check a specific possible problem. A negative control can reveal background or an effect of handling; a positive control can show that the assay responds in the medium being tested. Neither shows whether an unidentified factor survived a manipulation. If you cannot check that the factor remains active after restoring N, a loss of response will leave its possible role unresolved.

title: Connecting questions, models and experiments
text:
Designing the experiment
Specify what is independently sampled or assigned to treatment. Many cells from one culture describe that culture more precisely, but do not replace independent cultures when the question concerns variation between cultures. Split samples can provide useful paired comparisons; preserve that pairing in the analysis. State the direct contrast that answers the question. A significant response in one condition and a non-significant response in another do not establish that the responses differ [4].
Keep treatment groups comparable in handling, timing and measurement. Calibrate the assay and consider how a systematic error could survive repeated runs. A second method is useful when it challenges a different possible error; repeating the same proxy with a new label may preserve the same weakness [1, chapter 5]; [4].
Suppose all treated cultures are measured on Monday and all controls on Tuesday. A difference then combines treatment with whatever changed between days. Measuring more cells on each day can make that difference look precise without separating its causes. If both conditions can be measured on each day, the within-day comparison is more informative. Random allocation reduces systematic assignment differences; blinding addresses a different problem, such as scoring borderline cells more generously when you expect a treatment to work. Neither repairs an assay that measures the wrong quantity. [4]; [1, chapter 5].



Experimental plan for the fictional medium comparison
Question: Does N depletion account for the reporter increase, or does activity remain after N restoration?

Manipulations: Prepare the four medium conditions in the prediction table. Verify N concentration after preparation. Match pH, added volume and vehicle, exposure time and recipient starting density.
Measurement: At the specified sampling time, measure background-corrected reporter fluorescence and viable-cell count separately, then calculate fluorescence per viable cell. Track growth to identify physiological differences that complicate the ratio.
Sampling and allocation: Grow independent donor cultures and split each conditioned-medium preparation between untreated and N-restored conditions. Use independent recipient cultures and distribute all four conditions across experimental batches. Preserve donor pairing and recipient identity; extra aliquots are not extra donor cultures.
Assay checks: Include a reporter-free background control and a validated reporter-inducing positive control in each medium matrix. Verify that the recipient population remains viable. These checks address detection and recipient competence; they leave the preservation of an unknown factor unresolved.
Analysis and decision: Estimate N-lowered fresh medium versus fresh medium, N-restored conditioned medium versus untreated conditioned medium, and N-restored conditioned medium versus fresh medium. Retain the paired structure for the conditioned-medium comparison. Choose replication after assessing variation and the smallest response difference that would separate the predictions. Fix the primary comparisons, sampling time and exclusion criteria before the discriminating experiment; record additional analyses as exploratory.
Assumption that could defeat the test: N restoration may interfere with the factor. If that cannot be excluded, an A-like pattern will remain compatible with an N-dependent extracellular mechanism. A B-like pattern would motivate identifying the active component and challenging its action with a different approach; it would not establish direct promoter regulation.


When you cannot check the key assumption. Suppose the factor is still unidentified, so you cannot measure its activity independently after restoring N. You could develop that measurement before running the comparison. Alternatively, you could run the comparison now to find out whether restoring N changes the reporter response. A loss of response would then leave two explanations open: N depletion caused the increase, or restoring N interfered with a factor that caused it. Decide whether learning about the reporter response alone is worth the experiment, or whether you need a different way to distinguish the explanations. Repeating the same ambiguous comparison more precisely will not settle which explanation applies.

title: Connecting questions, models and experiments
text:
Interpreting negative and inconclusive results
A result can challenge your preferred model only if the manipulation worked and the assay could detect the predicted response. Check these points whether the result agrees or disagrees with your expectation. A failed control, a failed manipulation and an imprecise estimate each require a different next step [3].









Possible outcome
What it establishes
Next action




The manipulation and assay checks pass; the estimated response is precise enough to exclude the increase predicted by the model
Evidence against that prediction under the tested conditions
Revise the model or its stated domain; develop a new discriminating prediction


The positive control fails in the experimental matrix
The absent response cannot distinguish biological absence from detection failure
Diagnose the assay or matrix before interpreting the biological comparison


The manipulation did not achieve its intended change
The proposed intervention was not tested
Repair or replace the manipulation


The checks pass, but uncertainty allows both little response and the predicted increase
The data do not resolve the relevant difference
Improve precision or choose a contrast with better separated predictions




A non-significant test alone cannot tell these situations apart. Define the response magnitude that matters for the prediction, then assess the estimate and uncertainty against it. A sufficiently precise result may constrain an effect of that size; it does not prove an exact zero or absence in every condition. Select any equivalence or other absence-testing procedure with its assumptions and decision threshold before using it to interpret the outcome. See showing observations and uncertainty for estimates and intervals [4].

title: Connecting questions, models and experiments
text:
Revising the explanation
If the medium comparison follows B’s predictions, something other than simple N depletion is needed to explain the response. The experiment would not identify the factor or show how it affects the reporter. Those questions would still need to be investigated.
An unexpected pattern may suggest a model you had not considered. Record which explanation arose after seeing the results, then test a prediction with observations you did not use to develop it. Check whether a technical problem could explain a contradictory result. If the measurements hold up, reconsider the explanation rather than changing analyses or rejecting observations until they fit it [7, pp. 5–6]; [8, pp. 4–6].

title: Planning and reviewing a research project
text:
Scope and milestones
Plan the work in stages. Decide what you can do now and which later steps depend on the results. Estimate the time and resources each stage needs, then revise the plan as you learn.
Define what the next stage should establish. “Understand heat stress” is too broad to plan. “Check whether this imaging method can measure division timing after a heat pulse” gives the first stage a specific purpose. The method may work even if the heat pulse does not change division timing.
Work out what you can do with the time, equipment and help available. Check sample access and any commitments already made to collaborators. If a stage depends on an instrument booking, confirm the booking before scheduling work that requires it. Do the same for other resources you are counting on [1, pp. 127–130].
Agree on scope with the people who will do and support the work. Include what this stage will leave unanswered. A first experiment may establish a response without identifying its mechanism; a technical pilot may establish whether a response can be measured at all. These are different milestones. For the scientific design itself, use connecting questions, models and experiments.
crumbs: Planning and reviewing a research project

title: Planning and reviewing a research project
text:
Feasibility checks
Check early for problems that would prevent the later work. Can you obtain the essential material? Can the assay distinguish the outcomes you want to compare? If these checks take little time or expense, do them before committing to the larger experiment [2].
Define what the pilot needs to establish. For an imaging experiment, you might check whether cells remain visible long enough to measure division and whether the control cells behave as expected. Decide what would justify proceeding and which failures would require changes to the method. A small pilot may establish that the assay works while providing too few independent observations to estimate the biological effect precisely.
Not every important uncertainty has a cheap test. A larger commitment may still be worthwhile, but consider what it would teach and which other work it would displace.
An unexpected observation may suggest a better question. Yanai and Lercher distinguish this evolution of a research programme from the design of each study within it: the programme can change direction while its experiments retain clear comparisons. Before following a new direction, decide which existing work to stop or postpone and whether the change affects commitments to collaborators. Keep exploratory work distinguishable from tests of predictions specified beforehand. [6, p. 667].
crumbs: Planning and reviewing a research project

title: Planning and reviewing a research project
text:
Scheduling the work
Break the near-term work into tasks, with a responsible person and a clear endpoint for each. Tasks taking one or two weeks can be a useful starting scale; unfamiliar procedures may need smaller steps. Plan distant stages more broadly and add detail as you learn what they will require [1, pp. 129–130].
Identify which tasks must wait for others. You can sometimes check an analysis script on existing data while preparing new samples. But two experiments that could run independently may still need the same microscope or the same person’s time. Check these conflicts before scheduling them together.
Estimate elapsed time as well as hands-on work. Culture growth, deliveries, training, access queues and feedback can determine the completion date even when they require little active work. Use records of comparable tasks to improve estimates, and name uncertainty where a method is new. Include data inspection, documentation and interpretation; a schedule that ends at acquisition has left part of the research unplanned [1, pp. 131–133].
A short table or shared document may be enough. For a larger project, a timeline can help you see which tasks overlap and where a delay would hold up other work.



Example: plan a feasibility stage before expanding
In this fictional project, Mira asks whether a short heat pulse changes the time to first division in yeast after return to standard temperature, compared with mock-handled cultures. Six weeks are available for the initial project stage. The imaging method has not yet been shown to retain identifiable cells through the observation period. These are local planning constraints, not recommended durations.

First two weeks — establish feasibility. Before imaging, Mira and her supervisor will agree on the observation window, the evidence needed to trust track identity, and the amount and pattern of cell loss that would prevent a timing comparison. Mira will use two confirmed pilot sessions to check handling, retention and event detection in both heat-pulsed and mock cultures, including whether mock cells can divide. She will inspect the raw movies alongside the tracks and record cells lost from view. The milestone is a documented judgment about whether the assay can answer the timing question, including unresolved limitations.
Support and preparation. Leo has agreed to one training session before imaging and a technical review afterward. Mira can prepare the tracking workflow on existing practice movies while waiting for the first session. The practice movies can reveal software problems; they cannot establish that the new experimental setup works.
Decision at the end of week two. Mira and her supervisor will review feasibility before committing the remaining four weeks. If tracking and handling are adequate, they will settle the biological sampling and analysis plan, confirm further instrument access and begin the comparison. If a specific technical problem remains, they will assess a bounded repair. If the method cannot answer the question within the available resources, they will reconsider the approach rather than collect a larger uninterpretable dataset.
Work held back. No additional conditions or mechanistic assays will be added during the pilot. Later imaging access is provisional, so the six-week allocation is not a promise of a completed biological answer.
crumbs: Planning and reviewing a research project

title: Planning and reviewing a research project
text:
Reviewing the plan
For an extended project, start with a monthly review, as Gosling and Noordam suggest. Compare progress with the previous plan, discuss why work took a different course and agree on the next goals [3, pp. 37–41]. Use a shorter interval when a decision cannot wait until the next month.
Review sooner if an essential control fails, access is lost or new evidence changes the question. Routine troubleshooting can usually stay within the current plan.
Revise the plan with the people affected. Record what will change and what will be postponed. If the remaining work no longer fits the time available, agree on a smaller scope, a later deadline or additional help. When a deadline slips repeatedly, address the cause of the delay before setting another date [1, pp. 134–135].
crumbs: Planning and reviewing a research project

title: Planning and reviewing a research project
text:
What have you learned?
Begin with the current question and what you agreed to do at the previous review. Explain any change of direction. Show what you learned, including control results and technical problems that limit the conclusions. Mention changes in access or support that affect what you can do next.
Explain what the work establishes, with a link to the experiment or analysis record. “We completed four imaging runs” says how much was done. “We can follow cells through the required period in one condition but not the other” explains why the planned comparison is not yet possible.
Compare this account with the previous plan. Was an estimate unrealistic? Did access disappear? Did the experiment answer a different question than expected? Or did useful new evidence change the aim? A regular comparison of planned and actual work can reveal recurring obstacles that a list of achievements conceals [3, pp. 37–41].
crumbs: Planning and reviewing a research project

title: Planning and reviewing a research project
text:
Understanding setbacks
A result that disagrees with the preferred explanation is not necessarily a failed experiment. If the relevant controls, measurement and comparison are sound, that disagreement can constrain the explanation. If the control fails or the measurement cannot distinguish the possibilities, the experiment may leave the question unresolved. KamounLab makes this distinction central to judging progress [4].
Even a technically successful experiment can be inconclusive. An uncertain estimate may allow both a meaningful effect and little or no effect. A negative finding may apply only to the tested dose, time, system or detection limit. Before treating it as evidence against a model, ask what that model actually predicted under those conditions. The fuller reasoning belongs in connecting questions, models and experiments and showing observations and uncertainty.
If work has stopped because samples, equipment or help are unavailable, discuss whether and when access can be restored. The scientific question may still be worth answering, but you may need another way to study it or a different project while you wait [1, pp. 131–135].
When discussing a setback, ask what prevented progress and what help would make a difference. If a control is missing, agree on how to establish it. If equipment is unavailable, resolve access or change the plan. Assess the work without treating the setback as a judgment of the researcher [3, pp. 43–48].
crumbs: Planning and reviewing a research project

title: Planning and reviewing a research project
text:
Deciding what to do next
Decide whether the next period of work is worth its time and cost. Having already spent months on a project is not sufficient reason to continue. Raj recommends setting dates to reconsider the project and seeking outside advice when there always seems to be “one more” experiment to do [5].
Before adding an experiment, ask what it could resolve and how the answer would affect the plan. If every possible outcome leads to the same next step, the experiment may not be needed for that decision. It could still be necessary to document a method or complete an agreed obligation; be clear about that purpose.
Compare credible alternatives. Continuing may be justified when the method is sound and the remaining question is valuable. A bounded repair may be preferable when one identifiable technical problem blocks an otherwise useful comparison. Changing direction can make sense when the evidence points to a more informative question. Pausing may be appropriate when a necessary resource cannot be obtained soon enough. Closure can be reasonable when the remaining contribution no longer warrants its cost [1, pp. 128, 134–135].
If another group publishes on the same question, read what their study establishes before deciding to stop. It may answer your question, leave a limitation you could investigate or make independent replication more valuable. Assess a new project just as carefully before replacing the current one.
When seeking advice, explain the current plan and the strongest alternative. Say what each could establish and what work it would take. Choose someone who knows enough of the science to challenge your assumptions, and explain the constraints they may not know about [5].
crumbs: Planning and reviewing a research project

title: Planning and reviewing a research project
text:
A constrained choice
The next step can remain debatable even after everyone agrees on the evidence. In the example below, repairing the assay preserves the original question but consumes time that could support a different project. The decision depends on how much that question matters and whether the proposed repair is credible.



Example: repair the measurement before expanding the study
This fictional review follows a two-week microscopy pilot within a six-week project allocation. Mira asks whether a short heat pulse changes time to first division in yeast after return to standard temperature, compared with mock-handled cultures. The pilot was intended to establish feasibility. The following outcomes are introduced for this review exercise; they are not real experimental findings.

Evidence reviewed. Temperature handling met the pilot’s checks. Mock-handled cells divide while visible, but cells frequently leave the field in both conditions, preventing reliable assignment of first-division times. The raw movies show the losses. The current records do not establish whether loss is unrelated to division timing or treatment.
Scientific conclusion. The heat-pulse question remains unanswered. A cell lost from view cannot be counted as a cell that did not divide. Comparing only the cells that stayed would require assumptions the pilot has not justified.
Options. Expanding the current assay would repeat the tracking problem. A specialist has identified a possible mounting change that can be tested in one further week; its effects on growth and observation still need checking. Measuring bulk growth is another possible project, but it would answer a different question from the timing of individual first divisions.
Decision. Suspend the biological expansion and spend one week on the mounting test. Mira will run it with the imaging specialist in one confirmed core session. Before the test, they will agree on the observation window and the criteria for trustworthy tracks and acceptable cell loss. They will inspect retention and event detection in both conditions, check whether mock-handled cells can divide under the revised mounting conditions, and assess whether losses could select cells by treatment or division timing. Retaining cells is not sufficient if the mounting prevents normal division or remaining losses still make the timing comparison unjustifiable.
Next review. Mira and her supervisor will review the records at the end of that week. If the revised assay supports an interpretable comparison, they will replan the remaining three weeks and confirm access before expanding. If tracking remains inadequate, they will pause this imaging route and assess a different approach. The review does not assume the repair will work or promise a completed biological result within the original allocation.


The one-week repair is a defensible choice because it targets an identified problem with confirmed help. It is not the only defensible choice. Mira could instead decide that learning about bulk growth is worth more than preserving the single-cell question within this short allocation. That would be a change of question, not an alternative measurement of the same outcome. If the specialist or core session becomes unavailable, the case for the repair weakens. A failed repair would not by itself show that choosing it was unreasonable with the information available.
For a pause or closure, record what the work established, where the data and materials can be found, and what would make reopening worthwhile. Agree on who will complete outstanding commitments. If the project continues, update its plan to reflect the decision. When the same obstacles affect several projects, consider reviewing how the group works.

title: Keeping up with the literature
text:
Choosing what to follow
Choose a few ways to find papers on your current questions and wider interests. If screening new papers takes all your reading time, reduce the number of alerts or narrow their searches.
Write down the question, method or research area you currently need to follow. “Single-cell biology” is a broad interest. A more focused question is how to distinguish a change in the abundance of a cell type from a change in gene expression within that type. You can search for methods that make this distinction while still reading more widely about single-cell biology.
How closely you read depends on what you need from the paper. In a new field, an article may help you learn the vocabulary and find earlier work. If you plan to adopt its method, examine the procedure, the assumptions it relies on and the evidence that it works under conditions like yours [1, Rule 1 and Table 1].
Alerts help you notice new work. Before designing an experiment or making a claim in a manuscript, also search for earlier studies that address the question. Reviews can help you find them; read the original studies when you need to assess their methods or rely on their findings [2, pp. 93–95].

title: Keeping up with the literature
text:
Finding relevant papers
A topic search can find papers across journals, but it depends on the terms you know to search for. Following a few journals or research groups may reveal work you would otherwise miss. Suggestions from colleagues and seminars can also take you beyond your usual searches [3].
Start with a query that describes the biological question or method, then inspect what it returns. Try alternative terms used by authors, including names for the system, intervention or measurement. Check whether it finds a few papers you already know are relevant. If an important paper is absent, ask why: missing terminology, a narrow condition in the query or a database that does not cover the material. An experienced colleague or research librarian can help with terminology and search strategy [2, pp. 94–95].
Use alerts or feeds for searches and publications you want to follow, or revisit their pages regularly. Check what each subscription adds: perhaps one finds new applications of your assay while another follows a neighboring field. When several alerts return the same paper, keep one record.
When you find an important paper elsewhere, check why your searches missed it. A different term or an additional source may help. Even several well-chosen searches can miss relevant work; adding subscriptions is useful only if they help fill a gap you have identified.

title: Keeping up with the literature
text:
Choosing what to read
Use a paper’s title and abstract to decide whether it addresses a question that interests you. Look at a relevant figure or method passage if the connection is unclear. Assessing its conclusions will take closer reading.
Decide what to do with the paper:

Read for a current question. Name what you need to learn. A result that could change your experimental plan, a method you may use or a paper you must explain to others warrants a focused reading slot.
Keep for a named later use. Save the reason to return: background for an introduction, a method for a possible extension or a study to revisit when a particular result appears. Keep these records separate from the active reading queue.
Leave it. If you cannot name a reason to return to it, you need not save it. This is a decision about your reading priorities, not a judgment of the paper’s quality.

Reading a selected paper may reveal a method or concept you need to learn first. Allow time for that background reading, and keep your note labeled as a screening note until you have examined the evidence [1, Rule 1 and Table 1]. Understanding a research paper explains how to follow the connection between a paper’s experiments and its conclusions.

title: Keeping up with the literature
text:
Saving papers and notes
Keep papers and their notes together in a searchable reference manager or document collection. Include the authors, title, year and a stable link or identifier so you can reopen the source [2, pp. 95–97].
For a screened paper, note why you saved it and what you have read. After closer reading, add the finding you expect to use and where its supporting evidence appears. Keep your interpretation and unanswered questions distinct from what the authors report. If you highlight a passage, add a note when you might otherwise forget why it mattered.
Use labels you are likely to remember when the paper becomes relevant again: a project question, assay, organism or unresolved problem. Before relying on the record in a new plan or manuscript, reopen the source and check the relevant passage. Check which version you retained and whether a later version or correction changes the point. When several records bear on the same question, move from individual notes to comparing and synthesizing papers.

title: Keeping up with the literature
text:
Making time to read
Reserve recurring time for discovery and selected reading. Weekly screening is a useful starting point, with frequency adjusted to the pace of the field and the decision ahead. Ulitsky emphasizes regular screening and warns that too many subscriptions can make researchers abandon the routine altogether [3].
If your reading queue keeps growing, check what is filling it. Revise searches that mostly return irrelevant papers and remove overlapping subscriptions. If the papers are relevant but you cannot read them all, choose which questions need attention now or set aside more reading time. During a busy experimental period, you may need to pause broad alerts while following work needed for an imminent decision. Return to wider interests when time allows.



Example: a routine for a method decision

In this fictional example, a researcher is deciding whether to pilot a new cell-segmentation method on crowded fluorescence images. During assay setup, they can give literature work 90 minutes each week. They initially reserve 20 minutes for screening and 70 for selected reading and notes; these times describe their available week, not a recommended reading rate.
Discovery: a focused method-topic search and a broader imaging-journal stream, with occasional suggestions from colleagues.
Current reading: paper A describes a method intended for crowded fluorescence images. Its abstract suggests a possible fit. The researcher assigns it the reading question “Does the evaluation include image conditions similar to ours, and how were errors assessed?”
Orientation: review B explains segmentation-evaluation metrics. The researcher keeps it for the pilot plan, beginning with the section needed to understand paper A rather than treating the whole review as an immediate assignment.
Later interest: paper C concerns a different tissue. It goes into a background collection to revisit if the project expands to that tissue, outside the active method-reading queue.
No further reading: paper D addresses microscope calibration. It is related to imaging, but the researcher has no current calibration question and the paper does not address segmentation. They leave it outside the reading collection.
The initial note attached to A reads:
Purpose: decide whether this method merits a pilot on our images.
Reading status: abstract and one figure inspected; methods and evaluation not yet assessed.
Next check: read the evaluation Methods and the crowded-image example in Figure 3. Identify the reference annotation, image conditions and types of error counted. The abstract’s claimed relevance is still unverified.
The incoming alerts double during a busy assay week. The researcher removes duplicate notices and pauses the broad journal stream. They keep the method-topic search and use the reading slot to continue A, postponing optional background reading. Before committing to the pilot, they also search for earlier evaluations of the method. If understanding A requires more background reading than fits this week, they postpone the decision.


Review the routine after using it for a few weeks. Can you find a saved paper when you need it? Which alerts led to useful reading, and which mostly added notices? Adjust the searches and reading time accordingly.

title: Keeping up with the literature
text:
References

Gosling, P., & Noordam, B. (2022). Mastering Your PhD: Survival and Success in the Doctoral Years and Beyond (3rd ed.), Chapter 13: Searching the Scientific Literature, pp. 93–98.

title: Understanding a research paper
text:
What do you need from the paper?
You may understand every word in a paper yet be unsure why an experiment supports its conclusion. Work through that connection using the figures, captions and relevant methods. Aim to explain what the study found and which questions remain open.
Decide what you need from this paper: orientation in an unfamiliar field, evidence for a particular claim, a method you might adopt or preparation for a discussion. That purpose changes where to spend time. For orientation, the Introduction can identify the question and useful earlier work. To adopt a method, concentrate on the procedure, its validation and conditions of use. To rely on a biological conclusion, follow the experiments supporting it, including controls and supplementary material [1, Rules 1–3].
Identify the article type as well. A review can orient you and lead to original studies; its account of an experiment is not a substitute for reading that experiment when your conclusion depends on it. A methods paper needs evidence about performance and limits. An original research article presents observations and an argument about what they mean. The workflow below concentrates on that argument.
Begin with enough of the abstract and Introduction to state the question and proposed answer. Then move between Results, figures and methods. Reading the figures first can work when you know the system; reading each Results passage alongside its figure can work when you need more context. Neither order is compulsory. Look up an unfamiliar term or follow a cited method when it blocks your understanding of a consequential step, rather than allowing every unfamiliar word to start a separate literature search [1, Rules 4 and 8].
For an overview, it may be enough to understand the question, approach and main finding. Before adopting a method, check how its performance was assessed and whether that assessment covers the samples you plan to use. Before citing a proposed mechanism as established, read the experiments that distinguish it from other explanations. Note anything you still need to check.

title: Understanding a research paper
text:
Following the argument
State the research question in your own words, then identify the comparison intended to answer it. What changed between the groups or conditions? What was measured? Why would that measurement help answer the question?
Follow the main claim through its supporting experiments. One may establish that the measurement works, another show a response and another test an alternative explanation. The order of Results usually expresses this logic rather than the order in which the work happened. Ask what each experiment adds and which later conclusion depends on it [3, Rule 7].
Write an observation before accepting the interpretation: reporter fluorescence was lower describes a measurement; the treatment suppresses a specific pathway proposes why it changed. Results headings and figure titles can contain interpretations too. Check whether the panels support them [1, Rules 3–6].



Example: what a reporter measurement establishes
In this fictional paper, cultured cells receive inhibitor Q or vehicle. At six hours, Figure 1A shows lower background-corrected whole-well reporter fluorescence with Q. The authors propose that Q suppresses the reporter through a specific molecular target. The material considered so far does not identify viable-cell number or fluorescence per cell.








Part of the argument
What the reader can establish




Question
Does Q suppress reporter activity through the proposed target?


Observation
Whole-well fluorescence is lower with Q than with vehicle at six hours.


Unresolved inference
Total signal depends on contributing cells and their signal. This measurement alone does not distinguish fewer cells from lower signal per cell, or establish target specificity.



To assess the proposed mechanism, look for measurements of cell number and signal per cell, then for experiments testing whether Q acts through the proposed target. The whole-well measurement alone cannot answer those questions.

title: Understanding a research paper
text:
Figures and methods
For each panel supporting the conclusion, establish what its points or other marks represent. A point may be a cell, a culture, an animal or an average across several measurements. Read the axes, units, group labels and legend. Check whether values are totals, proportions or normalized measurements. For a fold change, identify the baseline used to calculate it [1, Rule 4].
Use the caption to find the relevant method. Follow how samples were selected and measured, then how those measurements became the plotted values. For a normalized result, find the denominator; for an analysis that excludes observations, find the exclusion criteria. These details may be in supplementary methods.
In the reporter example, background correction does not account for how many viable cells contribute to the signal. The measurement also tells you only what happened at six hours, not when the response began or how long it lasts.
Ask whether the display supplies the evidence claimed. A representative image can show a phenotype, but to assess how common it is, you need to know how samples were selected and how the phenotype was counted. A smooth curve may be a fitted model rather than additional observations. For an unfamiliar figure type, consult specialized displays and explanatory diagrams, then return to the paper’s caption and methods to check how it was constructed.
If a necessary detail remains missing, name it specifically. “The caption does not identify whether points are cultures or repeated measurements from one culture” is a question you can resolve. “The experiment is unreliable” goes beyond what that absence establishes.

title: Understanding a research paper
text:
Assessing the evidence
Examine controls by the alternative explanation they address. In a before-and-after experiment, a change may reflect elapsed time or repeated measurement as well as the intervention. A suitable concurrent control helps separate these effects. In the reporter example, vehicle supplies a treatment comparison, but it does not by itself settle cell number, assay interference or target specificity. Read what the controls test and what they leave open [2].
Also identify the independent units behind the comparison. Repeated images from one culture can describe that culture more thoroughly; they do not create additional independently treated cultures. Check how the analysis handles this dependence and whether the replication supports the scope of the claim. If the paper says the treatment works differently in two conditions, look for a direct comparison of those effects. A significant result in one condition and a non-significant result in the other does not establish that they differ [2].
Read the estimated effect together with its uncertainty. Identify what error bars represent: standard deviation describes spread among observations; standard error or a confidence interval concerns precision of an estimate. To compare groups, look for an analysis of their difference rather than judging whether their separate error bars overlap [4, pp. 186–191]. See showing observations and uncertainty for an explanation of these intervals.
A non-significant result alone does not establish that an effect is absent. Check the range of effects compatible with the estimate and its uncertainty interval. If that range includes both no change and the change predicted by a proposed mechanism, the measurement does not resolve the prediction. A narrower interval may rule out an effect as large as predicted without establishing an exact zero. Base that judgment on the analysis the paper reports [2].
Distinguish an association, the effect of an intervention and evidence for its mechanism. Observational covariation can have several explanations. Manipulating a treatment strengthens some inferences, but the treatment may act through routes other than the proposed one. Ask which experiment distinguishes those routes before describing the mechanism as established [2].
Judge a descriptive study by the description it supports. An atlas need not identify a mechanism to be useful, but its coverage depends on which specimens, conditions and measurements it includes. Ask whether the sampling supports the claimed population and whether the method could miss the feature being described. A missing mechanism and an inadequate measurement are different limitations. [1, Rules 3–6].
Apply the same scrutiny to findings you agree with and those you doubt. Would you ask for the same control if the result supported your expectations? Distinguish a missing explanation of a method from evidence that the method was used incorrectly. Likewise, a study confined to one cell model may answer its stated question while leaving open whether the finding applies elsewhere [1, Rules 6–7].

title: Understanding a research paper
text:
Taking useful notes
Close the paper and explain the question, main evidence and conclusion in a few sentences, including any important limits. Then reopen it to check your account and add the relevant figure, table or method locations. If you cannot explain a step, reread it or discuss it with someone who understands the method [1, Rules 3, 8–9].
Keep the paper’s citation or stable link with the note. Include the experimental system, treatment and measurement time when these define the finding you plan to use. In the reporter example, the note needs to say that the measurement is whole-well fluorescence in cultured cells at six hours. Separate what the authors conclude from what you have checked yourself.



Example: a short reading note

The paper asks whether inhibitor Q suppresses reporter activity through its proposed target. In cultured cells, Q produces lower background-corrected whole-well fluorescence than vehicle at six hours (Fig. 1A). The authors interpret it as target-specific suppression, but I have not yet found viable-cell counts or per-cell signal measurements. Replication and estimate precision also need checking in the caption and Methods. Before using the paper as evidence for the mechanism, I need to look for cell-normalized measurements and experiments testing target specificity.


Suppose you then find an additional panel reporting fewer viable cells with Q. Update the note:

The additional viable-cell-count panel shows fewer viable cells with Q. Cell number may therefore contribute to the lower whole-well fluorescence. The findings still do not establish whether signal per viable cell changes or whether the proposed target mediates the response. I will look for a per-cell measurement, check how it was obtained and examine whether specificity experiments distinguish the proposed mechanism from other effects of Q.

Fewer viable cells alone do not establish how much of the fluorescence difference is explained by cell number.


If you are preparing a journal review, see writing the report for organizing your comments.

text:
References

title: Comparing and synthesizing papers
text:
Defining the review question
Before deciding whether papers agree, check what each study measured and under which conditions. An increase in RNA and no detectable increase in protein may both be accurate observations. To explain what the studies show together, you need to keep that difference in view.
State the question you want the papers to answer. “Does this pathway matter?” could mean a role in development, a molecular response or survival after treatment. “Does inhibiting the pathway reduce cell survival in this model?” is specific enough to guide paper selection. A developmental study may suggest a mechanism to investigate, but it does not directly answer the survival question.
Decide which systems, interventions and outcomes belong in the comparison before selecting papers by their conclusions. Record how you searched, when you searched and why you excluded papers; note papers you could not obtain. A reader should be able to tell whether your account covers a few selected studies or a search intended to find all the evidence on the question [3, Rules 1–2 and 9].
A review can orient you to the concepts and point toward original work. For a conclusion that depends on a particular experiment, inspect that experiment’s paper and relevant supplementary material. Keep a review’s account separate from your assessment of the primary evidence. Before describing an unresolved question, check both recent work and older studies that the current discussion may have overlooked [3, Rule 10].

title: Comparing and synthesizing papers
text:
Comparing methods and evidence
Compare the studies side by side, using the same fields for each. Record where you found each detail so you can return to the figure, table or Methods passage when a difference needs checking.








Record
What to establish




Question and system
Which biological question, organism, cell type, population or state does the study address?


Intervention and comparator
What changes, at what dose or intensity, and relative to what control? Is the study observational or experimental?


Timing
When does the intervention occur, and when is the outcome measured?


Measurement
What quantity is measured, with what assay, normalization and units?


Replication
What are the independent biological units? Which measurements repeat within them?


Finding and uncertainty
What is the effect estimate or observed pattern? How precise is it, and what analysis supports it?


Inference and limits
What conclusion follows, and what alternative explanation or missing control remains?




Do not fill an absent detail with an assumption. Mark it as unreported or not yet checked and return to the source if it affects comparability. These fields extend the distinction between question, approach, observation and interpretation used by Carey and colleagues [1, Rules 3–6 and 8].
Check what each study means by “pathway inhibition.” A drug may only partly inhibit its target and may affect other targets too. Deleting a gene produces a different perturbation. Check how long each treatment acts before treating the experiments as equivalent.
Also check how the measurements were normalized. Total fluorescence per well depends on how many cells are present as well as their fluorescence. A measurement divided by the number of viable cells accounts for cell number differently; the two values cannot be compared directly. For fold changes, identify the baseline in each study before comparing the reported effects.
Evaluate the evidence for the particular claim you need. A strong observational association may establish a relationship while leaving its cause unresolved. An intervention can narrow causal explanations, but its controls and possible additional effects still matter. Likewise, many measurements from a few cultures do not provide the same biological replication as independently initiated cultures [2].
Check whether papers reuse a cohort, dataset or experimental series. Analyses of the same observations may answer different questions, but they do not show that a finding recurs in a new sample. Record which papers share data. When studies address different questions or measurements, compare them in separate groups and explain how the groups relate.
Repeating an experiment in independent samples tests whether the finding recurs. Using a different method may help determine whether it depends on a weakness of the first assay. Check what changed in each additional study: repeating the same assay can repeat its bias, and a second method needs its own validation.

title: Comparing and synthesizing papers
text:
Explaining differences between studies
First ask whether the studies disagree about the same quantity under comparable conditions. An increase in mRNA and an unchanged protein estimate are distinct observations. They can both be accurate; neither alone establishes how RNA changes lead to protein changes. Similarly, a short perturbation and a long depletion can reveal different parts of a response.
Compare the estimated effects and their uncertainty, not just their significance labels. A statistically significant result in one study and a non-significant result in another do not establish that their effects differ. The second estimate may be too imprecise to distinguish no effect from an effect as large as the first study reports. To claim that the effects differ, you need an analysis of that difference; judging overlap or nonoverlap of their separate confidence intervals is not a general substitute [2]. See showing observations and uncertainty for the distinction between separate estimates and an estimate of their difference.
When studies of the same outcome still give different findings, examine how their methods differ. Start with differences that could affect the measurement or the biological response. For example, a longer exposure might allow a response to develop. That explanation predicts a change over time that could be tested. Finding a difference in exposure time does not by itself establish why the results differ.
If several explanations remain possible, say which ones and what evidence would distinguish them. Apply the same scrutiny to findings you favor and those you doubt. An unexplained disagreement belongs in the synthesis even when you cannot yet resolve it [4, pp. 4–6].



Example: compare the evidence behind different conclusions
The following three study summaries are fictional. They ask whether ligand L changes marker M in cultured epithelial cells. All use the same stated cell model, ligand dose, exposure conditions, vehicle comparator and two-hour endpoint. Independently initiated cultures are the biological replication units. The values are authored study reports, not results calculated from a dataset. Fold changes compare L with vehicle; CI denotes the reported confidence interval.





Study
Outcome
Fold change
95% CI




A
M mRNA
1.4
1.2–1.6


B
M protein abundance
1.0
0.9–1.1


C
M mRNA
1.3
0.9–1.7




A fold change of 1 means equal abundance. Study A supports increased mRNA. Study C’s estimate is in the same direction but is less precise, allowing no change as well as an increase. Its interval crossing 1 does not show that it contradicts A. No direct comparison of the study effects is supplied.
B measures a different outcome. Its protein estimate is near 1 with the stated interval; this does not refute A’s mRNA finding or prove that protein abundance cannot respond. A delay between the RNA and protein responses is one possible explanation, but these reports contain no later measurement that tests it.
Suppose you need to choose a follow-up now. If you need to know whether the RNA increase recurs, repeat the two-hour RNA measurement. If you need to know whether protein abundance rises later, measure it at later times. The reports alone do not tell you which question to prioritize, and they leave the delay explanation untested.

title: Comparing and synthesizing papers
text:
Writing the synthesis
Organize each paragraph around a question that the studies help answer. You might first explain whether the outcome changes, then discuss the evidence for a mechanism or for a response in other systems. Within each paragraph, show how the findings relate: one study may establish an observation while another tests whether it occurs under different conditions [3, Rules 4 and 6–7].
State what the studies establish together and explain which findings support that answer. Keep the relevant conditions and uncertainty beside the conclusion. “These results are consistent with a delayed protein response” allows other explanations; “the protein response is delayed” asserts that this explanation has been established. If the studies still conflict, identify what remains unresolved.
For the fictional studies, the completed synthesis could read:


Synthesis of studies A–C
Ligand L increased marker M mRNA after two hours in the epithelial-cell model examined by study A. Study C estimated an increase of similar magnitude, although its uncertainty interval also allowed no change. The mRNA findings therefore do not establish a disagreement between these studies. Study B measured protein abundance and reported an estimate near no change at the same endpoint. Together, the studies support an mRNA response at two hours more clearly than a protein response at that endpoint. Whether the mRNA change produces a later protein increase remains unresolved; measurements of both outcomes over time would help distinguish that possibility from a response confined to mRNA abundance.


Check each conclusion against the original studies. In the example, the measurements concern a particular marker in one cell model at two hours; they do not establish a general effect on gene expression or a response at later times. Ask a colleague to check your interpretation and identify missing details that could change it [3, Rule 8].
A synthesis for a whole field needs a search and appraisal design suited to that purpose. Quantitative pooling also requires comparable quantities and an analysis that accounts for their uncertainty and dependence.

Choose a display for the comparison you want to make. Try alternatives while exploring the data: a pattern hidden by a group average may become visible when you plot the individual observations. [4].
