title: Planning the paper
text:
Define the contribution
Which finding should the paper lead with, and which experiments support it? A working title and a short statement of the contribution can help you decide. Check them against the results before developing the figure plan and manuscript outline.

title: Planning the paper
text:
Identify the reader and question
The paper needs a question to answer or a problem for the new method to solve. Write that question with the intended readers in mind: what do they already know, and what background will they need to understand it? [1]; [3]; [2]. The relevant literature should establish what is known, what remains unresolved and why resolving it matters. [12]; [5]; [6].


State what the study establishes
Write a working title and a one- or two-sentence contribution statement that names the main finding and what it adds to existing knowledge. Specify the system or conditions when they limit the conclusion. [1]; [4]. Distinguish the observation from its interpretation: a measured response may support a functional role without identifying the mechanism. Choose the wording accordingly. [11].
A computational method and the biological insight it enables may belong in one paper. If two groups of results answer independent questions, consider separate papers. [1]; [2].

title: Planning the paper
section: Build the argument from the evidence
text:
Build the argument from the evidence

Connect claims to results
List the proposed claims in a table, with the supporting result and planned figure or panel beside each one. Add the assumptions on which the claim depends and any limits to its interpretation. Include results that challenge it and questions that remain unresolved. [3]; [7]; [8]. For a quantitative claim, include the effect estimate and its uncertainty. Note whether the analysis tested a planned prediction or suggested an explanation during exploration. [11].



Example: defining the contribution
Brake is a fictional bacterial defence system inspired by the antiviral gene-synthesis discovery of [15]. Genome annotation reveals a reverse transcriptase and an RNA template, but no conventional defence-effector gene. The researchers ask what this system produces and how it restricts phage infection.

Working title: An RNA-templated gene arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation
Working contribution: Brake assembles a protein-coding gene from an RNA template. Its protein product arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation, revealing a route to defence in which the functional gene must first be assembled.

Claim inventory












Proposed claim
Supporting analysis/result
Planned figure/panel
Assumptions
Interpretation limits




Brake restricts phage propagation.
Lower infectious phage yield with intact Brake than with empty vector or inactive reverse transcriptase.
Figure 1B–C
Matched infections and comparable titre measurements.
Establishes restriction in the tested host.


The RNA template supplies a protein-coding DNA product.
Repeat-junction sequences, DNA measurements and protein detection; template-deletion control.
Figure 2A–D
Product identification distinguishes newly assembled DNA from the construct.
The infection signal that activates the pathway is unknown.


The protein mediates growth arrest and defence.
Blocking translation preserves DNA production but removes growth arrest and phage restriction; separate protein expression restores both.
Figure 3A–C
The translation change leaves upstream RNA and DNA production intact.
The protein’s molecular target is unknown.


Activity differs among tested phages.
Restricted output of phages A and B; phage C remains productive.
Figure 4A
Infection conditions permit each phage to replicate in the control.
Three phages do not establish the full host–phage range.


Recovery after infection remains unresolved.
Infected cells stop growing during observation; subsequent recovery was not measured.
Figure 4B
Tracking captures the infected cells of interest.
Growth arrest does not establish survival or irreversible death.




The third row identifies the decisive control. If blocking translation also stopped DNA production, loss of defence would not distinguish a protein effect from a DNA effect.




Resolve gaps and conflicting findings
An incomplete argument may need a clearer explanation, a different analysis or additional evidence. Use the claim inventory to locate the missing step before planning more experiments. In Brake, checking that DNA production survives the translation-disrupting change is necessary to attribute defence to the protein. Identifying the protein’s molecular target would address a further question. [1]; [4].
When findings disagree, examine the conditions, measurements and analytical choices. If the disagreement persists, revise the interpretation and discuss it in the main text, even when the detailed displays are in supporting material. [2]; [3].

How to resolve incomplete arguments
[1]; [4]; [2]; [11].



Problem
How to recognize it
Next action




Missing explanation
The evidence is present, but a link in the reasoning is unstated.
Explain why the comparison answers the question. Note the missing explanation beside the relevant claim, then include it in the manuscript’s paragraph outline.


Missing essential evidence
The claim depends on an untested assumption or missing control.
Obtain the necessary evidence or narrow the claim.


Contradictory findings
Results support different answers to the same question.
Check conditions, measurements and analyses. If disagreement remains, include it and revise the interpretation.


Inconclusive findings
The estimate or assay is too uncertain to answer the question.
State what remains unresolved. If the central claim needs that answer, improve the evidence or narrow the claim.

title: Planning the paper
text:
Arrange the figures

Give each figure a purpose
Group results from the claim inventory around the question each figure will answer. Write its title early: a finding-based title helps you judge whether the panels support one conclusion, while a descriptive title suits a design or unresolved comparison. [7]; [8]; [3].
For an unfamiliar procedure or a comparison across several stages, include a schematic showing the starting material, important steps and measurement. Align corresponding stages when comparing conditions. Use recognizable schematic symbols and keep them distinct from the images or plots reporting observations. [13].
Plan the comparisons within each figure. Put the treatment and reference condition together; use a separate control panel when you need to establish that the intervention worked. Pair an illustrative observation with a population summary when readers need to judge how typical it is. Keep group names consistent across figures. Rough plots and panel notes are sufficient for this stage; refine the layout once the scientific content is settled. [5]; [7].


Choose the figure sequence
Order figures by the questions they answer. First establish the problem or observation; then present the tests needed to explain or resolve it. Arrange panels within each figure so the relevant comparisons can be read together. [1]; [6].



Example: planning the figures
The experiment log starts with a growth defect during protein expression, followed by phage-yield assays, sequence analysis, DNA measurements and tests of the translation-disrupted construct. The figure plan changes that order: first establish defence, then explain how it works.


Figure 1 — Brake restricts phage propagation

Does Brake reduce phage output?

A: Introduce the defence region and the control constructs.
B: Compare infectious phage A yield with empty vector, intact Brake and inactive reverse transcriptase.
C: Show host growth during infection alongside uninfected controls.


Figure 2 — Brake produces a protein-coding DNA intermediate

What does the reverse transcriptase make?

A: Map the RNA template and the coding sequence created across DNA repeat junctions.
B: Compare DNA products before and during infection.
C: Show expression of the encoded protein during infection.
D: Test the RNA-template deletion.


Figure 3 — The Brake protein mediates growth arrest and defence

Which product carries out the defence?

A: Introduce the translation-disrupting change and verify that DNA production remains intact.
B: Show loss of growth arrest and phage restriction.
C: Test restoration by expressing the protein separately.


Figure 4 — Brake responses across phage challenges

How do the tested phages differ in restriction and infected-cell growth?

A: Compare phage output for A, B and C.
B: Track growth of infected cells, retaining the observation window in the display.

Starting with protein expression would leave readers wondering why that protein was tested. Placing it after product identification makes it a test of the proposed effector.




Decide what belongs in supporting material
Keep the evidence essential to the main contribution in the paper, including controls on which its interpretation depends. Supporting material can hold extended analyses and additional checks. A result from another system belongs in the main paper when the claim depends on its generality. [4]; [7].
Read the figure titles in sequence and ask a colleague to explain the argument from the figures and provisional legends. If a figure needs several unrelated explanations, split it; if two displays establish the same point, consider combining them. [7]; [5].

title: Planning the paper
text:
Develop the outline

Section purposes
Build the manuscript outline around the figure plan, using the section purposes below. [6]; [1].

Section overview








Component
Purpose




Title and abstract
Identify the contribution and summarize the question, approach, main findings and meaning.


Introduction
Establish the relevant knowledge, explain the unresolved question and introduce the study.


Methods
Describe the design, materials, procedures and analyses needed to assess and reproduce the work.


Results
Present a logical sequence of findings, supported by figures, tables and the controls needed to interpret them.


Discussion
Answer the research question, relate the findings to prior work, assess alternatives and limitations, and explain the contribution.


Supporting material
Supply additional methods, data and analyses that support the paper while keeping its main argument easy to follow.





Adjust the outline to the journal’s format: Methods may appear later, Results and Discussion may be combined, or a separate conclusion may be required. [6]; [9].
Start the outline with the working title and contribution statement, then place the figure findings under Results. Work outward from those findings: list the background needed to understand them, the procedures to describe in Methods and the interpretations to examine in Discussion. [1]; [7].
Check the journal’s length and display limits before developing the manuscript outline. Use a rough word and figure budget to allocate space. [14].


Plan paragraph purposes
Outline what each paragraph will establish and which results or sources it will draw on. A figure may require several paragraphs if readers need to follow distinct steps in the reasoning. [1]; [8]. For Results, specify the finding and the comparison that supports it; leave sentence-level development to drafting. See building a Results paragraph. [5]; [6]; [12].
Read the paragraph statements in order. Does the reader have enough information to understand each new comparison? Combine repeated points and divide paragraphs that try to explain several things at once. Introduce each experiment through the question it addresses; you need not repeat the motivation for the whole study. [12].



Example: developing the outline
Manuscript outline for the Brake study

Introduction


Explain why understanding bacterial defence requires identifying the product that inhibits infection.
Introduce the puzzle: Brake contains a reverse transcriptase and an RNA template but no recognizable effector gene. Explain why identifying its products could resolve this gap.
State the question: what does Brake produce, and how does that product restrict phage infection?



Results


Intact Brake reduces infectious phage A output relative to the controls; host growth measurements distinguish infection-associated effects from growth without infection (Figure 1).
RNA-derived DNA repeat junctions create a coding sequence. Use the sequence analysis and RNA-template deletion control to explain the product’s origin (Figure 2A, D).
The DNA product is present before infection; double-stranded DNA and the encoded protein are detected during infection (Figure 2B–C).
Preventing translation removes defence despite continued DNA production; separate protein expression restores growth arrest and restriction (Figure 3).
Activity varies among the three tested phages, and infected-cell tracking shows growth arrest without establishing recovery (Figure 4).


Methods


Identify the host, defence constructs, phages and infection conditions.
Describe DNA-product identification, sequence analysis and protein measurements.
Explain growth measurements and infectious-titre assays, including independent cultures, technical measurements and matching by experimental day.
Describe cell tracking and the analyses behind each comparison.


Discussion


Explain how RNA-templated gene assembly supplies a defence protein, connecting product identification with the genetic tests.
Contrast this organization with a defence protein encoded by a conventional genomic gene. Identify the literature needed to support that comparison in an actual manuscript.
Explain why growth arrest leaves cell recovery unresolved and why the protein’s molecular target requires further work.
Close with the contribution: a functional defence gene can emerge from RNA-templated DNA assembly rather than exist as a conventional coding sequence in the genome.

Figure 2 supports two paragraphs: one identifies the DNA product; the next connects protein production to infection. The following paragraph tests the protein’s function. Product detection alone would not establish that role.


You can plan Methods alongside Results, noting software versions, analysis choices and experimental details while they are available. Check that every reported analysis has a corresponding method. [7]; [2].


Choose where to start drafting
If the comparisons are settled, starting with Results and Methods lets you describe work you already know well. If you are unsure what the paper contributes, try writing the title and Introduction first. If you have many results but no clear order, return to the figure plan. These are different ways into the draft; the finished paper’s reading order need not determine where you start. See Drafting and revising for starting a passage and organizing writing sessions. [9]; [5]; [3].

title: Planning the paper
text:
Plan the writing with coauthors

Agree the plan and responsibilities
Share the contribution statement, rough figures and manuscript outline before dividing the writing. Ask coauthors to challenge the claims and identify missing evidence or alternative interpretations. Agree on the main argument before authors develop separate sections. [4]; [3].
Assign a writer and a scientific checker for each part, set dates and choose who will integrate the manuscript. That person should reconcile terminology, transitions and repetition across contributions. Keep one current version with recoverable history, and record decisions that affect other sections. [10]; [3].
Assign data and metadata preparation early, allowing time for repository queries and corrections alongside the writing. [12].


Agree authorship and credit
Discuss who should be an author and the proposed order before drafting, then revisit the agreement when contributions change. Use the target journal’s criteria and relevant disciplinary or institutional guidance. Record the reasons for the order, including any shared-author designation, so that later discussion can refer to the work each person actually did. [10]; [16, section 2].
For a journal following ICMJE, a substantial contribution to the research alone does not complete the authorship requirements. Contributors must also help draft or critically review the paper, approve the version for publication and accept responsibility for addressing concerns about the work. Give eligible contributors the manuscript and enough time to participate; do not exclude them by withholding that opportunity. [16, section 2].
Prepare the contribution statement with the authors. If the journal uses CRediT, its roles describe the work performed; they do not decide who qualifies as an author or the order of names. Check the statement with each contributor, agree who will handle correspondence with the journal, and identify other contributions to acknowledge. [17]; [16, sections 2–3]. For a worked credit decision and guidance when contributions are disputed, see Contributions, authorship and order.


Organize feedback
Plan an early review of the contribution and figures, then a later review of the written explanation. Ask a domain expert to challenge the inference and a colleague less familiar with the project to identify missing context. Agree these roles and review dates with the coauthors. The chapter Drafting and revising explains how to request and resolve their feedback. [1]; [2]; [8].

Before drafting

Can a reader state the question, contribution and conditions without an oral explanation?
Can each retained claim be traced to supporting evidence, with important assumptions and limits identified?
Can readers find the controls needed to interpret each finding, including comparisons that remain inconclusive?
Do paragraph purposes connect the figures to the section plan, with each reported analysis assigned a method?
Have coauthors agreed who will write and check each section and how contributions will be credited?

title: Titles, abstracts and introductions
text:
Choose an informative title
A reader scanning search results needs to recognize what the paper is about and what it adds. The title, abstract and Introduction explain this at increasing depth. Draft the title and abstract from the main contribution identified in Planning the paper, then revise them as the manuscript develops. [5]; [6].
Three different jobs
The examples continue the fictional Brake study, inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [15]. Brake assembles an RNA-derived gene whose protein product arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation.

title: Titles, abstracts and introductions
text:
Identify the subject and contribution
Build the title around the biological subject and the main finding. For a methods paper, name the capability the method provides. Include the study system or condition when leaving it out would make the finding appear more general than it is. [1]; [2].
Use recognizable search terms and spell out unfamiliar abbreviations; secondary technical details can wait for the abstract. Replace phrases such as “new insights” with the finding itself. Choose a verb that matches the evidence. “Is associated with” reports a relationship; “activates” claims an effect, and “directly activates” makes a further claim about how it occurs. [3]; [4]; [2].


Choose a descriptive or finding-based title
A finding-based title works when one conclusion captures the paper’s main contribution; a descriptive title may better suit a paper that characterizes several related aspects of a system or resource. Draft both, then ask whether the promised finding or scope is what the paper actually delivers. [3]; [1].



Example: choosing a title
Brake produces an RNA-derived DNA intermediate whose protein product arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage output. The experiments identify the protein’s role but leave its molecular target and the recovery of infected cells unresolved.

Too vague: Characterization of the Brake defence system
The system’s name tells an unfamiliar reader little about the biological finding.
Overclaiming: An RNA-templated gene saves bacteria from viral infection
The study measures phage restriction and growth arrest, not recovery of individual infected cells.
Finding-based: An RNA-templated gene arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation
Use this title when the protein’s origin and function are the paper’s central findings.
Descriptive: RNA-templated gene assembly in the Brake antiviral defence system
This suits a paper organized around several properties of the system. It conveys less of the functional result, so the abstract needs to supply it promptly.


Draft several titles and ask a colleague what each leads them to expect. Revise any wording that suggests a different contribution from the paper’s. [1]; [2].

title: Titles, abstracts and introductions
section: Write an abstract that stands alone
text:
Write an abstract that stands alone

Connect the question, findings and implication
An abstract should explain the question, what the study found and why that finding matters. Include enough background to understand the question and enough of the approach to understand the evidence. The Nature summary-paragraph guide illustrates one way to arrange these elements. [1].

The Nature summary-paragraph structure









Stage
Purpose
Sentences in Nature’s guide




1. Broad context
Orient scientists outside the immediate field.
1–2


2. Specific background
Supply the knowledge needed to understand this study.
2–3


3. Problem
Identify the unresolved question.
1


4. Main result
State the central answer clearly.
1


5. What the result adds
Explain the finding through evidence and comparison with prior knowledge.
2–3


6. Wider meaning
Connect the answer back to the larger scientific problem.
1–2





Nature (2019) [9] also allows an optional 2–3 sentences of broader perspective when the editor judges that they improve accessibility. The allocations describe that guide; use the target journal’s current word limit and format.
Draft the question and answer first, then add the background an unfamiliar reader needs. [6]. Test whether the opening sentence helps explain the question: if deleting it leaves the abstract just as clear, it may be too general. [7]; [11].
Give the main finding enough space for its supporting comparison. Briefly introduce an unfamiliar experiment before stating its result. For a familiar comparison, begin with the finding and include the method in the same sentence. [8]; [1]. Nature’s annotated example introduces its assay with the supporting results, without a separate Methods block. [9].
End by explaining what the finding adds. A biological study might identify how a process works; a methods study might make a previously difficult measurement possible. Keep this closing statement within what the study demonstrated. [9]; [4].



Example: giving an abstract a clear argument
Both drafts describe the same fictional Brake study. The numerical comparison is the illustrative dataset developed in the reporting chapter.


Draft organized around procedures


We tested the bacterial defence system Brake using phage infections, DNA sequencing and protein-expression experiments. Intact Brake reduced infectious phage A yield 79-fold relative to the empty-vector control. Repeated RNA-derived DNA was detected, and infection was accompanied by double-stranded DNA and protein production. A translation-disrupting change preserved DNA production but removed growth arrest and defence. Separate protein expression restored both. Phages A and B were restricted, whereas phage C remained productive. These experiments addressed how a defence region encoding a reverse transcriptase and an RNA template, without an annotated effector gene, inhibits infection.


Revised abstract


Some bacterial defence regions encode a reverse transcriptase and an RNA template but lack an identifiable effector gene. How these regions inhibit infection is unclear. Here we show that the Brake defence system assembles an RNA-derived gene whose protein product arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation. Intact Brake reduced infectious phage A yield 79-fold relative to the empty-vector control, with activity differing among three tested phages. Sequencing identified a coding sequence spanning junctions in the repeated DNA product; double-stranded DNA and the encoded protein were detected during infection. Blocking translation preserved DNA production but removed growth arrest and defence, both of which were restored by expressing the protein separately. These findings reveal a defence pathway whose effector gene is assembled from an RNA template.

The revised opening explains why the gene’s origin is a puzzle before presenting the answer. The effect’s magnitude remains; the full interval and replication details appear in Results.




Select details that make the result understandable
Select details that establish what was compared and what the comparison showed. Name the system and any method central to the contribution; summarize routine procedures with the finding. [3]; [11]. Give the principal effect’s magnitude and reference group, adding uncertainty or sample information when interpretation or the journal’s format requires it. A percentage without its reference group, or an improvement without its comparator, leaves the result ambiguous. [4]; [9].
Include a limitation if leaving it out would misrepresent the answer. For Brake, stating that activity differed among the three tested phages prevents the abstract from implying that Brake restricts every phage. Secondary controls and exploratory findings can remain in Results. [4]; [1]. Read the abstract without the paper beside it: can readers identify the methods and groups, and understand its terms and abbreviations? Use the same names throughout. [12]; [4].


Adapt to the format and word limit
Check the article’s word limit, headings and required reporting elements before polishing. For a structured abstract, distribute the argument under the journal’s headings, commonly Background or Objectives, Methods, Results and Conclusions. Make sure the Results answer the stated objective. [5].
If the draft is too long, first cut background that does not lead to the question, repeated claims and secondary procedural detail. Then combine related statements, checking that the main comparison remains clear. Avoid saving words through unfamiliar abbreviations or overloaded sentences. [6]; [4]. Use the structural outline to check whether background has crowded out the findings. Studies linking writing features with citation counts do not establish that changing abstract length makes a paper clearer or more influential. [14].
Some journals also request a separate significance statement for a broader audience. Explain the problem and the value of the advance with less technical detail, following the journal’s instructions. Keep the approach and principal findings in the research abstract.


Give a methods paper its own emphasis
A methods abstract needs to explain what researchers can do with the method and how well it performs. Identify the limitation it addresses, such as an unreliable measurement or a time-consuming procedure, then explain what it changes. Give the benchmark or application that demonstrates its performance, including the conditions under which it was tested. Keep the method’s name and recognizable technical terms prominent. If the study also makes a biological discovery, explain how the method enabled it. [10].

title: Titles, abstracts and introductions
section: Build the introduction around the question
text:
Build the introduction around the question

Select the background the reader needs
Use the sequence below to select the background and plan the paragraphs. [1]; [12].

A common introduction structure








Stage
Purpose




1. Scientific context
Establish the process or problem and why understanding it matters.


2. Relevant knowledge
Explain the findings, ideas or methods on which the study builds. Select what the reader needs for the next step.


3. Unresolved question
Show what remains uncertain or inadequate, and why resolving it would matter. State the question or hypothesis the study addresses.


4. Present study
Introduce the approach and, where appropriate, the principal answer and contribution. Prepare readers for the Results.





Combine these functions when they form one point: a paragraph describing a method can also explain the limitation your study addresses. Start a new paragraph when the point changes. [1, Rule 6]; [12].
Choose background in relation to the question, rather than trying to summarize the whole field. Explain what remains unresolved and what an answer would change. For a methods paper, this means identifying the measurement that is difficult or unreliable and why researchers need it. [13]; [4].


Use the literature fairly and precisely
Organize previous work by the points it establishes, using reviews for orientation and original studies for specific findings. Where disagreement motivates the study, check whether the earlier experiments asked comparable questions under comparable conditions. Place citations beside the claims they support, splitting a sentence if different references support different parts. [5]; [4].
Before claiming priority, search alternative terminology and examine the closest studies. If priority remains uncertain, describe the specific advance. [4]; [13].


Connect paragraphs and introduce the study
Connect paragraphs through the scientific reasoning. After describing a method’s limitation, explain how the proposed method addresses it. After identifying an unexplained observation, introduce the question it raises. Reuse the same scientific terms so readers can follow the connection. In the Brake example, the missing effector leads to a question about the DNA product, followed by tests of the protein’s function. [1]; [4]. A closing interpretation can explain why the next step is needed. Omit a closing summary that merely repeats the paragraph’s opening. [12].
End with the study’s question and approach, usually followed by its main finding. Follow the article’s conventions if it calls for an aims-focused ending. Include a section-by-section roadmap only if the paper’s organization needs explanation. [13]; [3]; [12].



Example: introducing a biological question
This short introduction develops the question raised by Brake’s apparently missing effector gene. A real manuscript would need background citations and more context about the system.


Bacterial defence relies on molecules that interrupt phage replication. A protein-coding gene provides a starting point for identifying and testing a defence effector. When a defence region contains no recognizable effector gene, the origin of the protective molecule remains unresolved.
Brake contains a reverse transcriptase and a conserved RNA template, but no annotated effector gene. Its reverse transcriptase suggests that an RNA-derived DNA product may be involved. What does the reverse transcriptase produce, and how could that product contribute to defence?
Here we combine sequence analysis with genetic perturbations to determine how Brake restricts phage infection. We find that repeated RNA-derived DNA forms a continuous coding sequence whose protein product arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation. Preventing translation abolishes defence while preserving DNA production; expressing the protein separately restores it. These findings reveal a defence pathway in which the functional gene is assembled from an RNA template.

The final paragraph includes the genetic tests because detecting the product alone would not establish its role in defence. Phage range and the numerical effect can remain in the abstract and Results. The absence of an annotated effector gene is part of the fictional study’s starting analysis; a real manuscript would cite the source of that annotation.

title: Titles, abstracts and introductions
section: Check the opening against the paper
text:
Check the opening against the paper
Read the title, abstract and final Introduction paragraph together, then compare them with Results. Check that they describe the same contribution and that the evidence answers the question posed. [4]; [1]. Trace numerical statements back to their comparisons, including the population, condition and reference group. [5].
Some repetition between the abstract and Introduction is necessary because each must make sense independently. Within either section, remove explanations that do the same job twice and check that each paragraph advances the argument. [12]; [4].
Ask a colleague from the broader field to explain the question and answer after reading the opening. Revise where their understanding differs from the intended meaning. [7]; [1].
Final opening checklist

The title identifies the subject and gives a supported finding or clear scope.
The abstract explains the question, approach, main result and implication independently.
Quantitative statements name the comparison, and shortened passages retain the conditions needed to interpret the findings.
The introduction supplies the background needed for a specific, worthwhile question.
Citations support the precise statements made, and prior work is distinguished from this study.
Paragraphs lead into one another, and the ending prepares readers for the Results.
Terminology and claim strength agree across the opening, figures and main text.
The chosen article format is satisfied, and an unfamiliar reader can explain what was learned.

title: Methods, results and figure legends
text:
Plan what readers need
Draft Methods from the experimental records and analysis code, Results from the figures, and legends alongside each display. As you write, check that all three describe the same samples, measurements and comparisons. A change to the analysis may require a correction in each place. [1]; [2].
The examples continue the fictional Brake study, inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [12].

title: Methods, results and figure legends
text:
Where details belong
Place details according to the question they answer. [3]; [4].

Where the information belongs










Component
Main question
Information to provide




Methods
How was the evidence obtained?
Design, materials, procedures, measurements, processing and analysis choices needed to evaluate and reproduce the work.


Results
What did the study find?
The question or comparison, principal finding, quantitative support and qualifications that affect its interpretation.


Figure legend
What am I looking at?
Figure topic, panel descriptions, experimental context, visual encodings and statistical details needed to read the display.




The same treatment may need three different descriptions: how it was applied in Methods, what it changed in Results, and which marks represent it in the figure legend. Give readers the context they need at each point, while describing the full protocol once. [2]; [5].


Choose how much detail to include
State which population was sampled and what was compared, even for a specialist audience. Define scores developed for the study. Before describing an unfamiliar analysis, explain the question it answers so readers know why you used it. [3]; [6].
Use prose for procedures and reasons, tables for repeated fields, and a schematic when several inputs follow different paths into an analysis. Keep exact settings in Methods. [4].
Supporting material can hold detailed procedures and extended analyses. Keep the evidence essential to the main conclusion accessible in the paper, with precise references to supporting displays and controls. [3].

title: Methods, results and figure legends
text:
Write reproducible Methods

Organizing Methods
Begin with the design and materials, then describe measurement, processing and analysis. Within a procedure, preserve the order of operations; across procedures, group shared methods so readers encounter each protocol once. [7]; [8]. Open each subsection with its purpose or material, explaining unusual choices that affect interpretation before describing the steps. [4].
Write completed work in the past tense, choosing the subject that makes the procedure easiest to follow. Active sentences often clarify responsibility; passive wording works when the sample or procedure is the natural subject. [6]; [4]. Have contributing authors check the account against their records and final code, including the steps where data passed between collaborators. [1]; [2].


Include the details that determine the outcome
Identify the materials or datasets and their sources, inclusion criteria, conditions and controls. Give laboratory settings needed to repeat the procedure, and identify datasets by accession or durable reference and relevant release. A table can collect reagent or dataset identities; the prose should explain how they were used. [2]; [7].
Consult study-specific reporting requirements for additional details. Obtain details of the required ethics approvals and compliance information from the responsible investigators, identifying the samples or procedures they cover. [2]; [7].
Describe how samples were allocated, when measurements were taken and how randomization or blinding operated when used. If a safeguard was absent, report that accurately and assess its effect on the conclusion. [9].
For an established protocol, cite the version used and describe what you changed. The phrase “with minor modifications” does not tell someone repeating the work which steps to follow. [7]; [2]. For computational procedures, report filtering, reference annotations, normalization and thresholds because they can affect the result. Routine file-handling operations usually need no description. [2]; [4].



Example: describing a matched comparison
The Brake study compares infectious phage output across three bacterial genotypes. The values and design details below are invented for teaching. This excerpt covers titre calculation and analysis; the host, constructs, infection conditions and collection protocol would be specified elsewhere in Methods.



Infectious-titre analysis

We compared empty-vector cultures, cultures carrying intact Brake and cultures carrying Brake with a catalytically inactive reverse transcriptase. On each of six experimental days, one independently started culture of each genotype was infected with phage A and sampled at the same endpoint.
For each culture, we estimated infectious titre in plaque-forming units per millilitre (PFU/mL) from technical duplicate plaque counts, accounting for the plated volumes and dilution factors. We combined the duplicate measurements into one culture-level estimate.
The primary comparison was intact Brake versus empty vector, matched by experimental day. We divided the intact-Brake titre by the empty-vector titre within each day and took the log10 of that ratio. We estimated the mean log10 ratio and its two-sided 95% confidence interval using a Student t distribution with five degrees of freedom. We exponentiated the estimate and interval limits to obtain a geometric mean titre ratio. Fold reduction was its reciprocal, with the interval limits inverted accordingly. The inactive reverse-transcriptase measurements were displayed as a mechanistic control.

What to notice. Each day contributes one matched contrast. Duplicate plates improve the measurement of a culture; they do not double the sample size. The analysis is specified for the between-genotype effect, rather than inferred from separate error bars on each group.




Describe the analysis from input to inference
Describe how the input becomes the reported result. Identify the input data and version, then explain processing in order, naming the software and settings that affect the output. For genomic analyses, give the reference assembly. State what the final comparison or model estimates. Readers should be able to follow that account in Methods without having to reconstruct it from the code. [2]; [6].
Explain selection and exclusion before presenting findings from the selected data. State how samples, genes, cells or regions entered the analysis and how many remained where counts affect interpretation. Distinguish prespecified decisions from choices made after inspecting the results. A subset selected because it shows the desired effect cannot also supply an independent test of that effect. Report exploratory analyses as exploratory and describe any separate data used for confirmation. [9].
Name the statistical comparison, not merely the software command. Describe the outcome, explanatory variables and relevant pairing or grouping; state how uncertainty was estimated and how multiple testing was handled when many comparisons were made. If different panels use different analyses, make those assignments clear. [7]; [2]; [9].
Identify the data and code in durable repository records, subject to applicable access restrictions. Prepare those records early and specify the version or retrieval date for changing datasets. [2]; [6].


Make the sampling and replication clear
Explain which samples were independently collected or treated and which measurements came from each. Hundreds of cells from one culture describe that culture more thoroughly, but do not establish consistency across independent cultures. Individual cells can be independent treatment units when the design assigns them that way and supports their independence. [10].
Give sample sizes with their meaning: independent cultures, repeated readings or analysis runs. Where the study has more than one level, report the counts and their relationship, including exclusions. In the Brake example, there are six cultures per genotype, each measured on duplicate plates, and the primary effect is estimated from six contrasts matched by day. [10]; [9].
Preserve that structure in both the analysis and its description. State whether the comparison uses sample summaries or a model that accounts for measurements nested within samples. Identify pairing when corresponding control and treatment observations belong to the same experimental run. A display can show individual observations and sample summaries together, provided the legend distinguishes them and identifies the unit used for statistical inference. [10].

title: Methods, results and figure legends
text:
Present results as an argument

Order findings by what they establish
Introduce each result before relying on it. In the Brake study, identifying the protein-coding DNA product prepares the experiment that tests the protein’s role. Presenting that test first would leave readers unsure why the protein was chosen. [3]; [6].
Use finding-based Results headings when one statement covers the evidence. “The Brake protein mediates phage restriction” is more informative than “Protein experiments.” A descriptive heading suits a resource, procedure or unresolved comparison. Read the heading with the figure title to check that the written claim and display answer the same question. [2].
One figure may support several paragraphs, and a claim may draw on several figures. Refer to the panels that support each finding and give the values needed to explain it. [2]; [3].


Build a paragraph around a finding
Build the paragraph around a finding, bringing together observations that support it. Briefly introduce the question and approach for an unfamiliar experiment; begin with the finding when the comparison is already clear. Name the treatment, comparison and outcome, then give the evidence, panel reference and any necessary qualification. Keep the full procedure in Methods. [8]; [2].
When introducing the next experiment, explain what you still needed to find out after the previous result. You do not need to repeat the paper’s broad motivation. [4]; [6]. Explain what each result supports where readers need that connection to follow the next experiment. Reserve extended literature comparisons and broader implications for Discussion. If Results and Discussion are combined, still distinguish the observations from your proposed explanations. [3]; [4].
A closing interpretation is useful when it connects several observations or motivates the next experiment. If the paragraph has already made and supported its point, move on without restating it. [6].


Report magnitude, comparison and uncertainty
State what changed, relative to what and by how much, with units and the scale of comparison. Give the important difference or proportion explicitly. The display or underlying data can carry the remaining values. [6]; [3].
Report the estimate together with appropriate uncertainty and, where used, the statistical test result. A small p-value cannot convey the magnitude of an effect, and “significant” alone does not tell readers its direction or biological importance. Distinguish variability among observations from uncertainty in an estimated effect. Make clear whether an interval describes a group mean, a between-group contrast or another quantity. [7]; [9]; [10].
A claim that two effects differ needs a direct comparison between them. A significant response in one condition and a non-significant response in another can occur even when their estimated effects are similar, because the estimates have different precision. Separate significance tests do not answer the comparative question. [9].
Name what was measured before giving its biological interpretation. In the Brake example below, the measurement is endpoint infectious titre; the interpretation concerns phage restriction. [6].



Example: reporting a quantitative finding
Endpoint infectious titres were compared within each experimental day, as described in the Methods above.

Brake reduced infectious phage A output. Across six experimental days, the geometric mean of the day-matched titre ratios indicated a 79-fold reduction with intact Brake relative to the empty-vector control (95% confidence interval, 55–116-fold; Figure 1B). Cultures carrying the inactive reverse transcriptase retained high phage titres. These results support a requirement for reverse-transcriptase activity in phage restriction.


What to notice. The interval belongs to the fold reduction. The final sentence gives a local interpretation of the control; it does not identify which downstream product causes defence. That question motivates Figures 2 and 3.
A lower endpoint titre is not automatically a smaller burst size per infected cell. Keep the result named after the quantity measured.




Negative and inconclusive findings
Report results that disagree with the prediction. State whether they provide evidence against it or are too imprecise to assess it. Also report controls that leave an alternative explanation unresolved. [9]; [3].
Give the estimated effect and uncertainty even when a test is non-significant. If you want to claim that any difference is too small to matter scientifically, specify how small it would need to be and whether the design and analysis can rule out larger differences. An inconclusive control leaves open the explanation it was intended to test. [9].
When an unexpected result prompts exploration, explain how that analysis arose and label it accordingly. Report what it establishes and which questions remain unresolved, preserving the distinction from the original test. [9].

title: Methods, results and figure legends
text:
Figure captions and legends
The figure caption, often called a figure legend, is the text beneath or alongside the display. Here, “legend” refers to that text rather than the key inside a plot. Include the conditions, label definitions and statistical details needed to understand the figure without searching the main text. [5]; [2].

Identify what each panel shows
Write the legend while looking at the figure. Begin with a concise title identifying its subject or principal finding, then describe the panels in their labeled order. Explain what readers are looking at before interpreting it: a schematic needs its relationships explained; an image needs the specimen, displayed signal and relevant scale; a quantitative plot needs the measured quantity and comparison. Add a brief finding when the journal permits and the title has not already conveyed it. [5]; [11].
Label figures directly where practical, using the legend to define remaining symbols, abbreviations and encodings. Describe shared conditions once and identify panel-specific exceptions. Use the same names for conditions in the legend and display. [5]; [2].


Make the statistical display interpretable
Identify sample sizes, what each plotted point represents, the summary statistic and the meaning of error bars or intervals. Distinguish individual observations from independent-sample summaries. [2]; [10].
State which comparison each test or annotation refers to. Include the test and relevant sidedness, pairing and multiple-comparison information where applicable, following the journal’s reporting format. For box plots, define the boxes, central line, whiskers and any separately plotted points. For normalized data, explain the reference used for normalization if it is needed to interpret the values. [2].
Keep the full analysis in Methods, but define the displayed samples and error bars in the legend. Shorten a long legend by describing shared procedures once. If the panels require unrelated explanations, consider whether they belong in separate figures. [5]; [2].



Example: a panel and its legend
This is the quantitative panel from Figure 1 in the Brake figure plan. It uses the same illustrative data as the Methods and Results passages above.
Original teaching figure; all plotted values are illustrative.



Figure 1B. Brake reduces infectious phage A yield. Endpoint titres from cultures carrying empty vector, intact Brake or Brake with a catalytically inactive reverse transcriptase (inactive RT). Each point represents one independently started culture; lines connect the three cultures assayed on the same day. Six days were measured, with technical duplicate plaque counts combined for each culture. The vertical axis is logarithmic. The geometric mean titre was 79-fold lower for intact Brake than for empty vector (95% confidence interval, 55–116-fold), calculated from the six day-matched log10 titre ratios.

A legend for the complete Figure 1 would also describe the construct schematic and growth curves in panels A and C.




Adapt the explanation to the publication stage
An initial legend can explain the figure’s takeaway to reviewers; some journals retain that style, while others require shorter descriptions for publication. [11]. Use a finding-based title when it accurately summarizes the figure and the journal permits it, or a descriptive title otherwise. When shortening the legend, move necessary procedural or interpretive detail to the appropriate Methods or Results passage while retaining what readers need to decode the display. [5]; [11].
Keep figures and legends together in a review copy when the submission format allows it. To test a legend, first give it to a colleague without the figure and ask them to sketch the panels they expect. Compare that sketch with the figure: a missing comparison, unexplained image or ambiguous panel identity tells you what to clarify. Then inspect the figure and legend together to check the labels and statistical details. [11].

title: Methods, results and figure legends
section: Check reporting across text and figures
text:
Check reporting across text and figures
Check each result against its figure, legend, Methods and underlying analysis, following the same samples and comparison through to the reported numbers and interpretation. [2]; [3]. Contributing authors should verify technical details; a second reader can identify missing explanations or unclear figure labels that the authors overlook. [1]; [2].
Make the final pass on the assembled manuscript and supporting files, checking figure letters, units, terminology and statistical labels. Test data and code links, and carry each correction through all affected files. [1]; [6].

Reporting checklist

Each result states a clear comparison and points to its supporting evidence.
Methods identify the materials, design, procedures and analysis choices needed to follow the work.
Selection, exclusions and exploratory decisions are reported where they affect inference.
Sample counts distinguish independent units from measurements within them.
Quantitative claims include the relevant magnitude and uncertainty, with suitable statistical support.
Findings that limit the conclusion remain visible; inconclusive evidence retains its uncertainty.
Legends identify the panels, conditions, encodings, summaries and statistical comparisons.
Text, figures, legends, Methods and supporting files agree, and data/code access has been checked.

title: Discussion and conclusions
text:
Opening and structure
The Results tell readers what happened; the Discussion asks what those findings establish. Begin with the study’s answer, then explain how it relates to previous work, where it remains uncertain and what follows from it.
The examples continue the fictional Brake study: an RNA-derived gene produces a protein that arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation.

title: Discussion and conclusions
text:
Start with an answer the evidence supports
Answer the Introduction’s question in the opening paragraph, using the few findings needed to support that answer. State the conditions in which it holds. Save detailed comparisons and controls for the passages that discuss them. [1]; [2]; [3].
If the study answers only part of the question, say what was resolved and what evidence is missing for the rest. A study may show that a protein mediates an effect without identifying its molecular target; the unknown target limits the mechanistic explanation, while the functional conclusion can stand. [5]; [4].


Give the argument a clear order
The following sequence is a starting point; limitations may belong within an interpretation or comparison rather than in a separate block. [1]; [6].


A working structure for the Discussion


Answer: State the central finding and the essential evidence behind it.
Interpretation and comparison: Explain the major findings alongside the most relevant previous work. Show what agrees, differs or becomes clearer.
Limits and alternatives: Evaluate the explanations the evidence can distinguish and the conditions under which the answer remains uncertain.
Implications: Explain what the findings change and which unresolved question is worth pursuing next.
Closing contribution: Leave the reader with a concise statement of what the study adds.


Follow the Results order when it supports the same argument. Group experiments that jointly answer one question, and give an unexpected finding early attention when it changes the interpretation. Use subheadings for a long Discussion; a short one may read better without them. [9]; [10].
A combined Results and Discussion can interpret each finding as it appears, then draw the findings together at the end. With separate sections, report new measurements in Results and their procedures in Methods; the Discussion can then concentrate on what they mean. [7]. Some formats permit a preliminary observation within Discussion, but it still needs enough methodological and reporting detail to be evaluated. Place any result essential to the central conclusion in Results. [6]; [10].

title: Discussion and conclusions
text:
Explain findings alongside previous work

Comparing findings
Start with the studies that motivated the question, adding work needed to interpret the findings and relevant papers published during the project. The Introduction may only have needed their central conclusions; here, a particular comparison may require closer attention to the evidence. [10]; [5]. Read the relevant Results and Methods, noting the system, intervention, measured outcome and conditions before deciding whether the findings agree or conflict. [4].
Explain how your finding confirms, extends or conflicts with earlier work. Distinguish confirmation under similar conditions from extension to a new setting. [5]; [3].
Compare studies through their effect estimates and uncertainty, alongside experimental context and analysis choices. Different significance labels do not establish different effects; see comparing effects. Likewise, similar directions do not establish close agreement when estimates are too imprecise to distinguish substantially different effects. [8].
Differences in conditions may suggest why studies disagree, but they do not by themselves establish the explanation. Identify the evidence that would distinguish it from alternatives, and leave the conflict unresolved if that evidence is unavailable. Apply the same care to contrary and supportive findings: cite the specific result, and discuss methodological limitations where they affect the comparison. [5]; [4].


Build paragraphs around an interpretation
Build each paragraph around one point. A paragraph explaining a mechanism needs the evidence for it; a paragraph about disagreement needs the findings being compared. Give readers any unfamiliar background before asking them to follow the interpretation. Add a closing consequence or next question when there is something further to explain. [7]; [4].
As you move between your results and published work, make clear which experiment established each finding. Name the biological subject and use consistent terminology so that a phrase such as “this finding” does not leave readers choosing between several studies. [3]; [4]. The paragraph should explain what the evidence establishes together; a sequence of paper summaries that does not affect the interpretation is usually unnecessary. [5]; [6].

title: Discussion and conclusions
text:
Evaluate limitations and alternatives

Explain why one interpretation is better supported
Consider plausible alternatives that would change the conclusion, and compare their predictions with the observations. Explain which control distinguishes the alternatives and where more than one explanation remains possible. An intervention may establish that a protein contributes to a response while leaving open how it acts. [5]; [4]; [8].
Unexpected findings require the same scrutiny. Examine the conditions and possible measurement problems before developing a biological explanation, and identify explanations developed afterward as hypotheses generated by the result. [8].


Explaining limitations
Explain what each limitation prevents you from concluding. Testing one cell model leaves generality uncertain; an assay that cannot distinguish two mechanisms leaves the mechanism unresolved. Qualify the affected claim and state what the checks did resolve. [1]; [9]; [2]; [5].
Instead of simply noting a small sample, explain whether the estimate is too imprecise to distinguish effects that matter. For a method tested under limited conditions, state which uses remain untested. [6]; [4].


Inconclusive results
Use the estimates and uncertainty described in the reporting chapter to explain what an inconclusive result leaves open. If the uncertainty includes effects large enough to change the interpretation, that uncertainty belongs in the conclusion. Establishing a practically negligible effect requires a suitable design and analysis, such as a justified equivalence analysis; a non-significant test alone cannot establish it. [8].



Example: connecting mechanism, limits and implications
Here RNA-templated defence-gene assembly is a new discovery, as in the main Brake case.


Brake assembles a functional defence gene from an RNA template. Sequence analysis identified a coding sequence spanning DNA repeat junctions. Genetic tests established the encoded protein’s role: blocking translation preserved DNA production but removed defence, and separate protein expression restored it. The effector therefore becomes available through gene assembly rather than expression of a conventional genomic coding sequence.
These experiments establish the protein’s role without identifying its molecular target. Growth arrest could result from interference with a host process needed for both cell growth and phage replication, but the current measurements do not identify that process. Determining the target would help explain how arrest is initiated and why activity differs among the tested phages.
The fate of infected cells is a separate question. They stopped growing during observation, but we did not measure subsequent recovery. Reduced infectious output therefore establishes phage restriction without showing that individual cells survive the infection. Recovery measurements would distinguish reversible arrest from a lasting loss of growth capacity.
These findings show that a functional defence gene can emerge in an RNA-derived DNA product. Searching those products for coding sequences could reveal effectors missed by conventional genome annotation.

The molecular target and cell recovery need different follow-up experiments, so they receive separate paragraphs.





Example: comparing a follow-up with its precedent
In a follow-up version of the Brake paper, RNA-templated antiviral gene synthesis is already known, and the study tests the effector’s function in another system. Tang and colleagues (2024) [11] serves as real prior work. This is also the premise of the second cover letter.










Question
Published DRT2 study
Fictional Brake study




What connects gene assembly to defence?
RNA-derived DNA encodes Neo, whose expression causes growth arrest.
A translation-disrupting change preserves DNA production but removes defence; separate protein expression restores it.


What happens to arrested cells?
The study includes viability and recovery measurements.
Recovery after infection was not measured.


What remains unresolved?
The protein’s molecular function requires further investigation.
The molecular target of the Brake protein is unknown.





RNA-templated gene synthesis was previously established as a route to bacterial defence in DRT2 systems. [11]. Our Brake experiments identify the protein encoded by the assembled gene as an effector of defence in this system. Blocking translation preserves DNA production but removes defence, and separate protein expression restores it. These results distinguish the protein’s contribution from a direct effect of the DNA product alone. Whether Brake-arrested cells recover remains unresolved: recovery was measured in the DRT2 study but was not tested here.

title: Discussion and conclusions
text:
Develop implications and conclusions

Explain what follows from the finding
Explain how the finding changes an explanation, prediction or measurement capability. The implication should follow from the result: identifying a previously unrecognized source of protein-coding genes, for example, gives researchers a reason to examine material that conventional annotation overlooks. [3]; [7]. For a method, distinguish a newly available capability from better performance on an existing task. A performance claim needs a specified comparator and benchmark, together with the conditions tested. [4]; [6].
Use a model or schematic to connect findings when it clarifies the explanation. Distinguish established relationships from proposed links in the labels and legend. Explain the evidence for each important connection and a testable prediction for a hypothetical one. [6]; [4].


Identify the next question to resolve
Identify the most important remaining question and explain how its possible answers would change the interpretation. [1]; [9]. If that answer is essential to the present conclusion, obtain the evidence now or narrow the claim. [2]; [4].
If you propose an explanation that the study has not tested, show how it follows from the results or previous work and what evidence could challenge it. For a proposed practical application, identify the test still needed before recommending that use. [5]; [4].


Finish with what the study changes
Close with the contribution and its most important implication, retaining any qualification essential to its meaning. The ending should draw out what the findings change, without recounting the experiments again. [7]; [3]. Use a separate Conclusion when the format requires it or a substantial Discussion benefits from a final synthesis. A short Discussion may already have the ending it needs. [2].

title: Discussion and conclusions
text:
Check the interpretation
Read the Introduction’s question and the Discussion’s opening and ending together. If the answer changed during writing, revise the framing while preserving the distinction between the original prediction and interpretations developed afterward. [3]; [8]. Then follow the argument paragraph by paragraph: check claims against results or publications, retain important alternatives, and use the paragraph openings to locate repetition or abrupt changes of subject. [4]; [5].
Before asking for sentence edits, ask a colleague to identify the main answer, unresolved issue and contribution. Where their account differs from yours, find the missing or misleading step in the reasoning. [1].

Before finishing the Discussion

Does the opening give a supported answer to the question in the Introduction?
Do the main comparisons explain what the study adds, including relevant disagreement?
Can readers follow the evidence favoring the interpretation over plausible alternatives?
Does each important limitation explain what cannot yet be concluded or recommended?
Can readers distinguish an established mechanism from a proposed one, and see what inconclusive findings leave open?
Would the proposed future work extend the findings, or is it needed to support a claim the paper already makes?
Does the ending leave a clear contribution without repeating the experiment summary?

title: Discussion and conclusions

title: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper
text:
Starting a draft
Writing can reveal that you have not explained why an experiment supports a conclusion. Resolve such problems before polishing sentences. As the draft develops, check the evidence, arrange the results so readers can follow the reasoning, and then edit the paragraphs and sentences. New findings or feedback may require you to revisit earlier decisions.
The examples use the fictional Brake study, inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [12].
crumbs: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper

title: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper
text:
Choose a passage you can develop
If the question and figures are settled, start with a Results passage whose comparison you understand well. Explain the finding and draft the corresponding Methods from the records. [1]; [2].
If you have results but are unsure how they fit together, draft a working title and a short statement of what the study adds. Sketch the question and background for the Introduction. Then check the figures: do they support the answer you have proposed? [3].
State the paragraph’s purpose, then develop it with the figures, analysis outputs and sources beside you. Mark missing information precisely—for example, “confirm which samples enter this comparison”—and continue where you can. [4]; [2].


Make writing sessions manageable
Choose a task you can tackle in the available writing time: draft one result, revise a transition or check a Discussion claim. If you stall, make the task smaller. Allow a longer session when you need to reread the whole argument. [5]; [2].
If sentence polishing prevents progress, explain the finding aloud or write an informal version before refining the terminology. Correct errors that block your thinking, but leave equivalent wording choices for later. [5]; [6].
When stuck, ask why. If you do not understand a result, inspect it or discuss it with a collaborator. If only the opening sentence is troublesome, draft the evidence and return to it. A break may help when concentration has faded. A shared writing session or an agreed date for sending a draft can help you return to the work. [5]; [2].
crumbs: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper

title: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper
section: Read for the question and answer
text:
Read for the question and answer
Read the draft through before making extensive local edits. If you have just finished writing it, a break can help you notice what the page actually says. Record places where the explanation stops making sense, but continue far enough to see whether the missing information appears later. [8, pp. 124–126]; [14, rule 8].
Write a brief account of the paper’s question, answer and decisive evidence. Include the condition or unresolved issue that most limits the answer. Then compare that account with the title, abstract, final Introduction paragraph and Discussion. These passages can differ in detail, but they should identify the same contribution. An abstract that promises a mechanism while the Results establish an association creates a substantive discrepancy, even if each section reads smoothly on its own. [4, rules 1 and 5–8]; [9, tips 4 and 9].
Ask whether the answer addresses the question the Introduction led readers to expect. Sometimes the experiments have resolved a narrower question, or an unexpected finding has become the main contribution. In that case, revise the framing without presenting an explanation developed afterward as the original prediction. If the answer is supported but difficult to recognize, identify the missing connection before deciding to collect more data. [14, rules 1–5]; [15].
Check what the paper adds to existing knowledge. If the contribution depends on differing from an earlier study, reread that study’s relevant result and method. Did it use the same system, measurement and intervention? A difference may explain why the findings disagree, or show that your work extends a finding to another setting. See comparing with previous work. [9, tips 1 and 10].
Ask a colleague who is less immersed in the project to explain the paper’s question and answer. If their account differs from yours, reread the passage that led to it and check whether the problem lies in the explanation or the evidence. [4, rules 2 and 10]; [2].

title: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper
text:
Checking claims against the evidence
Start with the claims needed for the paper’s main conclusion. Follow each claim through the cited panels and legend to the Methods, supporting material and analysis. What was measured, what was compared, and why does that comparison support the claim? Pay particular attention when the conclusion combines several experiments or proposes a biological explanation for a measurement. [14, rules 4–5]; [9, tips 6 and 9].
A legend may omit the meaning of n even though the analysis uses the correct units. Check the analysis before deciding whether the problem is an unclear description or repeated measurements treated as independent samples. [15]; [16].

Reconstruct the comparison
For a quantitative claim, identify the measured quantity, reference group, sampled or treated units and any pairing or nesting. Then check which observations entered the analysis and how the reported effect and uncertainty were calculated. A label such as “six replicates” does not explain whether the six are independently treated cultures, measurements within a culture or matched experimental runs. The appropriate unit follows from the design and the intended inference. [16, pp. 1–3].
Follow the same samples through exclusions, transformations and summaries. If the reported counts differ between a figure and Methods, establish whether different subsets were intended and whether the distinction is explained. Reconcile the reported number with the final analysis output rather than choosing whichever version appears more plausible. For a ratio or fold change, check its direction and denominator as well as its magnitude. See reporting quantitative findings. [9, tips 15–17]; [17, pp. 1514–1515].
Examine whether the analysis answers the comparison stated in the prose. A significant change in one condition and a non-significant change in another do not establish that the changes differ. Likewise, an imprecise estimate may remain compatible with a biologically substantial effect. If a claim depends on the absence of that effect, a non-significant test alone cannot supply the required evidence. [15].


Test the interpretation against an alternative
Choose a plausible alternative that would change an important conclusion and identify what distinguishes it from the preferred explanation. For an intervention experiment, ask what else the intervention changes and which control separates those effects. If the two explanations predict the same observed result, that experiment cannot choose between them. [15]; [9, tip 9].
Include findings that challenge the preferred explanation. Check whether the difference reflects conditions, samples or analytical choices; if it persists, decide how it limits the answer. Preserve the distinction between a prediction tested as planned and an explanation suggested by inspecting the results. In particular, selecting observations because they show an effect and then using them to confirm that effect can make apparently strong support circular. [15].
A study can establish that a protein is required for a phenotype without identifying its molecular target. But if the perturbation also removes an upstream product, the loss of the phenotype could result from either change. Further evidence would be needed to distinguish them. Decide which unresolved question affects the conclusion you intend to retain, and update the claim inventory accordingly. [9, tips 4 and 9]; [4, rule 7].


Figures and legends
Read the figures and legends independently of the main text, then compare the inference they invite with the analysis actually performed. Visual grouping can suggest a comparison the authors never tested; connecting points can imply pairing that did not occur. Check whether the display reveals the variation needed to assess the summary and whether exclusions or overlapping points hide relevant observations. [17, figure 8].
For a schematic, follow the material or process from beginning to end. Check that symbols, colors and names remain consistent and that the sequence agrees with Methods. [18].
For light-microscopy results, compare the selected image with the range of observations it is meant to illustrate. Check that readers can identify the specimen, channels and scale, and trace image processing into the reported measurements. Example input and output data can expose a segmentation or processing problem that a polished final image conceals. Use the applicable Schmied and colleagues (2024) [19] checklist to investigate missing information; it does not establish that the experiment itself was well designed.
Inspect the assembled figures at their intended reading size for unreadable labels and inconsistent colors. [9, tips 31–32].
