title: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper
text:
Deciding what to revise
For each concern, name the passage, explain the problem and state what needs checking. Replace “Strengthen the Discussion” with a task such as “The abstract infers survival from growth arrest; check whether recovery was measured and revise the claim accordingly.” [14, rules 8–10].
If the evidence supports the claim but the explanation is incomplete, clarify the comparison or explain what a control rules out. Put any needed background before the result that depends on it. If the analysis is wrong, correct it and reassess the claim before rewriting the conclusion. If essential evidence is absent, obtain it or narrow the claim. Another interesting question can remain future work when its answer is not needed for the conclusion. [4, rules 7–8]; [15]; [9, tips 4 and 9].



Example: assessing the complete Brake draft
An early draft of the fictional Brake study, inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [12], describes RNA-templated gene assembly, growth arrest and phage restriction. Its abstract additionally claims survival, although recovery was not measured. The numerical result uses the handbook’s illustrative dataset.


Draft packet

The title is An RNA-templated gene arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation. The Introduction asks what the reverse transcriptase produces and how that product contributes to defence. Figures 1–4 respectively establish phage restriction, identify the protein-coding DNA product, test the protein’s function and examine activity across the tested phages.

Abstract, final sentence


By arresting growth during infection, Brake enables infected bacteria to survive phage attack.


Figure 1B, display and legend excerpt

The plot shows endpoint infectious phage A titres for empty vector, intact Brake and inactive reverse transcriptase. Lines join observations across the three genotypes. The Results report a 79-fold reduction for intact Brake relative to empty vector, with a 95% confidence interval of 55–116-fold.

Endpoint infectious titres for the three genotypes. Six replicates were measured in duplicate; lines connect matched measurements.


Figure 3, Results excerpt

We next disrupted translation of the Brake protein. DNA production was retained (Figure 3A), but growth arrest and phage restriction were lost (Figure 3B). Expressing the protein separately restored both phenotypes (Figure 3C).


Only in the Discussion does the draft explain that retaining DNA production is necessary to distinguish the protein’s contribution from an effect of losing the upstream DNA product.

Checks against the full manuscript and records

The author checks the cell-tracking records and Methods behind Figure 4B: growth arrest was observed, but subsequent recovery was not measured. The phage assays establish restriction of A and B; C remains productive. None of these findings measures whether an individual infected cell survives.
For Figure 1B, the culture log records one independently started culture per genotype on each of six experimental days. Technical duplicate plaque counts were combined into one titre per culture. The analysis already compares intact Brake with empty vector within each day, using six log10 titre ratios to estimate the mean and a two-sided Student t confidence interval with five degrees of freedom. Converting back to a ratio and taking the reciprocal reproduces the reported fold reduction and interval. The Methods give this analysis; the legend fails to identify its units clearly.
For Figure 3, the author checks the construct description and product measurements against the panels. The translation-disrupting change preserves the RNA and DNA products, and separate protein expression restores arrest and restriction. The control needed for the protein inference is present. Its purpose becomes apparent too late in the written explanation.

Author’s assessment

The checked evidence supports an RNA-templated route to a protein effector of growth arrest and phage restriction. The repairs are specific: remove the unsupported survival claim, clarify the six day-matched cultures and comparison in Figure 1B, and move the protein-versus-DNA rationale before the Figure 3 results. These repairs require no repeat experiment on the records checked here. The protein’s molecular target and recovery of arrested cells remain unresolved.

Prioritized revision plan








Work and responsibility
Completion criterion




1. Settle the claim. The lead author and coauthors retain gene assembly, growth arrest and phage restriction as the contribution. Remove the survival inference throughout the manuscript.
Title, abstract and Discussion agree; none infers survival or irreversible death from growth arrest. Recovery remains an explicit unresolved question.


2. Clarify Figure 1B. The analyst verifies the culture log, plotted values and analysis; the figure author clarifies cultures, technical duplicates and day matching. Proceed alongside task 1.
Figure, legend, Methods and Results agree: six cultures per genotype; six day-matched contrasts; 79-fold reduction (95% confidence interval, 55–116-fold).


3. Explain the Figure 3 test. The Results author introduces the protein-versus-DNA question before the perturbation results. The contributing experimentalist checks the explanation against panels 3A–C.
Readers can explain why retained DNA production matters and how complementation supports the protein’s role. The wording does not identify an unmeasured molecular target.


4. Review the assembled revision. After the changes are integrated, the lead author circulates one version with the revised figures and supporting material. Technical contributors check their results; a colleague less familiar with the project reconstructs the argument.
The scientific concerns are resolved in the manuscript itself, and no stale claim, inconsistent legend or broken transition remains elsewhere. Any new substantive concern returns to the plan.




Two targeted repairs

Replace the abstract’s survival sentence with a conclusion consistent with the paper’s discovery:

These findings reveal a defence pathway whose effector gene is assembled from an RNA template.

Replace the Figure 3 paragraph’s first sentence with the question its controls answer:

We next asked whether the protein encoded by the RNA-derived DNA mediates defence. We disrupted translation while preserving the RNA and DNA products, allowing us to test the protein’s contribution without removing the upstream products.

The existing Figure 3 results then provide the answer. Had the translation-disrupting change also prevented DNA production, moving this explanation would not resolve the concern: the evidence would no longer distinguish the protein’s contribution from loss of the upstream product.

title: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper
text:
Revise the argument and organization

From the argument to the paragraphs
Once you know which claims the evidence supports, decide how to explain them. Check the paragraph order before polishing passages that may move or disappear. If rearranging the draft reveals a claim you cannot explain from the evidence, investigate it before continuing. [7]; [4].


Reviewing the paragraph order
Summarize each paragraph’s point in one sentence. Read these sentences in sequence to find repeated points, paragraphs trying to do too much and missing steps in the reasoning. Revise the paragraph order before editing individual sentences. [3]; [4].



Example: reorganizing a Results draft
The Brake draft follows the order in which experiments were completed. Protein expression appears before readers know why that protein was tested. The paragraph summaries below expose where the explanation arrives too late.


Paragraphs in the draft


Expressing the Brake protein arrests growth.
Details of expression-vector construction.
Intact Brake restricts phage output.
DNA sequencing identifies a coding sequence across repeat junctions.
Phage activity differs among the three tested phages.
Infection is accompanied by double-stranded DNA and protein production.
Blocking translation preserves DNA production but removes defence; separate protein expression restores it.


Revised paragraph plan


Establish the defence phenotype and the reverse-transcriptase control (Figure 1).
Identify the RNA-derived DNA product and the coding sequence across its repeat junctions (Figure 2A, D).
Describe the DNA products and protein expression before and during infection (Figure 2B–C).
Test the protein’s role using the translation-disrupted construct and separate expression (Figure 3).
Define the tested phage range and describe infected-cell growth (Figure 4).

Protein expression now answers a question raised by product identification. Vector-construction details move to Methods. Rewrite the transition into Figure 3 so it asks whether the protein is responsible for the defence already observed.


Once the order is settled, check what each paragraph contains. Keep an explanation or limitation beside the finding it concerns; move detailed procedures to Methods and remove background already established. If successive additions have obscured the paragraph’s point, list the facts and qualifications to retain and write it again. Compare the versions for changed meaning. [9]; [4].
To meet a word limit, first remove duplicated explanations, tangential background and details already clear in figures or Methods. Then shorten sentences. Read across each cut to check for lost definitions or premises. [9]; [4].



Rough word and figure budget
For a 3,000-word body, start with about 500 words for the Introduction, 1,700 for Results and 800 for Discussion. For 4,000 words, the corresponding starting allocation is 600, 2,400 and 1,000 words. Shift space between sections as the argument requires. These totals exclude Methods; check the journal’s counting rules. Plan around 4–6 main figures and tables combined. [13].





Make each paragraph advance the explanation
Open with the finding when the comparison is familiar; otherwise introduce the question and essential design first. Develop that point with the observations and reasoning it needs. A closing interpretation helps when it connects several observations or leads to the next experiment. If it merely repeats the opening, remove it. [3]; [4]; [9]; [7].



Example: giving a Results paragraph a clear point
Both passages use the illustrative titres from the reporting chapter.


Draft


We measured phage A titres in empty-vector cultures, intact-Brake cultures and cultures carrying inactive reverse transcriptase on six experimental days. The inactive reverse-transcriptase cultures retained high titres. The matched comparison of intact Brake with empty vector gave a 79-fold reduction in geometric mean titre (95% confidence interval, 55–116-fold; Figure 1B). Brake therefore restricted phage output.


Revision


Brake reduced infectious phage A output. The geometric mean of the six day-matched titre ratios indicated a 79-fold reduction with intact Brake relative to empty vector (95% confidence interval, 55–116-fold; Figure 1B). Cultures carrying the inactive reverse transcriptase retained high titres, supporting a requirement for reverse-transcriptase activity.

The control follows the main comparison because it addresses whether restriction requires reverse-transcriptase activity. The revision retains the matching by experimental day.

title: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper
text:
Edit sentences for clarity

Subjects and verbs
Start with the main clause: who or what did what? Direct verbs often make it easier to find—“we measured induction” instead of “we performed an assessment of induction.” Keep the subject and verb close, and place modifiers beside what they describe. Long qualifications may need a separate sentence. [9]; [3]; [7].
Check that introductory phrases attach to the right subject. In “Using regulatory analysis, the candidate was identified,” the candidate appears to perform the analysis. “Using regulatory analysis, we identified the candidate” makes the actor clear. [9]; [7].
Use a short phrase to identify an unfamiliar subject: “Brake, the candidate defence system, was tested in phage infections.” Once it is familiar, omit that reminder. Give longer explanations their own sentence and check that moving a qualifier preserves its meaning. [10].
Choose the subject that continues the paragraph’s topic. “We measured induction” attributes an action; a passive construction can keep attention on the sample or process. Read both in context. [3].


Connect sentences and comparisons
Connect each sentence to what the reader has just learned: after introducing the RNA-derived DNA, explain what that DNA encodes. In comparisons, parallel constructions put interventions and effects in corresponding positions, making differences easier to follow. Repeat the relevant terms rather than introducing synonyms that might suggest a different measurement or condition. [3]; [4, rule 4]; [10, pp. 217–218].



Example: choosing the focus of a comparison
In the Brake study, preventing protein production removes defence; expressing the protein separately restores it. Choose the subject that connects to the preceding sentence.


Continuing a discussion of defence


Intact Brake restricted phage propagation. Phage restriction was lost when translation of the Brake protein was blocked and restored when the protein was expressed separately.


Continuing a discussion of the genetic tests


We used two genetic tests to examine the Brake protein’s role. Blocking its translation removed phage restriction; expressing the protein separately restored restriction.



Words such as “however” and “therefore” signal a relationship that the sentences must also explain. Check what is being contrasted or what evidence supports the stated consequence; add the missing connection if necessary. [10, pp. 239–240].
Keep related findings together when one sentence makes their relationship clear. Split a sentence when competing points hide the subject or comparison. A short sentence can emphasize a conclusion; a longer one can keep a result beside its necessary qualification. [10, pp. 9–10]; [6].
Read aloud to find awkward phrases and ambiguous pronouns. Then read silently, checking the text against figures and equations. [6]; [9].


Keep terminology and notation stable
Use one term for each scientific concept. Distinguish measurements from inferred quantities, such as RNA abundance and regulatory activity. Agree on terminology with coauthors. [9]; [3].
Use past tense for completed procedures and observations, and present tense for interpretations or figure descriptions where appropriate. Check that tense changes reflect the intended meaning and the journal’s conventions. [9].
Define useful abbreviations on first use, including in the abstract and legends where readers may encounter them independently. Spell out terms used only once or twice unless the abbreviation is familiar. Likewise, name quantities before using symbols and define terms beside equations. For ratios, specify the numerator and denominator, including whether they are measurements or means. Check units, normalization and notation against the figures. [9].
Delete phrases such as “It is important to note that.” Replace vague results with the direction, comparison and relevant magnitude, including uncertainty where needed. [7]; [9]; [3].


Cut words without cutting meaning
Remove repeated caution but retain qualifications that affect the conclusion. Check that edits preserve the subject, comparison, scope and strength of the original statement. [9].



Example: replacing vague caution with a specific limit
The genetic tests establish a role for the Brake protein, but the study has not identified its molecular target.


Draft


The results suggest that the Brake protein may play a role in phage restriction, although further work is needed to understand the mechanism.


Revision


The translation and complementation experiments identify the Brake protein as the defence effector. Its molecular target remains unknown.

“May play a role” understates the genetic evidence. The uncertainty concerns the molecular target, so the revision places it there.


Word searches and readability scores can flag passages to inspect; read those passages before changing them. Studies relating writing features to citation counts do not establish which edits improve understanding. After an edit, check that readers can still identify the comparison and its limitations. [11].

title: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper
text:
Use coauthor feedback

Ask for the review the draft needs
Match the reader and request to the draft’s main problem. A knowledgeable collaborator can check the science; someone less familiar with the project can identify missing context. When the contribution is disputed, ask about the argument and missing evidence before requesting language edits. Once it is stable, ask readers to mark passages they reread and to summarize the contribution. [2]; [8]; [4].
Send one current version with those questions, a response date and a note identifying unfinished material. [4]; [2].


Working through comments
Read the comments together before accepting edits. Group comments about the same passage or claim, then identify what confused the reader. Their proposed wording may not solve the problem, but the confusion still needs attention. [4].
Discuss edits that change scientific meaning with the coauthors responsible for that work, using the sentence and its supporting figure. Ask why the change was proposed before choosing wording. For stylistic alternatives that mean the same thing, choose the version that fits the paragraph and agreed terminology. [2]; [9].
Maintain one working version with recoverable history. Assign an editor to integrate separate files, or agree ownership during simultaneous editing. Check surrounding definitions and transitions after substantial changes, and return unresolved scientific questions to the responsible coauthors. [9]; [2].
crumbs: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper

title: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper
text:
Resolving substantive disagreements
If coauthors disagree about a central conclusion, settle what the evidence supports before polishing that conclusion’s wording. Investigate possible analysis errors early and update any changed estimate in the figure, Results and abstract. Coauthors can continue work on unaffected sections. [14, rules 8–10]; [4, rules 9–10].
For a disputed control, state which explanations it would distinguish. An author may reasonably want to finish a paper with a narrower conclusion while another wants to pursue the larger mechanism. Agree first on what the existing evidence supports, then discuss whether the additional question belongs in this paper. Combining their preferred wording will not settle a disagreement about its scope. [15]; [4, rule 10].
Check whether the authors are answering different questions. An experiment can be technically successful yet leave the proposed mechanism unresolved. If disagreement remains, record the assumption or missing evidence that would settle it. [2]; [4, rule 10].

Check the revised paper against the original concern
Return to each concern with the revised passage and its evidence beside you. Check whether the change resolves the problem. If a claim has narrowed, read its other appearances; if an analysis has changed, verify every reported value derived from it. [9, tip 30]; [2].
Local repairs can leave an Introduction promising an abandoned conclusion, a Discussion relying on an old figure or a legend describing an earlier analysis. Read the complete revision for those consequences. [14, rules 8–9]; [4, rule 10]; [2].
crumbs: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper

title: Drafting, reviewing and revising a paper
text:
Finish and verify the manuscript

Check the final version as a connected document
Check the manuscript against figures, tables and analysis outputs. Verify numbers, units, group names, citations and cross-references. Inspect the rendered output even when citation and cross-reference tools maintain the links. [7]; [3]; [2].
Allow time for repository records, metadata corrections and coauthor approval. Check the journal’s submission requirements, then inspect the PDF and figures at their intended size for conversion errors. [9]; [8].


Decide when to stop revising
Continue revising while the contribution is unclear, support is missing or coauthors disagree about the interpretation. Once those issues are resolved, circulate the final version for approval. Use this reading to catch errors; return to structural editing if it reveals a problem with the argument, and leave equivalent wording choices settled. [2]; [8].

Before sending the final version

Can an unfamiliar reader summarize the contribution and follow the evidence supporting it?
Do paragraph purposes, transitions and figure references form a coherent sequence?
Have sentence edits preserved comparisons, terminology, scope and uncertainty?
Are substantive coauthor comments resolved in one agreed version?
Have numbers, units, citations, cross-references and supporting files been checked together?
Does the rendered manuscript satisfy the journal’s requirements and have final coauthor approval?

title: From thesis plan to finished text
text:
Choose the thesis scope and structure
A thesis explains the contribution of your research. Published papers may supply much of the material; the thesis also needs to explain how the projects relate and what their findings establish together.
Agree the local expectations.
Thesis format and length vary between countries, universities and programmes, and with supervisors’ expectations. Check the current requirements and look at recent accepted theses. Before substantial drafting, agree a provisional contents page and length with supervisors, including how much background and general discussion they expect. If you plan to include papers, check the conditions for doing so. [8].
Plan the length as well as the contents.
Check which components count toward the word limit. [7]. Agree provisional lengths for the chapters, allowing more space for those that need fuller explanation. Page counts are harder to compare because figures, spacing and appended papers affect them. Revisit the estimates after drafting a representative chapter.
Identify how the projects relate. For example, one may test an explanation suggested by another, or provide a method used in a later study. Projects can also examine different aspects of the same problem. An unfinished project can belong if its available findings contribute to the thesis; explain what those findings establish and what remains unresolved.
Develop the agreed contents into headings, figure and table titles, with notes about what each chapter will explain. [1, chs. 19–20, pp. 143–159].
Select a format that the programme permits.
Three useful starting patterns are:
A continuous monograph. An introduction establishes the problem, a literature review develops the background, and methods, results and discussion build one sustained account. The review may sit within the introduction, and results and discussion may be combined. This arrangement works when the studies are best understood as parts of one argument. [5].
A monograph organized around studies or themes. A general introduction and, where useful, shared methods precede several research chapters. Each chapter introduces its own question, explains its methods, presents findings and discusses them. A general discussion then brings the studies together. This is a useful option for several related projects, including work that has not become a paper. Whether that work is sufficient for the degree remains a local academic judgment.
An article-based, compilation or cumulative thesis. Papers form part of a larger account that explains their shared background, aims and combined contribution. Connecting chapters may surround the articles, or an integrative account may precede the collected papers. The arrangement and terminology vary, but the intellectual task is similar: explain how the studies fit together and what they establish beyond their individual conclusions. The integrating text needs its own critical argument, even when the papers are already published. [9].
Front matter usually includes the title, declarations, abstract and contents; references and appendices complete the document. Their required order, additional summaries and any separate impact statement are local choices or requirements. A hybrid structure can be sensible where permitted, but agree its logic before drafting.
Check which parts of published papers you may edit for the thesis. Where changes are permitted, adapt the opening to explain the paper’s place in the thesis, update references and remove repeated overview figures that add no new information. Shared methods can reduce repetition, but each chapter still needs enough context to understand its experiments and assess its findings. [1, ch. 20, pp. 155–157].
crumbs: 5  From thesis plan to finished text

title: From thesis plan to finished text
text:
State the thesis question and contribution.
Write a short statement of what the thesis investigates and what the completed work adds. If the projects do not answer one question, explain the topic or approach that connects them.
crumbs: 5  From thesis plan to finished text

title: From thesis plan to finished text
text:
Map the completed projects

Map the chapters.
Before drafting the general introduction, list each research chapter’s question, main finding and contribution to the thesis. Add the shared background and final synthesis. Check whether readers will understand why one project follows another and which findings the synthesis needs to compare.




Example: connecting three completed projects
In this fictional thesis, three projects examine whether brief heat pulses affect lateral-root emergence in young seedlings.









Chapter
Question or main finding
Role in the thesis




General introduction
Can brief heat exposure alter root branching during seedling development?
Introduce the biological question, relevant literature and the three approaches.


Project 1: greenhouse observations
Seedlings under an afternoon heat regime had fewer emerged lateral roots; primary-root length was similar between groups.
Establish the pattern. Because other greenhouse conditions also differed, Project 2 isolates heat exposure.


Project 2: controlled heat pulses
Heat pulses in sterile culture reduced lateral-root emergence without changing primary-root length.
Establish a heat-pulse effect under controlled conditions. Project 3 tests whether it depends on developmental timing.


Project 3: timing test
Early exposure reduced emergence; later exposure did not produce a comparable reduction. Each exposed group was compared with age-matched controls at the same interval after exposure.
Locate the stronger response in early development under the tested pulse regime. The molecular cause remains unresolved.


General synthesis
How do the controlled effect and timing result help interpret the greenhouse observations?
State the combined answer and distinguish the experimentally established effect from the explanation proposed for the greenhouse pattern.






Give chapters enough local context.

Put broad background and shared methods in a common chapter where the format permits. Give each research chapter a short introduction to its question and enough methodological context to interpret its results. Cross-reference the common account for detail. [1, ch. 20, pp. 155–156].
A schematic may need to appear again if readers use it to understand a new comparison. A general overview figure usually belongs in the introduction. Revisit the literature for paper-derived chapters: work published since submission may change how you interpret their findings.
crumbs: 5  From thesis plan to finished text

title: From thesis plan to finished text
text:
Develop the introduction and background
Write an introduction for the whole thesis.
Introduce the research area, explain the unresolved problem and state the thesis contribution early. Use the chapter map to select the background readers need before the first research chapter. Explain the scope of the work and finish with a brief account of how the chapters develop the answer. [2]; [3].
Draft a short introduction early to test the proposed structure. Keep collecting relevant literature and notes, then develop the full account once the research chapters are stable. [1, ch. 20, p. 157]. For project-level openings and literature transitions, see Titles, abstracts and introductions.
Introduction, background, motivation and significance
These are functions, not mandatory headings. Their order and emphasis depend on the work and the agreed format. [6].
Introduction: orient the reader. Establish the topic, question and route through the thesis. The opening may lead to a separate background chapter or incorporate the fuller literature review.
Background or literature review: establish the basis for the question. Explain the necessary concepts and critically compare what is known, disputed or missing. Include the breadth needed to understand the studies, while connecting each topic to a later question, design choice or interpretation.
Motivation or rationale: explain why the investigation matters. Explain why the question is worth answering and how your approach could help. Saying that little is known leaves the reader to work out why knowing more would be useful.
Aims, questions or hypotheses: specify the task. State what the thesis investigates and how the studies contribute. If a study tests a hypothesis, explain the prediction used to test it. Do not invent prior hypotheses for exploratory or resource-building work.
Contribution and significance: preview what the thesis adds. Name the new evidence, method, resource or understanding and why it matters. Keep this preview proportionate to the completed work; develop the interpretation in the discussion.
Impact: explain possible or demonstrated use. Identify who could use the work and how. Benefits may lie within research itself. Distinguish prospective uses from demonstrated effects, and place this account where it fits the thesis rather than assuming a separate statement is needed. [10].

Build the background around the thesis questions.
Work backward from the chapter map to select the background and arrange it so that the aims follow naturally. Comparing and synthesizing papers explains how to compare evidence and evaluate conflicting accounts.

For the fictional seedling thesis, introduce heat exposure and root development, then explain why lateral-root emergence and primary-root length are different outcomes. Review what is known about their dependence on developmental timing. Because conditions other than heat differed in the greenhouse, the second project tests heat exposure under controlled conditions. The third asks whether the response differs with the seedlings’ age. Together, the studies help identify which effect needs a mechanistic explanation. They may guide later experiments, but do not demonstrate improved crop performance.
crumbs: 5  From thesis plan to finished text

title: From thesis plan to finished text
section: Write the methods and results chapters
text:
Write the methods and results chapters
The principles in Methods, results and figure legends apply to theses too: describe what was done reproducibly, organize findings around questions and comparisons, report uncertainty, and keep prose, figures and legends consistent. A thesis gives these principles more room and may distribute them across several chapters.
Methods explain both how and why. Describe the procedures and analysis, including why you chose them and which assumptions or limitations affect the conclusions. Include validation or method development needed to show that a measurement can answer the research question. Common procedures can appear in a shared account; explain each study’s design and modifications in its own chapter. [11].
Results establish what the evidence shows. Introduce each question or comparison, present the finding and direct readers to its support. Include negative or inconclusive findings when they affect the answer. A thesis can accommodate fuller controls, validation and exploratory work than a short article, but each addition should serve the argument. Keep essential evidence in the main account and use appendices for supporting detail. Whether interpretation accompanies each result or follows in a separate discussion, make the distinction between observation and explanation clear.
crumbs: 5  From thesis plan to finished text

title: From thesis plan to finished text
text:
Bring the findings together
Begin the final synthesis with what the thesis establishes. Use the findings from different chapters to explain that answer: one study may test an explanation suggested by another, or show that a result depends on particular conditions. Discuss disagreements and explain which conclusions remain uncertain. A reader should finish with an understanding of the combined contribution, rather than another summary of each chapter.

Discussion, synthesis and implications
A research chapter’s discussion interprets that study; the general discussion asks what the whole thesis establishes. The functions below may form sections or recur within a discussion organized by theme. Use the detailed advice in Discussion and conclusions at both scales.

Overall answer: return to the thesis question. State what can now be concluded, including a partial answer where necessary. Use a brief summary of the decisive findings to support it.
Interpretation and synthesis: explain the relationships. Show whether studies reinforce, qualify or challenge one another. Differences between systems, measurements or conditions may explain an apparent conflict. A methodological chapter may enable a later result rather than provide another test of the same claim.
Comparison with the literature: locate the contribution. Explain how the combined findings change, extend or support existing understanding. Discuss relevant evidence that disagrees, and distinguish what your work establishes from explanations proposed by others. [12].
Limitations and alternatives: explain what remains uncertain. Identify conclusions that depend on an untested assumption or a measurement limitation, and discuss other explanations that still fit the findings. Consider weaknesses shared by the studies: repeating a result does not remove a bias present in every experiment.
Significance and implications: explain what follows. Develop the contribution previewed in the introduction. Separate a change in scientific understanding from a potential application, and state what further evidence the application would require.
Future work: choose the questions that follow. Select a few unresolved questions raised by the findings. For each, explain what the proposed experiment would help you learn.
For the fictional thesis, the central synthesis paragraph could read:



Example: a general-synthesis paragraph


Brief heat pulses reduced lateral-root emergence in sterile culture, with a stronger response to exposure early in seedling development. Primary-root length remained unchanged, suggesting that the treatment affected root branching rather than uniformly slowing root growth. These controlled experiments provide a possible explanation for the reduced emergence observed under the greenhouse heat regime, where other environmental conditions also varied. The timing result now directs attention to the developmental processes that make early seedlings more sensitive to heat exposure.

The synthesis starts with the controlled result, then uses it to interpret the greenhouse pattern. Its order differs from the chapter map because the paragraph is organized around the answer.


For a complex synthesis, use a table to compare what different projects establish about the same question, including conditions under which their findings differ.
The conclusion
A separate conclusion is useful after a substantial general discussion. State the overall contribution, its scope and the next question that follows from it. Develop detailed interpretations and present essential evidence in the preceding chapters. [4].
crumbs: 5  From thesis plan to finished text

title: From thesis plan to finished text
text:
Plan the route to submission
Work backward from the submission date.
List what already exists and what each unfinished chapter still needs. Working backward from submission, allow time for final checks and approvals, review of the complete draft, chapter revisions and any unfinished analysis or figures. Include permissions and declarations. Assign each task to a person and agree when it will be ready, leaving time for anyone whose work depends on it.
For work that may not finish, agree when to decide whether to continue and what you need to know to make that decision. Also agree what the thesis will contain if the work stops. You can then complete the document without leaving its scope dependent on an open-ended experiment.










Work item
Finished item
Dependency or decision




Revise the three research chapters
Complete chapter drafts with final figures and local methods
Supervisor comments returned before the general synthesis is revised


Integrate the heat-exposure findings
General-synthesis draft comparing the greenhouse, controlled-pulse and timing results
Research-chapter findings and interpretations settled sufficiently to compare them


Attempt the optional mechanistic follow-up
A reviewed result and analysis, if the measurement and controls support interpretation
At the agreed decision date, assess what has been learned, including negative or inconclusive findings, and decide whether to include the completed work or proceed without this follow-up


Prepare the submission copy
Rendered thesis, declarations, permissions and deposit files
Programme checks and committee review started early enough to finish before submission





Discuss what you would do if a critical step is delayed. You may need to narrow a claim, change the chapter order or revise the submission date. Agree the response with supervisors and update the affected chapters and schedule. [1, ch. 19, pp. 145–150].
Decide what to do with the last project.
When the last project has not yet become a paper, decide which deadline matters more. Write the paper first if competition, priority or a coauthor commitment requires rapid submission. Write the thesis chapter first if the thesis needs the fuller account and publication timing allows it. Reconsider the choice when the data, competition or graduation deadline changes. [1, ch. 20, pp. 157–159].
If the selected thesis format requires accepted publications, include that dependency in the submission plan. Finishing the prose cannot substitute for a publication requirement; discuss permitted alternatives early if acceptance is uncertain.
crumbs: 5  From thesis plan to finished text

title: From thesis plan to finished text
text:
Check the complete document
Read the general introduction, research-chapter openings and final synthesis together. They should name the same question or framework, assign each chapter a distinct role and state compatible conclusions. Then inspect the rendered thesis against the current programme requirements: chapter order, cross-references, references, figure and table numbering, declarations, permissions, acknowledgements and deposit files. Return to the map if this check exposes a chapter that promises or concludes something different.

Before submitting the thesis

Can a reader state the thesis question or framework, its contributions and their scope from the general introduction and final synthesis?
Have supervisors agreed the structure, background depth and provisional length within the current programme rules?
Does the background prepare the reader for the research questions, and are motivation, significance and potential impact explained without inflated promises?
Does every research chapter contribute a distinct finding, test or boundary to that answer?
Do article-derived chapters give readers the local context and method detail needed to assess them?
Does the final synthesis compare findings across projects instead of repeating chapter summaries?
Does the completion plan include analysis, review, administrative dependencies and a decision for each critical uncertainty?
Has the rendered document been checked against the current local submission requirements?

title: Explaining research to an audience
text:
Start with audience and purpose
The same study can call for very different explanations. A colleague may want to know whether a control distinguishes two mechanisms; someone outside the field may first need to understand why the result is surprising. Before preparing slides or writing a summary, decide who needs the explanation and what they should understand when it ends.
Find out who will attend and why. For an invited talk, ask the host which departments were invited and what the audience knows about your topic. A room of biologists is not necessarily one audience: some may know the biological problem but not your methods, while others know the methods but not the system. [1]; [3].
Purpose changes the explanation, too. A departmental seminar might introduce an unfamiliar discovery; a meeting with potential collaborators might need to show where their contribution could help solve an open problem. In the second setting, spend more time on the unresolved work and the help you are seeking. Write the intended outcome in one sentence before selecting material. [1].
With a mixed audience, everyone needs access to the question and main finding, even if only some listeners need the technical detail that follows. Introduce an unfamiliar concept when it becomes necessary to understand the next step. A long preliminary glossary asks listeners to remember terms before they know what the terms are for. [2]; [3].

title: Explaining research to an audience
section: Choose the message and the evidence
text:
Choose the message and the evidence
Before choosing results, try stating the main finding in a sentence. “Bacterial antiviral defence” names a subject; “Brake uses an RNA template to produce a gene encoding an antiviral protein” makes a claim the explanation can develop. A longer talk may need supporting messages for different parts of that finding, but they should still lead toward the central claim. [3].
That sentence gives you a test for each result: does it support the claim, or rule out a serious alternative? A colleague may need the control that separates two mechanisms, though not every preliminary experiment that led to it. Explain the comparison, measurement and distinguishing test whenever they determine what can be inferred. Procedural detail can wait for discussion or the accompanying paper. [1].
The harder decision may be what to leave out. An additional result that needs several new concepts yet adds little to the conclusion can wait for another occasion. A result that changes the conclusion belongs in the explanation, even if something else must be shortened. For an unfinished study, explain what the current result shows and what question it leaves open. [3]; [5].

title: Explaining research to an audience
text:
Organize the explanation
Begin with a question or observation listeners can understand, then give enough context to show what needs explaining. For unfamiliar work, that may mean introducing the biological process or experimental comparison before stating the finding. [2].
When the finding emerges through several tests, let each result answer a question and raise the next one. In Brake, identifying a coding sequence in the DNA does not by itself show that the encoded protein causes defence. The next question is whether defence survives when translation is blocked but DNA production continues. Framing that comparison before its result lets listeners see why the experiment matters. [4].
For a short update or an audience already familiar with the question, give the conclusion first and work through its support. Successive questions are more helpful when listeners need to see how a mechanism was resolved. In either order, the reasoning should determine the sequence; the dates on which experiments were performed need not. [1]; [4].
Some relationships are easier to follow when they can be seen. If listeners must keep track of several intermediates or transformations, a simple schematic can show how one leads to another. Introduce its objects and arrows while explaining them, using the same names in speech and in the diagram. Specialized displays and explanatory diagrams covers its design. [6]; [7].
Return to the opening question at the end. Give the answer and explain what remains unresolved. If the audience is interested in an application, say what would still need to be tested before the result could be used that way. [1].

title: Explaining research to an audience
text:
Adapt detail and language
Explain an unfamiliar technical term when you introduce it: “the enzyme that copies RNA into DNA, a reverse transcriptase.” Specialists can usually start with “reverse transcriptase.” Then use the same name throughout, so listeners do not have to work out whether different labels refer to the same thing. [1]; [2].
Vocabulary is only one part of the adjustment. Researchers studying bacterial defence may need the construct comparison and the timing of DNA production. Biologists outside that field may first need to know why producing a gene from RNA is the finding. Both still need the experiment that supports the conclusion. The two explanations below use the fictional Brake study, inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [8].



Example: explaining the finding to two audiences


For researchers studying bacterial defence


Brake posed a puzzle. Its locus has a reverse transcriptase and a conserved RNA template, but no conventional effector gene. The DNA product contains repeated units, with a coding sequence spanning their junctions. We detect single-stranded DNA before infection; during infection, we also detect the double-stranded product and the Brake protein.
But is the protein responsible for defence? In a translation-disrupted construct, DNA production continues, yet growth arrest and restriction of phage A disappear. Expressing the protein separately restores both. That supports an RNA-templated route to a protein effector; it does not identify the protein’s molecular target. Brake also restricts phage B, while phage C remains productive.


For biologists outside the field

Some bacteria use proteins to restrict viruses called phages. Brake was puzzling because we could not find a conventional gene for its defence protein. Instead, it copies an RNA template into DNA that carries the instructions for that protein.
Was making the DNA enough for defence, or did the system also need the protein? We blocked production of the protein, but the DNA was still made. The bacteria no longer stopped growing, and phage A multiplied again. Supplying the protein separately restored growth arrest and restricted phage multiplication. So Brake builds a functional defence gene from RNA. It restricted two of the three phages we tested; the third still multiplied. We do not yet know what the protein acts on.


The specialist version can name the DNA intermediates, coding junctions and construct comparison because its listeners can use those details. The broader version asks whether DNA production alone is enough, then gives the same decisive comparison in ordinary language.


An analogy can help listeners grasp an unfamiliar relationship, provided the correspondence is clear: which part of the familiar example stands for which object or process? Keep it brief, then return to the actual system for the evidence. If the analogy implies intention or a mechanism the study has not established, use another explanation. [2, pp. 83–92]; [5].

title: Explaining research to an audience
text:
Test and refine the explanation
Try the explanation with someone whose background resembles the intended audience’s. Ask them to summarize the finding and explain how the main experiment supports it. Where did they need more background, or lose the connection between results? [1]; [2].
Their response tells you what to revise. Someone who knows the terms but cannot explain why the result supports the conclusion needs a clearer comparison or transition. Someone who cannot follow the comparison may need a concept introduced earlier. If the main point disappears among details, remove a secondary result and try again.
Use a short outline to plan the explanation or review its order. The outline below connects the broader Brake version’s question, evidence and answer before any slides are designed.



Example: an explanation outline for a biology seminar

Purpose: explain how an RNA template can supply an antiviral gene to biologists unfamiliar with this defence pathway.

The puzzle: Brake restricts phage propagation, yet its annotated region has no conventional effector gene. Introduce the reverse transcriptase and adjacent RNA template as the clues to where a gene might come from.
Where the gene comes from: show how repeated DNA contains a coding sequence. Connect the template and junction analysis to the observations of DNA and protein production.
What causes defence: compare intact Brake with the translation-disrupted construct. The continued production of DNA makes the loss of defence informative; separate protein expression then restores growth arrest and restriction.
What this establishes: the RNA template supplies a gene encoding the defence protein. Close with the tested phage range and the protein’s unresolved molecular target.



Keep more detailed results available for questions about the experiments in the outline.

title: Explaining research to an audience
text:
References

LeFever, L. (2012). The Art of Explanation: Making Your Ideas, Products, and Services Easier to Understand. Wiley.

title: Designing a presentation
text:
Plan the sequence
Before polishing individual slides, arrange the questions and results into a sequence your audience can follow. Work out what listeners need to understand before each experiment appears.
Write a short sentence for each main point and place the supporting results beneath it. Arrange these groups so that each result answers a question the audience already understands. Add the background and experimental design needed to interpret it. A research talk will often move from the biological problem through a few connected questions to the answer and its implications. A lab meeting about a proposed experiment may instead compare designs and end with a decision for discussion. [1]; [2].
Sketch each slide with a proposed title, its figure or diagram, and a note about what you will say. Paper, a whiteboard or an unformatted slide list all work. Then read the titles in order. If one finding does not lead clearly to the next question, add the missing explanation or rearrange the slides before working on their layout. [4, pp. 26–40].
The following four-slide sequence uses the fictional Brake study. It introduces the unfamiliar route before asking listeners to interpret the decisive experiments.
Decide which details belong in the main talk and which can be reserved for questions. A control that distinguishes two explanations belongs with the result it supports; an extended protocol can usually wait unless the method itself is under discussion. End with the answer to the opening question and its significance. Keep this conclusion visible during questions, with acknowledgments on the preceding slide or alongside it. [1]; [3, Rules 4–5].
Allow more time for an unfamiliar experiment than for a short transition. A fixed slides-per-minute target is unreliable when some slides build a diagram and others contain several comparisons. Determine the length by rehearsing the explanation aloud. [5]; [1].

title: Designing a presentation
text:
Example: a connected four-slide storyboard


Slide 1: Brake restricts phage propagation although no effector gene is annotated
On screen: A compact locus diagram labels the reverse transcriptase and RNA template; the missing conventional effector is marked as the puzzle.
Spoken transition: “If there is no ordinary effector gene, how does this system restrict phage propagation?”


Slide 2: The RNA template is copied into DNA that encodes a protein
On screen: Introduce the RNA template, then add the single-stranded DNA detected before infection, followed by the double-stranded DNA and protein detected during infection. Keep earlier elements visible and label when each product was observed.
Spoken transition: “This gives us a possible route to defence. Does defence depend on the enzyme that makes this DNA?”


Slide 3: Brake reduces infectious phage yield, and reverse transcription is required
On screen: Show the three-condition culture plot at readable size: empty vector, intact Brake and inactive reverse transcriptase, with matched days retained.
Spoken transition: “Reverse transcription is necessary. Next, we need to test the protein’s role while leaving DNA production intact.”


Slide 4: The encoded protein is required for defence
On screen: Show that disrupting translation leaves DNA production intact but loses defence, and that expressing the protein separately restores defence. Conclude that the protein is required for defence; its molecular target remains unknown.
Spoken transition: “So Brake uses an RNA template to make the gene for a defence protein. The genetic tests establish the protein’s role, but we still do not know its molecular target.”

The third slide can use the quantitative plot below. The fourth needs the translation-disruption and restoration results: the three-condition culture plot alone cannot establish the protein’s role.

title: Designing a presentation
section: Give each slide a clear message
text:
Give each slide a clear message
Use the title to state the finding or question. “Brake reduces the yield of infectious phage A” tells listeners what to look for; “Phage restriction assay” names only the experiment. A question works well when the slide introduces a test or asks colleagues to consider an unresolved choice. Keep the title short enough to read at a glance and specific enough to describe the evidence below it. [3, Rule 3]; [2].
Choose one main message for the slide, then include the comparisons needed to establish it. This may require two related plots, an image and its quantification, or a schematic beside the result. If the slide contains several independent conclusions, split it. Keep plots together when listeners need to compare them directly. [3, Rules 1 and 5].
Write the spoken explanation in your notes. On the slide, retain the title, labels and brief annotations that help people interpret the visual. Replace a paragraph describing an experimental sequence with a diagram when the sequence is easier to see than to read. Short text can still be the best choice for a definition, a question or a small set of alternatives; a decorative image adds little. [3, Rules 6 and 8]; [4].

title: Designing a presentation
text:
Adapt figures for live viewing
Prepare a presentation version of a manuscript figure. Select the relevant panels, enlarge the labels and place brief explanations beside the features you will discuss. Keep the units, controls, observations and uncertainty needed to assess the claim. If these cannot fit legibly, spread the explanation across slides rather than shrinking the complete publication figure. [2]; [4, pp. 64–77].
For an unfamiliar assay or display, first explain the experimental comparison and how to read the result. A small schematic or an illustration of the expected patterns can help. Distinguish predictions from measurements. For a familiar plot, a brief spoken orientation to the conditions and axes may be enough. [2].
The following slides use the fictional Brake study, inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [6]. Brake is a bacterial defence system containing a reverse transcriptase. The experiment compares the infectious yield of phage A from cultures carrying an empty vector, intact Brake or Brake with an inactive reverse transcriptase.



Example: turning a manuscript result into a slide



A draft slide with a method-based title, a small three-condition graph and a manuscript-style explanation beside it.






The revised slide enlarges the same observations and states the finding in the title. The annotation reports a 79-fold reduction in infectious phage A yield versus empty vector (95% CI: 55–116 fold).


Both slides retain all observations, day matching and the inactive-enzyme control. The revised slide gives more space to the comparison and replaces the paragraph with labels. The presenter can explain how the cultures were assayed while listeners inspect the result. The control remains visible, although the numerical estimate refers specifically to Brake versus empty vector.
Original teaching figure; all plotted values are illustrative.


Highlight the condition or region you are discussing while keeping the other evidence visible. Across slides, preserve condition colors, axis limits and plot positions when viewers need to compare results. If a scale changes, make the change explicit. [4, pp. 70–75].

title: Designing a presentation
text:
Make the slide readable
Build a simple layout with a consistent title position, generous margins and aligned visual elements. Put labels next to what they describe and separate unrelated groups with space. Give the central figure most of the slide rather than squeezing it between a large institutional banner and a long caption. [4, pp. 92–110].
Check the smallest essential label at the size and distance the audience will see it. A graph that is readable on your laptop may fail on a projector or in a shared screen. Increase the figure and its labels together; enlarging the title alone does not help. If the slide is still crowded, remove a secondary point or split the explanation. [3, Rules 6–7].
Use strong text–background contrast and consistent sizes for titles, labels and annotations. Pair color with labels, symbols or line styles so that viewers can distinguish conditions with poor projection or differences in color vision. Avoid placing text directly over a photograph; put it on a solid background if the image interferes with reading. For ways to distinguish groups without relying on color alone, see Color, symbols and accessibility. [3, Rule 7].

title: Designing a presentation
section: Use builds and prepare the shared version
text:
Use builds and prepare the shared version
Reveal a complex diagram in stages when you need to explain its parts in sequence. Keep the existing elements in place as new ones appear. A few duplicate slides with additional labels or arrows are often easier to edit and export than a complicated animation. Check every copy after a revision so that an old label or value does not reappear. For a comparison that requires simultaneous inspection, show both alternatives together. [3, Rule 1]; [4, pp. 180–191].
Use video or animation when motion, timing or a change in state is part of the explanation. Plan where to pause and what to point out. Keep a still image or short sequence that supports the explanation if playback fails, and test the exported deck as well as the editable file. [3, Rule 10].
Credit published figures and ideas on the slide where they appear, and identify collaborators’ contributions. A compact author–year reference can point to full details in the notes or reference slides; retain any required image credit. For unpublished work, agree with collaborators what can be shown and shared. [3, Rule 4].
If people will read the deck afterward, add the explanations they would otherwise hear from you in notes or a companion document. Check that the shared file includes those notes or explanations, and that diagrams revealed in stages can still be followed in the exported format. [5]; [3, Rules 8 and 10].
Before rehearsal, review the sequence in slide-sorter view. Then display the slides at presentation size to check small labels and crowded figures.

title: Delivering a talk and answering questions
text:
Rehearse and revise
Rehearse the complete talk aloud while it is still easy to change. Listen for awkward wording and results whose explanation takes longer than expected. Where the move from one result to the next feels abrupt, check whether you have explained the question the next experiment answers. Revise the transition or reorder the material before trying another run. [3].
Time the complete talk, including the opening, transitions and close. If the run reaches the end of the allotted slot, remove a secondary result, shorten a detour or move a detail to material for discussion. Keep the comparison that makes the central claim credible, and leave the agreed time for questions. [2].
Mark a few timing checkpoints in your notes, and decide which slides you can skip if questions or interruptions use the spare time. Use a visible timer during the talk. If you fall behind, move to the prepared shorter version and preserve the conclusion. [1, p. 10].
Rehearse the shorter version, including what you will say between the slides that remain. Skipping a result may leave a later reference or explanation without its context.
Practice the beginning and end until you can deliver them without searching for the next sentence. They need not be memorized verbatim. The opening can introduce the question and help listeners follow the first result; the close can state the answer and what remains unresolved. If possible, rehearse with someone outside the immediate project, who is less likely to fill in missing explanations from memory. Ask what they took to be the main claim, which comparison supported it and where they lost the thread. [4].
Record one run if you can. Check whether you rush through transitions or spend long stretches speaking to the screen. Notice whether a repeated movement distracts from what you are explaining. Choose a specific change to try in the next run. [3].
crumbs: Delivering a talk and answering questions

title: Delivering a talk and answering questions
text:
Rehearsal tool: revise after each complete run









Run
Observe
Revise before the next run




First complete aloud run
Where did a sentence become hard to say or a transition sound like a jump?
Rewrite the spoken link; state the question that the next result answers.


Timed run
Which material puts the close or discussion period at risk?
Cut a supporting detour or reserve it for a question; do not compress the decisive comparison.


Listener run
Can a colleague outside the immediate project identify the claim and explain the key comparison?
Add the missing premise or replace a term that obscures the comparison.


Recovery run
After a planned interruption, can the shorter route still reach the conclusion without dropping its decisive control?
Skip a named secondary result and rehearse the bridging sentence into the next essential comparison.


Delivery check
Can you speak to the displayed evidence without relying on a moving pointer or an unreadable note?
Add a label or annotation, and simplify the spoken cue.
crumbs: Delivering a talk and answering questions

title: Delivering a talk and answering questions
text:
Explaining figures aloud
Before explaining a dense figure, tell the audience what to look at. Describe the observation and what you conclude from it, then introduce the next question: “This shows that the DNA is made. The remaining question is whether its encoded protein causes defence.” [3].
Give listeners time to read unfamiliar axes and locate the groups being compared before explaining the result. A pause after the display appears can help. Speak clearly enough for the room or call, at a volume you can sustain. If nerves make you rush, pause at the next transition and take a breath before continuing.
Use a pointer briefly to identify a feature, then hold it still or switch it off. Put essential arrows, labels or staged annotations in the displayed material so the explanation still works without it. Explain the visual material in the order in which you want it inspected, then turn back to the listeners. [3]; [2].
crumbs: Delivering a talk and answering questions

title: Delivering a talk and answering questions
text:
Room, equipment and remote setup
Before an in-person talk, check the room’s display and audio, or ask the host what is available. Confirm how your computer connects and whether you need an adapter. Open the deck you will use and check that the figures are legible from the audience’s seats. Test the slide controls, bring a backup copy and decide how you will continue if the pointer or clicker fails. Confirm whether questions will come during or after the talk and how much time is reserved for them. [3].
For a remote talk, test screen sharing, microphone and camera in the meeting software. Check what a participant can see and hear, and how you would reconnect if the connection drops. Ask the host about captions and question handling. Tell listeners whether to use chat or speak when both are available.
Keep additional slides ready for likely questions, such as a control or methods detail omitted from the main talk. Practice finding them and returning to the slide where you left off. [3].
crumbs: Delivering a talk and answering questions

title: Delivering a talk and answering questions
text:
Answering questions
Let the question finish. If its target is unclear, ask a short clarification or repeat the part you will answer: “Are you asking whether the protein, rather than the DNA intermediate, accounts for phage restriction?” Repeating the question lets the room hear it and gives you a moment to formulate the response. Then answer that part first, using the relevant comparison. [3].
If you do not know the answer, say so. Explain what the study can establish about the question and, when useful, suggest how the unresolved point could be tested. If a challenge reveals a limitation, acknowledge it and explain how it affects the conclusion. If it rests on a false premise, correct that premise before answering. When repeated interruptions prevent you from continuing, ask the chair to help or suggest returning to the discussion in the question period. [1, pp. 11–12].
When a question requires a separate conversation, say so and offer to continue after the session. If the chair closes the discussion, stop. [2].
The fictional Brake study below is inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [5].


Example: a focused answer to a mechanistic challenge
Question: “If the translation-disrupted Brake construct still makes the DNA intermediate, how do you know the DNA does not itself cause phage restriction?”
Answer: “The DNA could still contribute, but this experiment shows that it is not sufficient. When we block translation, the DNA is still produced, yet growth arrest and phage restriction disappear. Supplying the protein separately restores both. That is why we interpret the defence as protein-mediated.”

title: Posters
text:
Choose the content
A poster is read in fragments. Someone may notice the title while walking past, approach the central result, ask a question, then leave with a contact or a link.
Decide what you want to discuss: a finding, an unresolved problem or a possible collaboration. Choose content for the people you expect to meet. A poster that will also circulate afterward needs enough explanation to be read without you. [1].
Write the main finding as a sentence, then choose the evidence readers need to assess it. Give the decisive comparison the largest area. Include enough background to explain the question and enough methods to interpret the result. Put secondary analyses and procedural detail in a handout or linked material unless they are needed to evaluate the central finding. [2, pp. 2–3]; [3].
Identify the presenter, affiliation and contact details. Place them where they are easy to find but do not displace the claim or evidence. [2, pp. 4, 6].
Adapt manuscript figures for the poster: select the relevant panels, enlarge labels and annotate the key comparison. Retain the controls and uncertainty needed to interpret the result. [3].

title: Posters
text:
Arrange the poster
Sketch the reading order before refining fonts or colors. Make the main finding prominent, place related text and figures together, and separate sections with whitespace. Align blocks along a few consistent edges. Use headings or numbers where the sequence would otherwise be unclear. [2, pp. 3–4]; [3].
The fictional Brake study below is inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [5].

Example: a focused poster portion






Figure 1: This focused poster portion gives most of its space to the quantitative restriction result, then uses a compact test strip to separate the DNA intermediate from the encoded protein. Original teaching figure.




The quantitative result occupies the largest region. The smaller translation test answers the next mechanistic question without competing with the main plot.
When several results need to be compared, place their evidence blocks beside one another and give each a heading that states its local finding.
Use headings that state the finding where possible: “Translation is required for phage restriction” tells a visitor more than “Results.” Use consistent type sizes for headings and body text, and align related blocks. Color can reinforce a grouping or emphasis, but readers should also be able to identify conditions from labels or symbols. [3]; [2, p. 5].

title: Posters
text:
Print and digital readability
Check the conference specification before committing to orientation, dimensions, logos, file format or display method. For a conventional A0 print poster, make an early A4 reduction and read it at normal page distance; then inspect the full-size poster in the expected light from roughly 0.5 to 1.5 metres. In both checks, the title, headings, axes, annotations and contact details must be legible. Use the production and export checks in Preparing figures for publication. [2, pp. 2, 6]; [3].
For a digital poster, keep an overview visible so visitors can identify the topic and main finding even if they arrive halfway through an animation or explanation. Check which interactive features the conference platform supports and whether visitors can operate them. An animation can explain a process; a zoomable image can reveal detail. Neither helps if visitors cannot find the comparison or return to the overview. [4].

title: Posters
text:
Use the poster in conversation
Prepare a short orientation: the question, the finding and the decisive evidence. Give it when someone asks what the poster is about, then pause. For the model above: “Brake restricts phage propagation, but its locus has no conventional effector gene. The large plot compares intact Brake with an empty vector and an inactive reverse transcriptase. Infectious phage yield is much lower with intact Brake than with either control. Is the protein encoded by Brake’s DNA needed for defence? We blocked protein production but still detected the DNA. Growth arrest and phage restriction disappeared, and both returned when we supplied the protein separately.” Their next question tells you whether to clarify the method, discuss a limitation or offer deeper material. [1]; [2, p. 3].
Rehearse with the poster in front of you. For a visitor unfamiliar with the study, start at the question; for a specialist, start at the finding. Point to the relevant evidence as you discuss it. If the conversation becomes lengthy, invite others to join or arrange to continue later. [2, p. 3]. See Delivering a talk and answering questions for rehearsal and difficult questions.

title: Elevator pitches and chalk talks
text:
Elevator pitches
A short pitch introduces your research and invites a conversation. In a chalk talk, you explain a proposed research program while the audience questions its plans and experiments.
Think about what you would like to discuss with this person. If you want advice on a difficult experiment, introduce the problem and explain where you are stuck. If you hope to collaborate, explain how your work connects with theirs. [2].
Start with the scientific question or finding. Introduce your role first if it helps the listener understand the connection. Give enough evidence to make the point credible, then leave room for a reply. You can explain the methods or discuss further results if they ask.
Follow the listener’s questions: they may want more technical detail or need some background first. When rehearsing, ask your partner to explain what they understood and what they thought you were asking for. Revise where their account differs from yours. [2].
The fictional Brake study is inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [5].
Rehearse the pitch with these questions:

title: Elevator pitches and chalk talks
text:
Example: a pitch that opens a specialist conversation

“You work on bacterial defence, so can I run a strange result past you? Brake has no conventional effector gene. Instead, an RNA template supplies DNA that encodes an antiviral protein. When we block translation, the DNA remains but phage restriction disappears; supplying the protein separately restores it. Have you seen infection-linked DNA intermediates play a similar role in other systems?”










Check
Revision when the answer is no




Could this listener repeat the question or contribution without my field’s shorthand?
Replace one term with its role in the problem, or supply the missing premise.


Is the evidence enough to make the stated point credible?
Add the decisive comparison; remove a less informative detail.


Does the final sentence give the listener a natural way to respond?
Ask a focused question or name the conversation you would like to have.

title: Elevator pitches and chalk talks
text:
Chalk talks
A chalk talk usually presents a proposed research program through an interactive discussion of its questions and experiments. Ask the host about the audience, duration, use of boards or slides, and expected level of detail. Prepare to explain both the first experiments and what you would do with different outcomes. [1]; [3].
Begin with the overall question in terms a scientist outside your field can understand. Sketch the projects before questions take the discussion into detail, then start with the most important one. Explain who would begin the work and when, including which projects can run in parallel. [4]; [3].
For each project, explain the question and the experiment that could answer it. Discuss what different results would lead you to do next and what resources you need to begin. Show how the program develops your own questions, identifying which work you will lead and which depends on continuing collaborations. [1].
Keep an outline of the program in view as questions arrive. Write the project questions and their connections where everyone can refer to them; explain the details aloud. If a question exposes a flaw, address it and revise the plan when warranted. If discussion moves away from the program, offer to return to that question later and continue with the next project. [3]; [4].



Example: a spatial program map for the board

This hypothetical program asks whether a previous inflammatory exposure changes epithelial responses to a later injury. Keep the program question across the top of the board, then place the first two projects side by side because they can begin independently.

How does resolved inflammation change the next epithelial injury response?








Left board — Project 1, starts in year 1
Right board — Project 2, months 9–24




Retained state or changed cell mixture?
Does exposure history change repair?


After the cue is removed, compare exposed and control airway organoids. Measure cell composition, expression and accessibility.
Re-injure matched organoids. Measure barrier repair and inflammatory output.


Branch: if no retained difference appears, narrow the proposed scope and decide whether another exposure condition tests a distinct, justified question.
Branch: if no functional difference appears, do not call the earlier molecular pattern a memory response; ask what narrower biological conclusion the result supports.




↓ Continue only if the first projects establish a reproducible functional difference

Project 3 — What sustains that difference? Months 18–36, if warranted. Nominate candidates from Projects 1 and 2, perturb a candidate and repeat the injury-response test.
Board margin: residual cue? transferable factor? changed cell composition? Write these confounds where the room can return to them. Keep access to primary cultures, the cue-clearance assay and single-cell measurements beside the project that needs each resource.


Keep the top question and the two parallel projects visible while sketching detailed comparisons below them. Discuss staffing and access alongside the experiment that depends on each resource. The conditional third project should be physically downstream, so the board does not imply that a mechanism will be pursued regardless of the first results. A clear overview matters because questions may interrupt before every experiment has been discussed. [4]; [3].


Example: respond by sharpening the program
Question: “How will you tell a cell-state change from residual cue or a different mixture of epithelial cells?”
Response: “I would first measure the residual stimulus with an assay sensitive below the concentration that affects these cells. Transferring conditioned medium to untreated cultures would test for a soluble factor, whether residual stimulus or a new secretion. We would also compare the same cell types using lineage and single-cell measurements. A difference that remains would justify testing for a persistent cell state; the re-injury experiments would establish whether the exposure history changes function.”



Rehearse with interruptions
Run a mock session with close scientific colleagues and people less familiar with the topic. Ask them to interrupt and challenge your reasoning, including whether the work is feasible and distinct from your former supervisor’s program. Check that they can read the board from their seats. Afterward, identify where they lost track of the program. Revise experiments that could not distinguish the proposed explanations, and be ready to explain how you would obtain the equipment or expertise they need. [1]; [4].
Prepare more experimental detail than you expect to present. In a quiet session, use it to develop a comparison or discuss alternatives. In a lively session, return to the overview between exchanges so that questions about one project do not consume the whole talk.
