title: Choosing an opportunity and planning the application
text:
Eligibility and fit
Before drafting an application, check whether you can apply and whether the funder supports the work you want to do. Prepare an initial budget to see whether the available funding would cover it [2, pp. 883–884].
Start with a short list of plausible opportunities. Your institution’s research office, colleagues and funders’ previous awards can help you find schemes that support similar work. Read the current call before using a colleague’s successful application as a model: the scheme’s scope or requirements may have changed. Previous awards cannot tell you how likely your application is to succeed [2, p. 883].
Check eligibility. Read the current call’s requirements for applicants, host institutions and partners. If a condition is unclear, ask your research office or the funder’s contact and keep their answer with the application instructions.
Read what the funder wants to support. A fellowship may place substantial weight on your training, while a pilot grant may support testing whether a method works. Explain how your proposed work meets that purpose. Where the funder welcomes enquiries, send a brief project description and ask about the point you are unsure of [2, p. 883]; [1, pp. 161–165].
crumbs: Choosing an opportunity and planning the application

title: Choosing an opportunity and planning the application
text:
Application requirements
Read the application instructions and assessment criteria together. Check where the application asks you to address each criterion and how it will be weighted [2, p. 883].
List the required documents and portal fields, who will prepare them and when they are needed. Record the applicable length limits and use the supplied templates from the start. Allow time for another person to approve a letter or support statement before its due date. Check whether portal registration or institutional authorization must be arranged before submission; finishing the text may not be the last step.
Clarify questions that could change the proposed work before drafting in detail. For example, if institutional costs count towards the award limit, less money remains for the experiments. If a partner has not agreed to provide samples, you cannot yet rely on that access. Ask the funder or research office about an unclear rule, and the partner about their commitment. Check for official amendments to the instructions during preparation [2, p. 884].
crumbs: Choosing an opportunity and planning the application

title: Choosing an opportunity and planning the application
text:
Preparing a budget
Start with the work you propose to do. Estimate the staff time and materials needed, and ask facilities or service providers for quotes. If you plan to use existing equipment, check that time on it is available and include any running charges. Note what the institution or partners have agreed to provide.
Work with your finance or grants office to check which costs the funder allows. They can also establish whether institutional overheads count towards the funding limit. Direct costs pay for the project itself; indirect costs cover shared support, such as administration and building services. Include the applicable charges before deciding whether the project is affordable [2, p. 884]; [1, pp. 168–169].
Check whether the requested funding and confirmed contributions cover the work. If essential costs exceed that support, reduce the scope, secure an agreed contribution or choose another opportunity. Removing a necessary cost from the budget leaves the work unfunded. Request what the project needs, even if it is below the maximum award. Eisenstadter advises examining a foundation’s usual award scale and explaining each expense; her observations concern smaller foundations and do not establish that cheaper proposals generally win [3, p. 154].
The following fictional case concerns a researcher who wants to use spatial RNA profiling in plant tissue. A usable preservation and processing workflow has not yet been established; no pilot measurements or biological findings are available. Both opportunities and all limits below are invented for the example.



Opportunity decision: establish the workflow first
Chosen opportunity: A nine-month methods pilot with a maximum total request of €35,000.

Scientific fit: The pilot supports establishing a workflow and deciding whether it can support the planned biological study. It does not require us to promise the larger seasonal comparison within nine months.
Information checked: The research office confirmed applicant and host eligibility, the institutional submission route and that service charges are permitted. The facility supplied a quote and indicated capacity conditional on an award. Finance estimates €29,000 for staff time, services, consumables and the permitted institutional charge. That total includes €3,000 of institutional costs within the €35,000 cap. Existing space and equipment are institutionally supported; no equipment purchase is requested.
Alternative: A two-year biological project could fund a seasonal comparison, with a maximum total request of €180,000. It is also eligible and relevant. However, access to external seasonal material remains unresolved, and the workflow is untested. We cannot yet show how we would obtain and process the samples needed for that comparison.
Decision: Prepare the pilot application. Reconsider the larger study once sample access is agreed and we have evidence that the workflow can support the seasonal comparison.
Condition for reconsideration: If the facility cannot provide the required service within the proposed period, or revised costs leave essential work unfunded, revisit the pilot’s scope or choose another opportunity before completing the application.


The pilot proposal still needs to specify how the workflow will be assessed and what different results would mean for its use in the biological study.
crumbs: Choosing an opportunity and planning the application

title: Choosing an opportunity and planning the application
text:
Contributors and reviewers
Identify who will lead the proposal, who will supply scientific or technical contributions, who will cost it and who is authorized to submit it. Agree what each person will provide and when. Confirm what help the research office offers; support may include interpretation of the scheme, budget checks, editing or submission, and it differs between institutions. If no such office is available, identify experienced colleagues and the person who can authorize the application rather than assume those tasks will happen [2, p. 884].
Ask each partner what they will contribute and whether they can provide it during the proposed project. If a collaborator will supply samples or run an assay, agree the work and timing before describing that support in the application. Use collaboration, authorship and credit to agree scientific responsibilities and credit.
Invite readers before you need the review. A reader familiar with the method can examine feasibility and missing controls; someone outside the immediate field can test whether the question, rationale and contribution are understandable. Give them the call’s criteria and ask for specific criticism, with an agreed return date. Send a complete draft early enough to discuss a major objection and revise the science or scope [3, pp. 153–154].
crumbs: Choosing an opportunity and planning the application

title: Choosing an opportunity and planning the application
text:
Scheduling and submission
Begin with the institution’s internal deadline and the funder’s cutoff, including the specified time zone and who must complete each submission step. Work backwards: when must the package be ready for authorization, the costs agreed and reviewers’ comments returned? Set the drafting schedule around those dates. Request quotes and support statements early enough for the people supplying them to respond. Scientific writing and costing can proceed in parallel; send changes in the proposed work to the person preparing the budget.
Choose lead times from the work and people involved. Eisenstadter suggests that two months before a deadline may not be too early to finish a draft for review, and allowing a week or two away from it can expose buried information. The institutional committee example in Making the Right Moves also begins at least two months before its NIH deadline. These illustrate room for thinking and revision; they are not a universal timetable [3, pp. 153–154]; [1, p. 161].
If time is short, check whether the necessary access, review and authorization can still be arranged. A smaller proposal may be possible if it answers a worthwhile question with resources already available. But if cutting the work removes the experiment needed to answer that question, consider a later round. Waiting delays the research and may mean missing this opportunity; weigh that cost against submitting a project that no longer answers the question or still lacks essential support.
The fictional pilot applicant has seven weeks until the funder cutoff. The research office requires the final package five working days earlier and has agreed to begin checks before then. The applicant and contributors agree the following plan; its future tasks have not yet been completed.



Application plan: review before authorization
Seven weeks before cutoff — choose and assign. The applicant records the eligibility and fit checks above, confirms the current instructions with the research office and invites two readers. The facility and finance contact agree dates for support text and final costing.

Five weeks before — make the proposal assessable. The applicant completes a scientific outline and first full account of the workflow work, including how its performance will be assessed. Finance prepares the initial budget; the applicant sends draft access and support statements to their owners.
Four weeks before — obtain scientific review. A methods reader examines measurement, feasibility and risks. A colleague outside the immediate field reads for purpose and rationale against the pilot’s criteria. Both return comments within the agreed week; the applicant discusses substantial objections with them.
Three weeks before — reconcile revisions and support. The applicant resolves comments, revises scope where needed and sends changes to finance and the facility. Final costing and support text are agreed against the revised work.
Two weeks before — assemble for institutional checks. The applicant provides the narrative, budget, applicant information and required support documents to the research office. The office checks the assembled package and requests corrections before its internal deadline.
At least five working days before — complete authorization. The applicant delivers the corrected final package. The research office completes the required authorization and confirms who will submit.
Target three working days before — submit and confirm. The authorized submitter sends the application through the specified system. The applicant and submitter check validation messages and receipt, resolve correctable problems before cutoff, and retain the submitted version and confirmation.


Before submission, reconcile the assembled application with its commitments. The narrative, budget and support documents should describe the same scope, people and access. Inspect the generated application or entered fields where the system makes them available: an uploaded file does not establish that every required component has been accepted. Confirm receipt through the applicable system rather than treating a saved draft as a submission.
Retain the submitted version, its costing and the instructions used. Consider how you would proceed if funding were declined or delayed.
crumbs: Choosing an opportunity and planning the application

text:

title: Writing the proposal
text:
Research question and significance
A proposal explains why a question is worth pursuing and how you plan to answer it. Give reviewers enough detail to assess the experiments and judge whether your team can carry them out. Explain what you could learn from different outcomes.
Use the current call and application instructions to determine the required sections and supporting material.
Put the objective near the beginning, before a detailed history of the field or description of techniques. Introduce the unresolved problem, say which part you will address, and explain why the answer matters. If a hypothesis organizes the proposal, describe how you will test it and what would count against it [5, commandments 1–3 and 6]; [6, tips 2–6].
Make clear what is already known and what you propose to find out. Support claims about the field with evidence, identify hypotheses, and use future tense for planned experiments. Explain exactly what preliminary results establish. Images might demonstrate that you can measure a response without yet showing which mechanism causes it.
Significance explains why the answer matters. Innovation explains how the question or approach differs from existing work. If you propose a new instrument, explain which comparison it makes possible and why that comparison matters. A familiar method may be sufficient to answer an important unresolved question. Compare the proposal with specific prior work before calling it innovative. If you suggest a practical application, explain what further work would be needed: an experiment in a controlled system rarely establishes a therapy or field application by itself [6, tips 4–7]; [3, pp. 883–884].

title: Writing the proposal
text:
Aims and experiments
State what each aim will establish. “Determine whether a response depends on treatment order” gives the experiment a purpose; “perform imaging” leaves the question unanswered. Then describe the comparison and explain how the measurements and analysis will answer it. Include the controls needed to distinguish explanations and identify which samples or experimental runs provide independent replication [2, pp. 166–167].
Explain how the aims depend on one another. If a later experiment tests the cause of a response you have not yet established, say what must be learned before it can begin. Describe what useful work remains if that response does not appear. Aims can depend on earlier results, provided reviewers can judge the risk and the alternatives [6, tips 9–10].
For each aim, explain what different results would mean. A precise result inconsistent with the hypothesis may answer the question. Failure to deliver the treatment or measure the response leaves the proposed test incomplete. Plan for both possibilities [5, commandments 7–8 and 13].

title: Writing the proposal
text:
Feasibility and alternatives
Separate scientific uncertainty from technical uncertainty. Whether a mechanism operates is the question; whether you can impose the intended condition, obtain the samples or measure the endpoint is a feasibility issue. Show what you have already checked. Preliminary work may establish that a method works; an access agreement documents who has agreed to provide the samples and on what terms. Where a procedure remains untested, describe how you will assess it, how much time this will take and what happens if it fails. Burchardi’s account of an economics ERC panel emphasizes access to data and a design capable of answering the question. His examples illustrate feasibility concerns, rather than requirements for every funding scheme [1, point 4].
Explain what an alternative method would let you learn. If automated scoring fails, manual scoring may still allow a comparison at the final observation time. But observations made by hand may be too infrequent to test a hypothesis about response timing. State when you would switch, whether the alternative answers the same question, and whether you can complete it with the time and resources requested. If the method works and the result challenges the hypothesis, reconsider the hypothesis.
Use the applicant and environment sections to show how the work can be done. Connect your experience to the proposed tasks and identify collaborators who provide expertise you lack. Confirm access to essential facilities and distinguish agreed support from requests still awaiting an answer. These commitments should agree with the staffing and costs elsewhere in the application [3, p. 884]; [2, pp. 166–169].



A focused proposal excerpt
In this fictional basic-research proposal, a researcher plans to characterize seed accession S under a defined pulsed-light protocol. The researcher has seed-handling and image-scoring experience and confirmed access to programmable light chambers, but no preliminary biological result. Red/far-red order effects are already known; the proposed question concerns this accession and protocol. A real application would need literature showing why this particular characterization is still needed, calibrated treatment parameters and the sections required by the scheme.

Objective and significance. We will characterize accession S’s germination response to a defined red/far-red light protocol. We will determine whether exposure order changes germination timing when the dose of each exposure is held constant, and how the interval between exposures affects that comparison. We hypothesize that reversing the order produces different germination trajectories within this protocol. If changing the order or interval changes germination, that detail will need to be specified when the protocol is used for this accession. The project will not identify a receptor mechanism, establish a treatment for agricultural use or determine how other accessions respond.
Aim 1: Determine whether exposure order changes germination. Seeds will receive one calibrated one-hour red exposure (R) and one calibrated one-hour far-red exposure (F), in sequences R→F or F→R with a fixed dark interval. Each sequence will deliver the same dose of R and the same dose of F; temperature, hydration and seed age will be matched. All final pulses will end at the same seed age, followed by the same observation period. A dark-only group will establish germination without the pulses. We will record time to visible radicle emergence and retain the fraction that has not germinated by the observation limit. This comparison tests order under the specified doses, rather than attributing differences to total illumination.
Aim 2: Determine how the interval between exposures affects the order comparison. For both sequences, we will compare predefined short and long dark intervals. Compensating darkness before the first pulse will keep final-pulse timing and the subsequent observation period aligned. Doses will remain unchanged. We will estimate the order difference at each interval and compare those differences directly. A smaller difference after a longer interval would be consistent with a response that depends on the temporal separation of the pulses; it would not, by itself, identify molecular memory. This aim uses the predefined sequences and can proceed without selecting a favorable result from Aim 1. An imprecise order estimate would still limit what either aim can conclude.
Design and feasibility. Each chamber run will receive one complete light schedule. Schedule allocation will be randomized and balanced across chambers and run blocks; containers will be randomized across positions. Several independently sourced lots of accession S will be represented across schedules. The analysis will retain chamber and run blocks and the nesting of seeds within containers and chamber runs. Containers sharing a chamber run will not be counted as independent treatment replicates, nor will repeated runs from the same lot count as new independent lots. Before biological testing, we will verify delivered spectral doses and temperature stability and compare image scoring with manual scoring. Calibration variation and the precision needed for an informative order contrast will determine the replication plan. Our existing seed-handling and scoring experience supports this stage; reliability of this particular pulsed assay remains to be established.
Risks and interpretation. Poor seed viability could make an apparent lack of response uninterpretable, so each lot will have a separate viability check. If image scoring is unreliable, we will use manual scoring at planned observation times only if it can retain the timing resolution required by the aims; otherwise we will narrow the timing question or revise the design before scaling up. If dose or temperature control fails, we will repair and requalify the treatment system before testing the hypothesis. If the checks pass and the estimates exclude an order difference large enough to matter for the stated question, we will report that constraint at the tested doses and intervals. We will not call an uncertain estimate evidence that order never matters.


Treatment calibration, a justified precision target and the resulting replication plan remain unfinished. Those details would need completion before this became a submission-ready proposal.

title: Writing the proposal
text:
Structure and readability
Use the required headings. Open each section with its main point, then develop the explanation. A reviewer skimming the objective and aim statements should understand the question and how you plan to answer it. Explain terms that a scientifically trained reader from another field may not know. Give the reason for an experimental comparison where you describe it, even if the background section has introduced the problem [5, commandments 3–4 and 15]; [4, pp. 153–154].
A figure can help explain a complicated design. For a schedule with several interventions, show when each treatment occurs and when measurements will be taken. If one aim depends on another’s result, a diagram can show the dependency and the alternative you would pursue. Explain the comparison in the caption so readers can interpret the figure without searching the main text. Follow the scheme’s format and accessibility requirements [5, commandments 5 and 9–11]; [4, p. 154].
Ask a specialist to challenge the scientific logic and a reader outside the immediate field to explain the proposal back to you. Can they say what the aims will establish and why the work is feasible? What would you learn if the expected result did not appear? Where they struggle, check whether an explanation is missing, a comparison is ambiguous or a claim lacks support. After revising, read the whole application. A change to an aim may also require changes to the figures, staffing or budget [5, commandment 16]; [6, tips 16–18].

title: Funding interviews and preparing for an award
text:
Prepare for the panel’s questions
Prepare to discuss the proposal’s most important questions and its weakest points at interview. If the application succeeds, check the award’s terms with your institution before arranging the start of the work.
Read the invitation alongside the submitted proposal and assessment criteria. Confirm the presentation time, question period, permitted materials, submission arrangements and interview format. Use those instructions to choose what fits. A previous applicant’s slide deck can show how they explained their project; it cannot establish this year’s rules.
Prepare a concise opening that explains the question and the work proposed to answer it. Why does the question matter? Which comparison is decisive, and why can this team carry it out? Leave time for the panel to examine those choices. In his account of an ERC panel, Burchardi recommends short, focused answers about contribution and feasibility, with backup material for likely questions [1, points 4 and 7].
Reread the application for assumptions the panel may question. If a facility has not confirmed access, explain how you would obtain it and what happens if it remains unavailable. If an aim depends on an earlier result, prepare to discuss other outcomes. Check the evidence for an untested assay and the basis of a tight cost estimate. State what you have already checked and what still needs to be arranged.
Choose backup slides by the question they answer: a control, a sampling plan, a dependency or the basis of a cost. Label them so you can reach the relevant evidence without searching through the whole deck. Detailed slide construction belongs in designing a presentation.

title: Funding interviews and preparing for an award
text:
Rehearsing the interview
Rehearse aloud with someone who can challenge the science and someone less familiar with the project. Ask them to interrupt, request a simpler explanation and question a central assumption. Notice where you answer a different question, rely on an unexplained term or take too long to reach the point. Revise those passages, then rehearse again [3, §§ 1–2].
Listen to the whole question. Clarify an ambiguity if it changes the answer, then answer directly and explain your reasoning. If the answer is unknown, say so. Explain how the proposed work would investigate it, or why it lies outside the project’s scope. When discussing an alternative experiment, explain whether it answers the same question or changes what the project can establish.



Example: answer the limitation directly
This fictional proposal compares two preservation methods using paired aliquots from an existing collection of freshwater samples. The outcome is recovery of viable microbial isolates under specified culture conditions. Sample access is confirmed, but the comparison has not been performed. The applicant has experience with the culture workflow. No preliminary result establishes which preservation method works better.

Panel member: Your culture assay misses organisms that do not grow in those conditions. How will you know whether you have preserved the community?
Applicant: We will not be able to claim that we preserved the whole community. Our question is narrower: which method gives better recovery of isolates with this culture workflow? We will split each sample between the two methods and an untreated recovery control, then keep the culture conditions the same. That makes the comparison useful for choosing how to preserve samples for this collection. It leaves uncultured organisms and other culture conditions outside the conclusion.
Panel member: What if both methods give very low recovery?
Applicant: We would first look at the untreated control and the detection limits. If the control also gives poor recovery, the experiment may not tell us much about preservation. If the control works, low recovery would show a problem under the tested conditions, but it would not establish that the methods are equivalent. We would use the paired estimates and their uncertainty to decide whether the difference is resolved. If it is not, we would report that limit rather than select a winner from noise.


Test the presentation setup, including opening the files and sharing slides. For a remote interview, check that you can hear questions and know how to reconnect or contact the organizer if the connection fails. Arrange accessibility or technical support with the organizer and keep a permitted backup copy. For pacing, voice and general question handling, see delivering a talk and answering questions [3, § 3].

title: Funding interviews and preparing for an award
section: Read the decision before making commitments
text:
Read the decision before making commitments
If the application is unsuccessful, separate the funding decision from the lessons in the review. Identify whether the main concern was fit, scientific reasoning, feasibility or explanation. Decide what evidence or redesign would address it before polishing the same text. Check the scheme’s current rules before assuming that resubmission is available. Ask the funder or research office if those rules are unclear. Feedback can help improve the project even when another opportunity is the better next step [2].
If the proposal is selected, read what the notification actually confirms. It may begin a period of award preparation rather than settle every term. Bring the notification and proposed work to the institutional team responsible for research awards. Establish the agreed start date, funded activities, available resources, outstanding conditions and who has authority to make commitments. Check any proposed early spending through the applicable institutional and funder process; do not infer permission from an encouraging message.
Pina’s guide to EU research grants treats preparation of the grant agreement as substantive work for the researcher and institutional support staff. Its broader lesson is to understand the conditions attached to the award, including its financial form, rather than reading only the scientific description. The specific obligations come from the applicable agreement, not from a general guide [4, Rules 3–6].
crumbs: Funding interviews and preparing for an award

title: Funding interviews and preparing for an award
text:
Preparing to start
Reconcile the approved work with what is available now. A facility may have changed its schedule, a collaborator’s commitment may need renewal or the awarded budget may differ from the request. Identify which changes affect the scientific comparison and which affect only its timing. Bring a concrete proposal to the appropriate funder and institutional contacts when an adjustment needs agreement. Do not promise the original scope with resources that no longer support it [2].
Before the first substantive work, agree who owns the initial tasks, what records will be kept and when progress or problems will be reviewed. Include administrative colleagues where their work controls purchasing, appointments or reporting. For a collaboration, settle the partner contributions and access arrangements needed at the start; collaboration, authorship and credit covers those agreements in more detail.



Example: selection with an unresolved start condition
Later in the same fictional project, the proposal is selected for funding and award preparation begins. The core facility now reports an eight-week delay in access needed for the first experimental batch. The final start arrangements remain unconfirmed.

Decision. Hold the dependent sample-processing and purchasing commitments while the applicant and institutional grants officer seek agreement on the revised schedule. Do not substitute a different recovery assay merely because it is available sooner; that could change the comparison on which the award was assessed.
Action and owner. The applicant will obtain a revised access date from the core and show which milestones depend on it. The grants officer will establish what the award process permits and whether the proposed sequence or start date needs formal agreement. Together they will submit a specific adjustment with its scientific and budget consequences.
Work that can proceed. The team can prepare protocols and analysis documentation using resources already authorized for that preparation. This does not authorize new grant charges, appointments or processing of the unique samples.
Release condition. Begin the dependent work after the necessary award arrangements and facility access are confirmed. If access remains unavailable, assess an adequate alternative or seek an agreed change; financial authorization alone does not make the assay feasible.


Keep a short record of the agreed start arrangements. Name who will do the first tasks and which commitments are confirmed. Include reporting dates and where to raise a proposed change. The amount of coordination depends on the award: an individual fellowship usually needs less than a multi-institutional programme. Plan required outputs early and retain the records needed for reporting [4, Rules 7–10].

title: Choosing a journal and submitting a paper
text:
Choose a journal for the contribution
While planning the paper, identify the readers who would use its findings and journals that reach them. Return to that shortlist once the results and argument are settled, and compare each journal’s expectations with the evidence you have.
The examples continue the fictional Brake study, inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [10].
crumbs: 6  Choosing a journal and submitting a paper

title: Choosing a journal and submitting a paper
text:
Match the paper to its readers
Summarize the contribution and identify who would use it. Match both the subject and kind of advance: a journal that publishes work on your organism may have little interest in the particular question or method. [1, pp. 175–180].
Read the aims, scope and article types, then several recent papers close to yours in purpose. Compare their questions, evidence and intended readers with your own. One similar article can suggest a candidate journal; a pattern across several papers gives a firmer basis for judging fit. [1, p. 178]; [3].
Use the journal’s editorial criteria to judge what kind of advance it expects. A broad journal may expect relevance beyond the immediate system; a methods journal will usually look for a useful capability and evidence of its performance. [3].
Ask a colleague familiar with the journals to read the abstract and main figures. Which journal would they recommend, and what additional evidence might its editors expect? [1, p. 178].


Make a realistic shortlist
Agree a first choice and a few alternatives with coauthors, weighing scientific fit, practical constraints and likely delay. An ambitious first submission can be reasonable when the case for that readership is clear and the authors accept the time cost of a possible rejection. [2, pp. 125–126]; [1, pp. 177–179].
First rule out journals whose charges you cannot cover, whose license conflicts with your requirements or whose format would force you to omit essential explanation. Then compare the remaining choices. When weighing delay, check whether advertised decision times cover only the initial editorial assessment or also external review. They are estimates, not promises. Recheck the chosen journal’s current instructions before submission.

Journal comparison
Record brief reasons for keeping or rejecting each journal, including any question that must be resolved before choosing it.








Question
What to examine
Decision to record




Who would use this paper?
Scope and recent papers addressing comparable questions
The readers and the contribution that interests them


Does the evidence meet the journal’s expectations?
Article type, editorial criteria and comparable studies
A good match, or a specific unresolved concern


Is this the right first choice?
Scientific fit, practical constraints, likely delay and coauthor judgment
First choice, alternative, or remove from the shortlist







Example: matching a biological finding to a journal
Brake reveals a previously unknown pathway in which an RNA template supplies a protein-coding defence gene.









Journal profile
Relevant readership
Assessment




General science, such as Science
Readers interested in gene organization, expression and cellular defence, including researchers outside microbiology.
The unexpected origin of a functional gene provides the case for broad interest. The sequence and genetic evidence must establish the proposed pathway.


Molecular microbiology
Researchers investigating bacterial defence and phage–host interactions.
A close fit for the pathway and the experiments establishing its function; also a natural audience for a narrower follow-up.


Microbial biotechnology
Researchers seeking useful traits in production strains or other applications.
The current study lacks application tests; an appealing use alone would not make this the strongest fit.



The team chooses Science as its ambitious first submission because the origin of the coding sequence could interest researchers beyond bacterial defence. A molecular-microbiology journal remains an alternative for readers focused on the pathway and its function.




Presubmission inquiries
Send a presubmission inquiry when an answer about scope, article type or expected validation would change where or how you submit. Check whether the journal accepts inquiries and use its requested route. [4].
Briefly explain the scientific question, finding and approach, adding the abstract if requested. Ask the question that affects your decision. For example, if your paper tests a method in one system, ask whether the journal would consider that evidence or expect validation in additional systems.
An encouraging reply does not guarantee external review. Keep the correspondence and refer to it accurately when submitting. You can contact an editor directly without a prior meeting or senior introduction. [4]; [1, p. 179].
crumbs: 6  Choosing a journal and submitting a paper

title: Choosing a journal and submitting a paper
text:
Check the terms and requirements

Investigate unfamiliar journals
For an unfamiliar journal, verify its identity, publisher contacts, editorial board and stated review process. Check indexing and preservation claims with the named services, and verify directory listings or professional memberships at the organization’s own site. Confusingly similar journal names, unclear charges or promises of guaranteed acceptance warrant further investigation. [7].
Establish the total charges, when payment is due, available waivers, the publication license and the terms for sharing the work in a repository. Confirm that the proposed route meets your funder’s and institution’s requirements. A librarian or research-support office can help resolve unclear terms before you commit. Record the policy page and date consulted. [7].


Distinguish initial submission from later production
Read the instructions for the exact article type and submission stage. Some journals allow flexible initial formatting; others require specific forms or structures. Distinguish what is needed for initial assessment from what will be required later, while keeping editable text, figures and data ready for production. [5, pp. 8–10].
Check limits on text, figures and supporting material. If they prevent a clear account, reconsider the article type or journal before removing essential explanation. The reporting chapter helps decide what the scientific account needs.
Check policies on preprints, related manuscripts and previous dissemination. Disclose overlapping work where requested. Pursue alternative journals sequentially: the usual declaration requires that the manuscript is not under consideration elsewhere. [2, p. 126]; [5, p. 7].
crumbs: 6  Choosing a journal and submitting a paper

title: Choosing a journal and submitting a paper
text:
Prepare the submission package

Assemble the agreed manuscript and supporting files
Assign a submission coordinator and agree on corresponding-author responsibilities. Circulate the submission version, resolve coauthor comments and confirm names, order, affiliations and contribution statements. Resolve authorship disputes before submission. [2, pp. 125–126].
Assemble the agreed manuscript, figures, legends, tables, supporting files and forms in one submission folder. Label versions clearly and assign the remaining checks to named coauthors.
Start repository preparation early because metadata and access queries can delay release. Before submission, test accession numbers and reviewer links, check access permissions, and identify the code version accompanying the paper. [8, p. 5].
Check which declarations apply to the study and collect them from the responsible authors, including funding, conflicts of interest, ethics, consent, contributions and data availability as required. Include requested reporting checklists and follow anonymization instructions for blinded review.


Writing the cover letter
Use the cover letter to explain what was unresolved, what the paper establishes and why the finding matters to the journal’s readers. Draw on the abstract, keeping the findings that establish the advance and omitting secondary results or unnecessary technical detail. A concise letter, often about a page, is usually sufficient unless the journal specifies otherwise. [5, pp. 4–7]; [6].
Open with the title and article type, then state the scientific advance early. For a broad readership, explain how the finding changes understanding of a wider question. For a specialist readership, identify the particular uncertainty it resolves. Mention earlier work in the journal when the connection helps explain the contribution. [5, pp. 5–6]; [1, pp. 179–180].
Include requested declarations and relevant editorial information, such as an earlier inquiry, related manuscript or potential reviewer conflict. Use designated portal fields where provided. If you claim to be first, check the relevant prior work and state exactly what is new. [5, pp. 5–7].



Example: a discovery paper and a narrower follow-up
The letters use the same genetic findings in two different publication contexts. Both assume coauthor approval and exclusive submission.











Discovery paper
Follow-up paper




Starting knowledge
The route from an RNA template to a functional defence gene is unknown.
The pathway is known; the effector’s function in Brake remains unresolved.


Main contribution
Establishes an unexpected way of producing a protein-coding gene.
Distinguishes the protein’s role from a possible direct effect of the DNA product.


Reason to read
Changes how researchers can look for functional genes and defence effectors.
Resolves a mechanistic question for researchers studying bacterial defence.





Discovery paper — letter to Science

Dear Editor,
Please consider our manuscript, “An RNA-templated gene arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation,” as a research article in Science.
We identify a bacterial defence pathway that assembles its protein-coding gene from an RNA template. Brake contains a reverse transcriptase and an RNA template, but no recognizable effector gene in its genomic sequence. We show that repeated RNA-derived DNA creates a continuous coding sequence whose protein product arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation.
Genetic tests connect gene assembly to function. Blocking translation preserves DNA production but abolishes growth arrest and phage restriction; expressing the protein separately restores both. These experiments identify the protein as the defence effector and distinguish its activity from a direct effect of the DNA product.
The discovery connects bacterial immunity to an unexpected route for producing a functional gene. It suggests that genome annotation can miss an effector whose coding sequence emerges only after DNA assembly, a possibility relevant to studies of gene organization and expression beyond bacterial defence.
All authors have approved the manuscript, and it is not under consideration elsewhere.
Thank you for considering our manuscript.
Sincerely,
[Corresponding author], on behalf of the authors



Follow-up paper — letter to a molecular-microbiology journal

Dear Editor,
Please consider our manuscript, “An RNA-derived protein mediates phage restriction in Brake,” as a research article in [Journal].
RNA-templated antiviral gene synthesis provides a route to bacterial defence, but the product responsible for defence in Brake remains unresolved. We distinguish a protein-mediated effect from a possible direct effect of its RNA-derived DNA product.
Preventing translation abolishes phage restriction while preserving DNA production. Expressing the protein separately restores restriction and growth arrest. Together, these experiments identify the Brake protein as the functional effector.
By linking the DNA product to an active protein, the work explains how a reverse-transcriptase-associated defence region restricts phage propagation. It should interest researchers investigating the function of these regions and their encoded effectors. The protein’s molecular target remains an open question.
All authors have approved the manuscript, and it is not under consideration elsewhere.
Thank you for considering our manuscript.
Sincerely,
[Corresponding author], on behalf of the authors


The same experiments make different contributions depending on what was already known. In the discovery letter, the genetic tests help establish the new pathway; in the follow-up, they resolve the identity of its effector.




Suggest reviewers for complementary expertise
Suggest reviewers with complementary expertise in the paper’s main methods and scientific questions. Give a short reason for each nomination and follow the journal’s requested number and information fields. [6].
Check potential conflicts involving institutional colleagues, recent collaborators, mentors or mentees. Follow the journal’s definitions, disclose uncertain relationships and verify contact details independently. [9, p. 4].
For permitted exclusions, give a concise reason relevant to fair review. Scientific disagreement alone does not establish bias. Keep exclusions proportionate; the editor makes the appointments. [5, p. 6]; [9, p. 4]; [3].
crumbs: 6  Choosing a journal and submitting a paper

title: Choosing a journal and submitting a paper
text:
Submit and follow the paper

Check the actual submission
Enter metadata from the agreed manuscript, checking author order, affiliations, funding and special characters after pasting. Assign files to the correct categories and remove superseded uploads before generating the review PDF.
Inspect the assembled review PDF for text and figure order, legibility, equations and symbols. Open supporting files and check any figures converted or compressed by the system. [5, pp. 8–10].
Once the assembled files are correct, complete the final approval step and retain the receipt, manuscript identifier and submitted files. Share them with coauthors and agree who monitors correspondence. If no receipt arrives, check the portal or contact the office before submitting again.


Following the submission
Journal staff may return a submission for missing files, declarations or unreadable material. Supply the correction with the manuscript identifier. Direct portal problems to staff and scientific questions to the handling editor. [5, p. 3].
The editor assesses fit, contribution and whether the evidence warrants review. Read the reason for an early rejection before deciding what to change. After external review, the reports inform the editor’s decision. [3].
Follow the journal’s timing guidance. If an expected interval has passed, or a deadline makes an update necessary, send a brief inquiry with the manuscript identifier, submission date and question. Avoid parallel inquiries to several editors. [4].
If you discover a material error after submission, tell the editor promptly, identify the affected files or conclusions and ask how to supply the correction. Keep the coauthors informed. When a decision arrives, circulate the complete message and reports. For a requested revision, continue with Responding to peer review, which covers revision planning and the response letter.
For a rejection or transfer offer, see Rejection, transfer and published reviews.

Before you submit


The journal and article type suit the contribution and intended readers; coauthors agree on the choice.
Publication costs, rights and applicable institutional or funder requirements are resolved.
The submitted version, author information and declarations are agreed and complete.
The cover letter explains the contribution and journal fit; reviewer suggestions provide relevant, independent expertise.
Figures, supporting files and data or code access work in the form supplied for review.
The assembled submission has been checked, and the team knows who will confirm receipt and monitor correspondence.

title: Reviewing a manuscript
text:
Decide whether to accept
Explain what the paper establishes and identify any problems that affect its conclusions. For each concern, tell the authors what needs to be resolved and explain to the editor how it affects your recommendation. [1].
Read the invitation, abstract and reviewer instructions before accepting. Consider whether you can assess the central methods and conclusions within the requested time. You need not cover every technique in a multidisciplinary paper: tell the editor which parts you can evaluate and where another reviewer is needed. If you cannot take the assignment, decline promptly and, when possible, suggest suitable alternatives. [2, rules 1 and 5]; [10].
Disclose relationships or interests that could affect—or reasonably appear to affect—your judgment. These can include recent collaboration, supervision, financial interests or close competition. Follow the journal’s definitions and ask the editor about uncertain cases before reading further. If a conflict becomes apparent only after you receive the manuscript, pause the review and contact the editor. [3, pp. 4–5].
Check what the journal asks reviewers to judge. Some decisions depend mainly on technical soundness; others also require a particular advance or relevance to a defined readership. Distinguish disagreement with a conclusion from lack of interest in the question. A result that challenges your preferred explanation deserves the same examination of methods and evidence as one that supports it. [2]; [3, pp. 5–6].

title: Reviewing a manuscript
text:
Confidentiality and co-review
Establish whether your report will be published, whether your identity will be disclosed, and how communication with authors is handled. Published reports can be anonymous; signing a review and publishing it are separate choices. Follow the agreed process, including any later request to share a report. [3, p. 3].
Keep the submission and review correspondence confidential. Do not circulate them to colleagues, use unpublished information in your own work or contact the authors directly without the journal’s permission. Before involving a trainee or specialist, obtain the editor’s agreement and arrange how their contribution will be acknowledged. The invited reviewer remains responsible for the submitted report. [3, pp. 5 and 8].
Apply the same confidentiality check to external tools. Before entering manuscript material or an identifiable draft report into an AI service, check the journal’s current policy, the service’s handling of the content and any required disclosure. Ask the editor if permission is unclear. Permission to use a tool does not transfer responsibility for the assessment or its accuracy.
If you can no longer meet the agreed deadline, tell the editor early and propose a date you can meet. [2, rule 1].

title: Reviewing a manuscript
text:
Assess the manuscript
Read the complete submission, including relevant supporting material. Summarize the question, approach and main finding in a few sentences, then assess which weaknesses affect that finding. Check apparent omissions elsewhere in the submission before raising them. [4]; [9].
Return to the results on which the main conclusions depend. Read each figure with its legend and the relevant Methods. Note where a description is missing and where you have found evidence of a problem. “The legend does not identify the experimental unit” calls for clarification; “The analysis treats technical measurements as independent experiments” requires evidence that this is how the analysis was performed. [4]; [6].

Examine the evidence needed for the claim
Ask whether the design distinguishes the proposed explanation from plausible alternatives. Identify the role of the controls and whether the intervention changes other features that could explain the result. When important information is missing, identify the comparison you cannot assess and request the relevant detail. The whole-paper assessment chapter develops this reasoning in more detail. [6].
For quantitative conclusions, first identify the comparison and its independent units, including any pairing or repeated measurements. Check the uncertainty around the estimated effect. Examine how observations were selected and whether the analysis accounts for testing many outcomes. If an analysis was chosen after seeing the results, consider how that choice affects the conclusion. A significant result in one group and a non-significant result in another do not establish a difference between groups; non-significance alone does not establish that an effect is absent. If you cannot assess a statistical issue that could change a main conclusion, ask the editor for specialist review. [6]; [3, p. 6].
Inspect the supporting data and code to the extent needed for your assessment and expected by the journal. Check that the files are accessible, identifiable and connected to the reported results. If access is restricted, assess the stated reason and available review arrangements rather than assuming unrestricted release is possible. Tell the editor when inaccessible material prevents an important check. [4].
When novelty or interpretation depends on an earlier publication, check the relevant passage in that paper. If the manuscript overlooks it, explain the consequence: perhaps a claimed discovery was already reported, or an apparent disagreement arises from different experimental conditions. Give the reference and the specific connection. A list of loosely related papers, especially your own, does not establish a substantive omission. [1, pp. 1029–1030]; [3, p. 7].

title: Reviewing a manuscript
text:
Distinguish essential revisions from extensions
Sort your concerns by their effect on the paper’s conclusions and your ability to assess them. A major concern challenges an important conclusion or the claimed contribution, or prevents you from judging whether they are supported. A minor concern is a local clarification or presentation problem that leaves the main conclusions intact. The amount of work is a separate question: an unsupported claim may be fixed by deleting a sentence, while an optional experiment could take months. [1, pp. 1028–1029]; [5].
State what remains unresolved before proposing a remedy. If the Methods omit information, ask for it. If the analysis does not answer the stated comparison, explain the mismatch. If the evidence supports a narrower conclusion, identify that option. Make clear when a concern prevents you from assessing the paper, rather than presenting your suspicion as an established flaw. [1, pp. 1029–1030]; [7].

Request experiments for a stated reason
An additional experiment is justified when its answer is needed for a claim the paper retains. Explain which alternative it would distinguish or which essential observation is missing. You can suggest a design, but allow another valid way to resolve the concern. Sometimes an existing analysis, a clearer explanation or a narrower claim is sufficient. [3, p. 7]; [7].
Consider whether the requested work is needed for the paper’s conclusion or asks a new question. Identifying a protein’s molecular target may be valuable without being necessary to establish its role in a phenotype; label such work as an optional future direction. For an essential concern, consider whether a different analysis or narrower claim could resolve it without costly new experiments. If neither would leave the paper’s conclusions supported, explain to the editor which evidence is still needed. [8]; [9].

title: Reviewing a manuscript
text:
Write the report
Use the journal’s form. Where the format is open, begin with a short summary of the question, main result and overall assessment, then present numbered major concerns followed by minor points. Identify strengths precisely—for example, a comparison that separates two competing explanations—rather than adding generic praise. You do not need to manufacture a list of weaknesses in a sound paper. [1, pp. 1028–1029]; [5].

Writing specific comments
For each substantive concern, identify the passage or figure, explain the problem and state what would resolve it. Quote a short phrase when its wording is the issue. If a comment contains several independently answerable questions, split them. Use continuous numbering or a clear section scheme so the response can refer to each point. [1, pp. 1029–1030]; [5].
Write directly about the manuscript. “Figure 2 does not distinguish these explanations because…” is more useful than a judgment about the authors’ competence. Be equally clear when the problem is serious: courteous wording should still let the reader recognize a conclusion you consider unsupported. When you may have misunderstood, say what you could not determine and ask the authors to clarify it. [3, pp. 6–7]; [7].
Concentrate language comments on scientific meaning and readability. Show where an ambiguous sentence changes the interpretation or a missing transition obscures the argument. Correcting every stylistic preference can bury more important concerns; widespread language problems can be described with a few representative examples. [3, pp. 6–7].



Example: a report on the Brake manuscript
Brake is the fictional bacterial defence study introduced in Planning the paper, inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [11]. Here a submitted draft describes an RNA-derived DNA intermediate that encodes a growth-arrest protein. The experiments connect protein production to phage restriction, but recovery of infected cells was not measured. The draft nevertheless claims survival, gives an ambiguous replication description and introduces the rationale for a key control only in the Discussion.



Comments to the authors

The manuscript describes Brake, a bacterial defence system in which reverse transcription of an RNA template produces a protein-coding DNA intermediate. Disrupting translation preserves DNA production but removes growth arrest and phage restriction; separate expression of the protein restores both. This comparison provides strong support for a protein-mediated defence mechanism. The main concerns are the inference about infected-cell survival and the description of replication in the phage-yield analysis.

Major concerns


The abstract states that Brake enables infected cells to survive. Figure 4 shows growth arrest during observation, but I could not find a measurement of recovery after infection. These observations do not establish survival. Please remove that conclusion and describe the observed growth arrest, or provide evidence of recovery if such measurements are available. The RNA-to-DNA-to-protein pathway remains an important finding without the survival claim.
Figure 1B reports a reduction in infectious phage yield, but the legend’s description of replicates does not let me assess the uncertainty around that estimate. Please state how many independently started cultures were tested for each genotype, whether genotypes were assayed together on the same days, and how technical plaque measurements were combined. The Methods should explain which values entered the comparison and how any matching by day was handled. If the current analysis already accounts for this design, a clear description would resolve the concern; otherwise, please revise the analysis and the resulting estimate and interval.


Minor point


The reason for preserving DNA production in the translation-disrupted construct is introduced in the Discussion. Please explain it when introducing Figure 3A. This would make it easier to see how the loss of restriction in Figure 3B, followed by complementation in Figure 3C, separates the protein’s contribution from loss of the DNA intermediate.


Optional future direction

Identifying the protein’s molecular target would help explain how growth arrest occurs. I do not consider this necessary for the present paper, provided the mechanistic conclusion remains at the level established by the translation and complementation experiments.

The replication concern cannot be settled until the reviewer knows how the observations were analyzed. The survival concern is already clear: it requires a change to the conclusion or additional evidence, even though removing the claim would take little work.


Confidential comments to the editor

I recommend revision. The evidence connecting an RNA-derived DNA intermediate to a defence protein is compelling, particularly the separation of DNA production from protein function in Figure 3. The survival claim should be removed unless supported by additional evidence, and I need the replication and analysis details described in point 2 before reaching a final judgment on the phage-yield comparison. I would be willing to assess a revised manuscript addressing these concerns. Identification of the protein’s molecular target is not a condition of my recommendation.





Give the editor a consistent recommendation
In the editor’s recommendation field, explain whether the problem can be corrected, requires a different study design or concerns the journal’s scope and expected advance. State any clarification you need before deciding. Do not request a substantial revision if you would still recommend rejection after the authors resolved your concerns. [1, p. 1030]; [10]; [9].
The editor makes the publication decision, but may ask for your assessment of both scientific merit and journal fit. Explain which criterion underlies a negative recommendation. A sound paper may fall outside the journal’s scope or offer less of an advance than it requires. A result that would interest its readers may still lack the evidence needed for publication. [2]; [9].
Keep scientific criticisms visible to the authors. A favorable author-facing report paired with a hidden negative assessment leaves them unable to respond and makes the editor’s decision harder. Use confidential comments for matters requiring editorial handling, such as a competing interest, a limit to your expertise or a suspected ethical irregularity. [3, pp. 5–6]; [1, p. 1030].
For a suspected irregularity, describe the observation and give precise locations or a relevant reference. Do not turn a suspicion into an accusation or conduct your own investigation with the authors. Ask the editor how to proceed. A substantive problem may need correction regardless of its cause; establishing misconduct is a separate matter. [3, p. 5].

title: Reviewing a manuscript
text:
Review the revision
Read the decision letter, your earlier report and the response alongside the revised manuscript. For each substantive point, assess whether the underlying concern has been resolved. The authors may have used a different analysis, supplied an explanation you overlooked or narrowed the conclusion. Judge that answer on its merits rather than requiring your preferred solution. [3, p. 8]; [9].
Check the revised evidence and wording, not just the response letter. A clear reply may describe a change that has not reached the manuscript, or a new analysis may alter the interpretation elsewhere. If an experiment remains inconclusive, reassess what the retained claim requires. [9].
Avoid adding a new list of desirable experiments after the authors have addressed the original review. A revision can introduce a problem, and you may discover a serious issue missed earlier; raise it with a specific explanation of why it now affects your assessment. If your original criticism was mistaken, acknowledge that and withdraw it. [3, p. 8]; [9].
If another journal asks you to review a manuscript you have seen before, tell the editor about your earlier involvement. Assess the current version afresh against the new journal’s criteria. Obtain the original journal’s permission before sharing your earlier report. [3, p. 6].
Tell the editor which important concerns are resolved, what remains and how that affects your recommendation. When no substantive issue remains, a short report can be sufficient. [10]; [9].

Before submitting the report


The summary identifies the paper’s contribution and the evidence that matters to the assessment.
Each major concern has a location, a reason and a clear criterion for resolution.
Essential revisions are distinguished from optional extensions and stylistic preferences.
Scientific criticisms in the recommendation are also visible to the authors; confidential matters are directed to the editor.
The report states any limits to the review and meets the journal’s instructions on conflicts, collaboration, confidentiality and disclosure.
