title: Responding to peer review
text:
Understanding the decision
Reviewer comments often mix questions about evidence with requests for clearer writing or additional work. Identify the concern behind each request before deciding what to change. The revised manuscript must address those concerns, and the response should explain what changed, why, and where the editor and reviewers can find it.
Start the response letter while planning the revision. A reply you cannot yet write may reveal an analysis to check or a question to discuss with coauthors. Mark proposed work clearly, then replace those notes with what was actually done as you revise the manuscript. [2].
The examples continue the fictional Brake study.
[2]; [1]; [5].
Start with the editor’s decision, which sets the conditions and deadline for revision. Read those conditions alongside the reports, and ask the editor which requests are essential if this is unclear. [4]; [5].
Read all reviews before answering individual points. Identify recurring concerns and challenges to the central result; these may require more work than a long list of minor corrections. Read the relevant manuscript passages beside the comments. A question whose answer seems obvious may reveal an unstated assumption, while several questions may point to one poorly explained idea. [1, rules 2–3 and 10]; [2].
Work through possible responses privately with coauthors, then draft the reply around the scientific concern.

title: Responding to peer review
text:
Planning the revision

Comments and tasks
Copy the full comments into a working document and number the points. Separate the issues within a compound comment so that each receives an answer. Beneath each point, sketch a response or specify the work needed. [2]; [1, rule 5].
Name what to inspect and what to change: “Define the experimental unit in the legend and check that the analysis uses independent cultures.” An unclear error bar might need only a better legend, or its calculation might be wrong. Inspect the analysis before choosing the remedy. Likewise, check whether an overstated claim results from an analysis error or an interpretation that goes beyond the findings.


Additional experiments
Identify the conclusion the reviewer is questioning and ask what the requested experiment would establish. If you intend to retain that conclusion, you need evidence that resolves the concern—for example, a test of a necessary assumption or a comparison that distinguishes plausible explanations. The requested experiment may provide that evidence; propose a different test if it answers the same question more directly. [6, p. 7].
Other checks may strengthen a conclusion that is already supported. Weigh the concern they resolve against the time and resources needed. If you do the work, describe its result in the response and include evidence necessary for the published conclusion with the paper. [1, rules 1 and 8]; [6, p. 7].
A request may also open a new project. Establishing a cellular effect does not necessarily require explaining its mechanism or testing a treatment application. Whether that further work is needed depends on what the paper claims. Discuss the intended scope with the editor when a reviewer expects work beyond that question. [3]; [1, rule 8].


Alternatives and narrower claims
A narrower claim may resolve the concern when the available evidence supports it. Explain what the revised paper would establish and what would remain unanswered, then change the claim wherever it appears, including the title and abstract when affected. If you propose an alternative experiment instead, explain how it answers the reviewer’s question. Distinguish a scientifically unsuitable test from one blocked by access, equipment or time. [6, p. 7]; [1, rule 8].
Consult the editor when an alternative changes a revision condition or the paper’s scope. If essential evidence is unavailable, assess whether a narrower contribution remains sound and suitable for the journal. [5]; [4].



Example: narrowing a claim after review
An early Brake draft claimed that the system helps infected cells survive. A reviewer asks for recovery measurements. The authors have measured growth arrest and phage output, but not recovery. They propose removing the survival claim and ask the editor whether the paper can be assessed on that basis. In this scenario, the editor agrees.




The manuscript states that Brake promotes survival after infection, but growth arrest does not establish survival. Please track whether infected cells recover and resume division.



We agree that our measurements do not establish recovery. We have not performed the requested recovery experiment. Following discussion with the editor, we have removed the survival claim and focused the conclusion on growth arrest and phage restriction.
The abstract now states: “The Brake protein arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation.” In the Discussion, “Fate of infected cells,” we now write: “Reduced infectious output establishes phage restriction without showing that individual cells survive the infection. Recovery measurements would distinguish reversible arrest from a lasting loss of growth capacity.”


Recovery evidence is necessary for the original survival claim. The narrower paper can proceed only if the remaining contribution is supported and the editor agrees to assess it.




Responsibilities and timing
Agree on substantial changes early and assign the work. Account for dependencies when setting the schedule: a reanalysis must be settled before the affected figure, Results and abstract can be finalized.
Plan with the people doing the work, allowing time for equipment access, sample preparation, analysis and coauthor review alongside their other commitments. When one trainee carries most of the revision, check whether the proposed workload is feasible. Request an extension if the resulting schedule exceeds the deadline. [3].
Include those doing the work in scientific discussions and relevant exchanges with the editor. Record decisions and open questions in the revision plan. [5].

Revision worksheet
Use one entry per comment or subpoint to track the work and record the final answer. A shared document is often enough; a spreadsheet can help with a large revision. [2]; [1].







Field
What to record




Comment
Reviewer and point number, with the full comment


Issue to resolve
The question, missing explanation or disputed conclusion


Planned work
The edit, analysis, experiment or reason for retaining the current approach


Responsibility and timing
Who will do the work, what it depends on and when it is needed


Progress
Work still to do, questions awaiting a decision and completed changes


Final response
The answer supported by the work actually completed


Manuscript location
Where the reader can find the revised text, figure or analysis






Questions for the editor
Contact the editor before substantial work if the revision conditions are unclear. Describe the concern, propose the work that would address it and ask whether that plan is suitable. If the work will exceed the deadline, explain why and propose a realistic date. [5, p. 221].

title: Responding to peer review
text:
Carrying out the revision
After each experiment or analysis, check whether the result answers the reviewer’s question. Revise the plan if the question remains unanswered or the result reveals a new problem.

New experiments and analyses
For new experiments, report the additional data and findings. For reanalyses, identify the existing data and explain what changed in the analysis and why. If you uncover an error, describe its consequences and check all affected figures and passages before stating that the conclusions are unchanged. [1, rule 9].
Record which analyses were specified before examining the new results and which arose during exploration. Explain changes to the analysis plan and report relevant outcomes, including those that challenge the expected interpretation. [7].


Unexpected or inconclusive findings
When a result is inconclusive, check why. If the intervention or measurement failed, explain what failed and whether the requested test can still be completed. If the experiment worked but the estimate is imprecise, report the estimate and uncertainty; a non-significant result does not establish absence of an effect. To claim that an effect is too small to matter, define the magnitude that would matter for the question and use an analysis that can assess that claim, with assumptions you can justify. See estimates and intervals. [7].
If new evidence weakens the interpretation, revise it throughout the paper and explain what changed your judgment. Discuss loss of support for a central conclusion with coauthors and the editor before continuing the old plan. [4]; [5].


Supporting material
Include the evidence needed to assess the published conclusions in the paper and its supporting material, including findings that qualify those conclusions. A figure or table may remain only in the response when it answers a reviewer’s specific question and the published account is complete without it. Label response-only material distinctly and state whether any part was added to the paper. [1, rules 1 and 8].

title: Responding to peer review
text:
Writing the response

Letter structure
Thank the editor and reviewers, then summarize the major changes and the concerns they address.
Follow the overview with the reviews in order, placing your answer directly beneath each comment. If a long comment raises several issues, split it at natural boundaries and answer each part. Retain the full wording, order and meaning, including any shared context, and note that the comment has been divided for clarity. Keep the original point number when it helps the reviewer recognize the comment. [1, rule 5].
Make each reviewer’s section readable on its own. When concerns overlap, repeat the explanation, relevant quoted changes and manuscript locations in each section. A reviewer should be able to assess your reply without reading your answers to someone else.


Point-by-point replies
Lead with the correction, experimental result or reason for retaining the approach. Explain how it addresses the concern and identify the corresponding manuscript passage or figure. [1, rules 1 and 7].
Distinguish old and new material explicitly. “This is described in the Methods” leaves the reviewer unsure whether the description was already there or has just been added. “We have added a description of the exclusion criteria to the Methods” makes the change clear.
Quote short changes directly: ‘We have clarified the Figure 1B legend: “Each point represents one independently started culture.”’ Identify the revised figure, table or section for every change. Add page or line numbers when the passage is harder to find or the journal requests them, and state that they refer to the revised manuscript. For a long addition, summarize its purpose and give the section title. [1, rules 3–4 and 9].
Use consistent typography, spacing and indentation to distinguish comments, replies and manuscript quotations, including in print. [1, rule 6]; [2, footnote 2].



Example: clarifying the experimental unit
A reviewer asks about replication in the Brake phage-yield assay. The authors confirm that the analysis already uses one titre per culture and matches conditions by experimental day. They split the two-sentence comment below.



Dear Editor,
Thank you for the comments. We have clarified the sampling and analysis behind Figure 1B. We have divided the reviewer’s comment into its two questions; locations and quotations refer to the revised manuscript.



Please define what each point represents.



Each point represents one independently started culture. The Figure 1B legend now states: “Each point represents one independently started culture; lines connect the three cultures assayed on the same day. Six days were measured, with technical duplicate plaque counts combined for each culture.”



Explain how the technical duplicates and measurements on different days were handled.



We combined the duplicate plaque measurements into one titre estimate per culture, then compared intact Brake with empty vector within each experimental day. The six day-matched contrasts were the observations used to estimate the effect and its uncertainty. The analysis and results are unchanged.
Methods, “Infectious-titre analysis,” now states: “We divided the intact-Brake titre by the empty-vector titre within each day and took the log10 of that ratio. We estimated the mean log10 ratio and its two-sided 95% confidence interval using a Student t distribution with five degrees of freedom.” The preceding paragraph explains that technical duplicates were combined into one culture-level estimate.


The analysis already used one titre per culture and matched the cultures by day, so the reply describes a reporting correction. If technical plates had entered the analysis as independent cultures, the authors would also need to correct the analysis and report its consequences.




Disagreements and unchanged text
When you disagree with a request, explain how the existing evidence answers the concern or how an alternative would resolve it. If the request concerns a different question, name that question and explain why answering it is unnecessary for the claim you retain. The phrase “beyond the scope” leaves that reasoning unstated.
Reread the relevant passage from the reviewer’s perspective. If it omits an explanation, leaves an assumption unstated or makes information difficult to find, improve the manuscript as well as the reply. The analysis may be sound even when its description needs revision. [1, rule 3].
If the passage already answers the concern or there is a sound reason to retain the approach, explain that reason, give the evidence and manuscript location, and explicitly say what is unchanged. Quote the passage when useful. Before finalizing the reply, check whether it contains an explanation the manuscript itself needs. [1, rules 7 and 9]; [6, p. 7].
Discuss unresolved disagreements with the editor when they affect a revision condition or the central claim.
Read suggested references and add those that provide relevant context or correct an omission. Briefly explain why an unrelated citation was not added. [6, p. 7].
Concerns about a conflict of interest or inappropriate conduct belong in a separate communication to the editor. Describe the relevant facts and the action you are asking the editor to consider. Keep the point-by-point scientific reply focused on the manuscript. [1, rule 2].


Conflicting requests
First ask whether both requests can be met. More explanation and shorter Results can often be reconciled by moving analytical detail to Methods. If requests require incompatible analyses or contradict the editor’s conditions, explain which approach you propose and why, then ask the editor to clarify the requirement. [1, rules 2–3 and 8]; [5].



Example: more explanation in a shorter Results section
Reviewer 1 wants the day-matched comparison explained. Reviewer 2 wants a shorter Results section, which currently gives the calculation over several paragraphs. The authors keep the comparison and finding in Results and move the calculation to Methods.



Reviewer 1



Please explain why cultures were compared within each day and how the effect and confidence interval were calculated.



Each experimental day included all three genotypes. Matching intact Brake to its same-day empty-vector control accounts for shared differences between experimental days. We have retained that comparison in Results, “Brake restricts phage propagation,” and moved the calculation to Methods.
The revised Results read: “We compared intact Brake with empty vector within each experimental day. Across six days, the geometric mean infectious titre was 79-fold lower with Brake (95% confidence interval, 55–116-fold; Figure 1B).”
Methods, “Infectious-titre analysis,” now states: “We divided the intact-Brake titre by the empty-vector titre within each day and took the log10 of that ratio. We estimated the mean log10 ratio and its two-sided 95% confidence interval using a Student t distribution with five degrees of freedom.” It then explains how the estimate and interval were converted to a fold reduction. The calculation is unchanged.


Reviewer 2



The Results contain too much detail about the titre calculation. Please shorten this passage and keep the focus on the finding.



We have shortened the Results by replacing the calculation paragraphs with two sentences under “Brake restricts phage propagation”: “We compared intact Brake with empty vector within each experimental day. Across six days, the geometric mean infectious titre was 79-fold lower with Brake (95% confidence interval, 55–116-fold; Figure 1B).”
The calculation now appears in Methods, “Infectious-titre analysis”: “We divided the intact-Brake titre by the empty-vector titre within each day and took the log10 of that ratio. We estimated the mean log10 ratio and its two-sided 95% confidence interval using a Student t distribution with five degrees of freedom.” The following sentences describe conversion to a fold reduction. This retains the day matching needed to understand the result while moving the analytical detail out of Results. The analysis is unchanged.

title: Responding to peer review
text:
Checking and submitting
Read the paper and response side by side to check that they describe the same revision. Verify every cited manuscript location and follow changes to results or conclusions through to the abstract and Discussion.
Ask each responsible researcher to check the relevant result and reply, then have a coauthor read the complete package for consistency. Resolve disagreements about the interpretation or response before submitting.
Update data, code and materials information affected by the revision. Test repository access and verify versions against the revised analyses. [4].
Prepare the required clean and marked manuscripts from the same final text. Check response locations against that version and remove working notes.

Before resubmitting, check the following. [1]; [2].

Every editor and reviewer comment, including each subpoint, has an answer.
Each reviewer’s section includes the explanations, quotations and manuscript locations needed to assess the reply on its own.
The letter reports the work completed and its actual results.
The manuscript contains the explanations and evidence readers will need.
Revised methods, sample counts, figure legends and supplementary files match the work reported.
New analyses and revised conclusions agree across the text, figures and supplements.
Inconclusive findings are described accurately, and any retained text or approach is justified in the reply.
Data, code, materials information and access links reflect the revised work.
All manuscript locations refer to the files being submitted.
Coauthors have reviewed the revision, and the required clean, marked and supporting files are ready.

title: Rejection, transfer and published reviews
text:
Understanding the rejection
Start with the editor’s reasons for rejection and discuss them with coauthors. If the paper does not suit the journal’s audience, another destination may be appropriate. If the main conclusion lacks support, address that problem before submitting elsewhere.
Read the decision letter alongside the reports. Identify the concerns the editor considers decisive: the journal’s audience, the contribution, a weakness in the evidence, or some combination. Reviewers can disagree, and the editor may give one concern more weight than several favorable assessments. [1].
Discuss the next step with your coauthors before writing to the journal. Separate work that would improve the paper wherever it is submitted from work intended to meet this journal’s expectations. Consider the time required, available resources and whether the revised contribution would justify another attempt there. Agree on an alternative destination as well. [2, pp. 126–127].
A rejection with an invitation to submit new work differs from a revision request: the journal may want to reconsider the project only after substantial changes. If the wording leaves this unclear, ask whether the proposed work would make a new submission appropriate and which concern it must resolve. Briefly describe the work rather than asking whether there is any chance of acceptance. [3]; [4].

title: Rejection, transfer and published reviews
text:
Choosing the next route








What explains the decision?
What to do next




The contribution does not suit the journal’s audience or selection criteria.
Reassess the destination. Appeal only if you can identify a consequential misunderstanding of the contribution.


A central claim lacks evidence.
Decide whether to obtain that evidence, narrow the claim or substantially rework the paper before submitting again.


A factual error appears to determine the rejection.
Check the appeal policy and show how correcting the error changes the assessment.


The editor explicitly invites a substantially revised new submission.
Clarify the expected changes, assess whether they are feasible and follow the specified resubmission route.

title: Rejection, transfer and published reviews
text:
Decide whether to appeal
An appeal is most useful when you can show why the reasoning behind the rejection should change. Correcting an incidental error is unlikely to help if another unresolved concern still justifies rejection. A successful appeal may lead to further revision or review. [4]; [1].
Check the journal’s permitted grounds, deadline, recipient and required documents. In the PLOS One process consulted for this chapter, an appeal must be written and sent through the stated route with the appeal form. A significant factual error or documented competing interest is considered only when correcting it would change the decision. Informal appeals are not accepted; while an appeal is active, the manuscript remains under consideration and must not be submitted elsewhere. Other journals may use different procedures. Recheck the applicable instructions before acting. [5].

Explain the decisive issue
Open with the manuscript title or identifier and the request for reconsideration. State the editor’s decisive concern, then explain the error or new information with precise manuscript locations. Where several concerns determined the decision, address each; do not select only the easiest criticism. Supply a point-by-point response if the journal requires one. [4].
New results may change an editor’s assessment if they resolve the reason for rejection. State what the completed experiments show and identify any work still proposed. If the concern is relevance to the journal, explain what its readers would learn that the editor’s assessment overlooked. [1].



Example: appealing a factual misunderstanding
In the fictional Brake study, inspired by Tang and colleagues (2024) [6], disrupting translation leaves the RNA-derived DNA product intact but removes growth arrest and phage restriction. Separate expression of the Brake protein restores both effects. Suppose the editor rejects the paper on the mistaken premise that the translation-disrupting change also prevented DNA production, so the protein’s contribution could not be distinguished from the DNA’s. The appeal can point to the control already present in Figure 3A.


Dear Editor,
We would like to appeal the decision on our manuscript, An RNA-templated gene arrests bacterial growth and restricts phage propagation.
The decision rests on the concern that our translation-disrupting change also abolishes DNA production. Figure 3A shows that the DNA product is retained in this construct. Growth arrest and phage restriction are lost despite this retained DNA production (Figure 3B), and both are restored by expressing the Brake protein separately (Figure 3C).
These results distinguish the protein’s contribution from DNA production and address the reason given for rejection. Would you reconsider the manuscript in light of this control? We can also revise the Results passage and Figure 3 legend to make the comparison more prominent.
Thank you for considering our appeal.

If the editor had also rejected the paper for insufficient novelty, the appeal would need to address that judgment too.




Resubmitting to the same journal
If the reports raise a possible conflict of interest or inappropriate conduct, describe the specific evidence through the journal’s complaints or appeal procedure. Explain separately whether it affects the scientific decision. PLOS One, for example, asks authors to raise concerns about correspondence with journal staff and sets explicit grounds for an appeal. [5].
A substantially revised manuscript may be eligible for a fresh submission to the same journal, but check its rules or obtain the editor’s agreement first. Disclose the previous submission and explain the changes. Wilke advocates this route as an alternative to appeal; its suitability depends on the journal and the extent of revision. [4].
If you abandon a pending appeal, notify the journal and resolve its status before submitting elsewhere. After a final rejection, return to the scientific concerns and the next journal’s criteria with your coauthors. Keep an appeal and a transfer or new submission as separate routes; do not pursue them at the same time. [5]; [7]; [2, pp. 126–127].

title: Rejection, transfer and published reviews
text:
Transfer or submit elsewhere
A transfer offer is worth considering alongside other suitable journals. Check the destination’s audience, publication criteria, article type, charges and licensing arrangements using the approach in Choosing a journal and submitting a paper. Agree the choice with your coauthors. [2, pp. 126–127].
Find out whether the offer is an automated suggestion, a recommendation from the original editor, or follows consultation with the receiving editor. Nature Portfolio describes all three; the receiving journal makes its own editorial decision, and authors choose whether to transfer. [7].
Check which files and correspondence will transfer, including earlier versions, and remove confidential material you do not want to send. The Nature Portfolio guide consulted for this chapter permits file changes during transfer. It also prohibits an appeal while the paper is being transferred for consideration elsewhere. Check the receiving journal’s applicable instructions before proceeding. [7].
Review transfer follows the journals’ agreements about confidentiality and identity. Do not forward an editor’s confidential material or reveal a reviewer on the assumption that permission to use the report also permits disclosure. COPE advises journals and reviewers to establish what can be shared in a transfer. [8, p. 6].

Prepare the next submission
Correct known errors and unsupported claims in the next version. For a new submission, address valid criticisms and decide whether requests for a broader study are necessary for the new destination. If a claim depends on missing evidence, obtain it or revise the claim throughout the paper. [2, pp. 126–127].
Some transfer routes allow a plan for outstanding work. Nature Portfolio advises distinguishing completed changes from proposed work and explaining the effort required. Establish the receiving journal’s interest before undertaking substantial destination-specific work. [7]. Detailed response planning is covered in Responding to peer review.
Update the cover letter and replace obsolete files. With an ordinary submission, previous reports may not reach the receiving editor automatically; follow its instructions on submission history and earlier correspondence. For transfers, check that the intended response and revised files accompany the manuscript. [7]; [2, pp. 126–127].

title: Rejection, transfer and published reviews
text:
Read and publish review histories
Published reviews can show how a paper’s evidence and interpretation were challenged and revised. Begin with the final article, then follow an important concern through the report, the authors’ response and the corresponding change. Note the dates, manuscript versions and journals involved. A report written for an earlier version may criticize a claim that no longer appears in the paper; a request from one journal may reflect its particular expectations. [9].

Follow the concern into the paper
For each concern that matters to your reading, identify what the reviewer questioned and how the authors answered. Did they add evidence, correct an analysis, explain an existing control, narrow a claim or leave the point unresolved? Check the final paper rather than relying on the response’s description of the change. If the corresponding manuscript version is unavailable, you may be able to assess the final claim without reconstructing exactly what the reviewer saw. [9].



Example: following a corrected claim
In this Brake example, the recorded experiment measured growth arrest; recovery was not tested.




The growth trajectories in Figure 4B do not establish survival. Did the arrested cells resume growth after infection?



We did not measure recovery after infection. We have removed the survival claim and now describe the observed growth arrest. The Results passage accompanying Figure 4B now states: “Infected cells stopped growing during observation; whether they subsequently recovered was not tested.”



Final Results passage


Infected cells stopped growing during observation; whether they subsequently recovered was not tested.

The claim is corrected; recovery remains untested.


When using published correspondence to learn about reviewing, examine how the reviewer explains a problem and whether the response resolves it in the manuscript. The number of review rounds and the severity of the language do not tell you whether a criticism was justified or a repair adequate. [10]; [9].


Check what becomes public
“Open review” can describe different arrangements. Reports may be published without reviewer names; a signed report may be visible to authors without being publicly available. Review transfer and post-publication commenting are further, separate practices. Check the journal’s model rather than inferring these choices from the label. [10].
Before agreeing to publish a review history, inspect what it includes and who can consent to publication. In the PLOS One process consulted for this chapter, authors can opt into publication of decision letters, reports, responses and attachments; names appear when reviewers have signed their reports, and ethical considerations can limit publication. Recheck the journal’s model and permissions for the history you intend to publish. [5].
If earlier reports came from another journal, ask how their publication is authorized and how the original context will be identified. Keep confidential correspondence private until the applicable permissions are clear. For teaching or quoting from an already published report, check its stated license and cite the particular report and version. [8, pp. 5–6]; [9].

Before taking the next step


Coauthors agree on the route and the work required before proceeding.
An appeal addresses a decision-relevant issue and meets the journal’s instructions.
The paper is no longer under consideration elsewhere when the next submission begins.
The next package addresses valid criticisms and contains the intended files and correspondence.
Any shared or published reviews follow the relevant permissions and identify their manuscript context.

title: Exploring career options
text:
Compare the work
Scientific training can lead to research, teaching, publishing, technology development, policy or managing shared facilities. The titles alone tell you little about the working day. An editor evaluates manuscripts; an applications scientist helps researchers use a technology; a facility manager organizes equipment, expertise and services for many groups. Compare what you would do repeatedly in each role and who would use the work [1].
Think about the work you would like to do regularly. You might enjoy troubleshooting instruments but prefer less time writing papers, or want to teach while staying involved in research. Being good at an activity does not necessarily mean you want it to fill your week. Also note conditions that could rule out a role, such as frequent travel or a location you cannot move to.
Compare actual posts within those categories. Research roles differ in freedom to choose projects, expectations for publication and the importance of a commercial application. Ask who sets priorities, how success is assessed and which decisions you would make yourself [2].
Scientific training develops skills in framing questions, evaluating evidence, learning unfamiliar subjects and explaining results. Identify which of these the role uses, then assess what else you need to learn. A supervised project or placement may provide relevant experience; a course may be sufficient for a specific knowledge gap.

title: Exploring career options
text:
Topic
Questions




Contribution
What problem does the role solve, and for whom?


Week of work
How much time goes to experiments, analysis, writing, meetings, documentation, training or coordination?


Responsibilities
Who sets priorities, and what limits the work?


Qualifications
What experience, knowledge or training does the role require?


A useful trial
What conversation, shadowing opportunity, short project or course would show whether the work fits?







Example: comparing two roles

Lena enjoys troubleshooting assays and explaining results to collaborators. She wants to remain in one region and prefers working with others to spending long periods writing alone.
Applications scientist: Lena spoke with two scientists who support genomics users and tried teaching a workflow to a new colleague. She enjoyed diagnosing the problem and watching the user become independent. Both conversations, however, described recurring travel outside her region. She will look for local or remote support posts and check the travel requirements of each one.

Research project manager: Lena observed a planning meeting and coordinated one defined part of a collaboration. She liked clarifying decisions and making sure one group’s delay did not block another. She missed doing the technical work herself, so she narrows the search to roles close enough to the science for her assay knowledge to matter.

Lena now gives locally based scientific project roles priority. She will accept less bench time for collaborative problem-solving, but not routine travel or work detached from the technical decisions.

title: Exploring career options
section: Learn from people doing the work
text:
Learn from people doing the work
Speak with people who hold the role in more than one organization and at different career stages. Ask them to describe a recent week and a difficult decision. Which responsibilities surprised them when they started? Find out how they learned the role and what experience they would look for in a new colleague. Ask how their work is assessed.
Ask similar questions across conversations. If people in the same role describe different weeks or constraints, ask what comes from the role and what comes from their organization or manager.
A conversation can suggest a way to try the work. Shadowing someone or taking on a short project may reveal more than another general discussion. For a postdoctoral position, ask what you expect to gain from the appointment and whether the group can provide it. Discuss how you would respond if the promised training or opportunities did not materialize. Choosing an advisor and research environment explains how to assess that support.

title: Exploring career options
text:
Experience and next steps
Keep a brief record of relevant work you have done. Describe what you did, who used it and what happened as a result. Include evidence you could show or someone who could confirm your contribution. Work beyond your research project may also be relevant: teaching a workshop can demonstrate training experience, for example. Compare these experiences with the responsibilities of the roles you are considering.
“Kept a shared project schedule up to date” shows coordination; it does not show that you led the project. “Completed a training module” may show interest in quality practice; it is not the same as having worked in that system. Check where you still need practical experience before applying.
Reconsider the options after the conversations or trials. Which work did you want more of after trying it? Did a working condition rule out an otherwise attractive role? Use what you learned to narrow the search or choose the experience you need next.

title: Exploring career options
text:
References



Sever, R., & Janssen, K. (2017). Career Options for Scientists. Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology, 9(9), a032755.

title: Choosing an advisor and research environment
text:
Decide what you need from the position
Two laboratories can work on equally interesting questions yet offer very different training. Read their work, talk with each prospective advisor, and ask current and former members how projects and supervision develop in practice. Compare the research, the support you need and the working environment before choosing. [1]; [2].
Start with the outcome you need from the training period. A PhD and a postdoc both involve research, but they make different demands of supervision.
Write down your priorities and any conditions you cannot accept. A student learning to design experiments may need frequent early feedback; a postdoc preparing for an independent position may need opportunities to develop and carry forward a distinct research direction. Ask about support for the career you intend to pursue, including work outside academia. [2].
For a PhD, identify who provides advice beyond the primary supervisor, such as a committee member or programme director. Ask how that person becomes involved if supervision or progress is difficult.
crumbs: Choosing an advisor and research environment

title: Choosing an advisor and research environment
text:
Stage
Central outcome
Questions that change the decision




PhD
Learn to frame questions, conduct and interpret research, communicate results, and leave with several viable directions.
How is a new student taught? How often is feedback available? Who can advise if the first project or supervision arrangement does not work?


Postdoc
Extend or redirect expertise while developing work, visibility and support for the intended next role.
What new capability, research direction or independent contribution can this position build? What work can the postdoc lead or carry forward? How does the supervisor support the next search?
crumbs: Choosing an advisor and research environment

title: Choosing an advisor and research environment
text:
Learning how the laboratory works
Keep notes for each serious option, recording who described a practice and what you observed yourself. Compare these accounts: do the advisor and trainees describe similar supervision, or do their experiences differ?







Topic
What to find out




Supervision
Meeting patterns, feedback on drafts and data, who provides day-to-day teaching. “Can you describe how a new trainee’s project is discussed in its first few months?”


Research and learning
Questions the group works on, project choice, access to methods and room to develop ideas. “How have recent trainees moved from an initial task to a question they led?”


Credit and collaboration
How ideas, data, authorship and shared projects are discussed. “Could you describe a recent collaboration and how contributions were decided?”


Resources and feasibility
Current support, essential equipment or collaborators, and realistic project scope. “What resources are already committed to this work, and what would require a new decision?”


Trainee trajectories
Completion, publications or other outputs, and the range of next roles people have entered. “May I speak with a recent alumnus about how the group supported their next step?”


Environment
How colleagues help one another, what happens when work stalls, and whether people can ask difficult questions. “What did the group do when a recent project ran into a serious obstacle?”



Read recent papers before these conversations. Ask how a possible project would build on that work, which methods you would need to learn and who would teach them. Confirm the funding and facilities available for your work, including what depends on a pending application. [1].
crumbs: Choosing an advisor and research environment

title: Choosing an advisor and research environment
text:
Conversations and visits
Talk with people at different points in the laboratory: a newer member, someone approaching a transition, and, where possible, a former member. A visit, rotation or attendance at a lab meeting can reveal how questions are handled and who participates. Conversations away from the immediate selection setting may make it easier for people to explain ordinary practice. Ask the same core questions of several people, but leave room for what they think matters. [2]; [3].
Ask for concrete examples: “Could you describe the feedback on the last paper or project proposal?” Follow up on how the advisor helped when a trainee was stuck or a project needed to change direction. Ask how decisions about credit were made. Compare the advisor’s account with those of current and former members.
Give people room to decline a question, and keep private accounts confidential. If several people describe the same problem with supervision, treatment or credit, take it seriously. Seek independent advice before committing, especially when a prospective advisor’s explanation conflicts with the accounts of current or former members. [2].



Example: compare a laboratory through evidence

In this fictional comparison, Mina is choosing between two PhD laboratories in the same field. She needs structured feedback while learning to frame a project, but she also wants room to develop an independent question.
Laboratory A: the advisor and two trainees describe weekly individual meetings. An alumnus recalls detailed feedback on an early proposal. A student explains how a lab discussion helped narrow a stalled project to a related, feasible question. The first-year project would sit within a funded collaboration, so its initial scope is relatively narrow and day-to-day teaching would often come from a senior postdoc.
Laboratory B: the research question matches Mina’s interests more closely, and two trainees value the freedom to shape their projects. The advisor schedules individual meetings every two weeks, and a staff scientist offers regular methods guidance. An alumnus describes developing a question in the group and carrying that line of work into the next position. When one project stalled, the trainee moved to a new question and another researcher took over the original work. The trainee says the advisor supported the change, although the first months required more independent planning than Mina expects to manage comfortably.
Mina chooses Laboratory A. She accepts a narrower starting project and more day-to-day dependence on a senior postdoc because weekly feedback meets her immediate training need. Laboratory B offers the closer topic, earlier ownership and a credible route to independence, but expects more planning between meetings. A student who already works confidently with that method might reasonably choose it.
crumbs: Choosing an advisor and research environment

title: Choosing an advisor and research environment
text:
Compare the opportunities
Compare the opportunities against your priorities. You might accept less freedom in exchange for closer initial supervision, but first establish what that supervision would involve. For a new group with no alumni, ask who will provide day-to-day training while it is being established. Observe scientific discussions where possible and find out what support the department offers. [1].
For a PhD, check whether the programme provides alternatives if the initial project or advisor arrangement does not work. For a postdoc, discuss how you could develop a distinct contribution and what support you would receive for the next position. Agree which projects you could take with you and which collaborations would continue. [2]; [3].
Resolve the questions that could change your choice before accepting. Record the agreed project, supervision and funding arrangements so you and the advisor can revisit them when work begins.

Before choosing an advisor or environment


I know what training and opportunities I need from this PhD or postdoc.
I have assessed research fit, supervision, environment, resources and trainee trajectories separately.
I have asked several people for concrete examples and compared their accounts with direct observation where possible.
I know which unanswered question would change my decision.
I have not treated prestige, a familiar topic or one positive interaction as sufficient evidence.

title: CVs, resumes, letters and references
text:
Choose the document
Read the advertisement to establish what the employer needs and which documents, format and deadline it requires. Choose examples that show how your experience meets the selection criteria. Use the requested letter or statement to explain connections that a reader may not see from a list of appointments and achievements.
An academic CV presents education, research, publications, teaching, awards and service. A resume selects the experience and capabilities most relevant to a particular role. Document names and conventions vary between countries: use the employer’s instructions to decide how much detail to include. [4]; [1].
Keep one private master record of roles, dates, contributions, outputs and collaborators. When preparing an application, select evidence from that record against the advertised requirements. A short working table can help you decide what to include:
Keep factual labels precise: submitted, under review, preprint and published do not mean the same thing. A stable PDF is sensible when the call permits it and layout matters; check the submitted file after export. [4].

title: CVs, resumes, letters and references
text:
What the reader needs to decide
Evidence I can show
Where it belongs




Can this person do the role’s central work?
A project, decision or deliverable with an identifiable individual contribution
Resume experience entry; letter example


Can this person work with the relevant people?
A collaboration, mentoring activity or communication task with a concrete outcome
Resume experience entry; letter example


What is this person’s scholarly record?
Education, appointments, publications with accurate status, talks and service
CV

title: CVs, resumes, letters and references
text:
Organize the CV or resume
Decide the section order before polishing individual entries. In an academic CV, research appointments and publications may lead an application for a postdoctoral position; teaching experience deserves more space in an application for a teaching position. Use clear section names and include grants, mentoring and service where relevant. Within dated sections, list recent work first and use consistent dates, role titles and publication details. [3]; [1].
In a faculty application, dates, project names and descriptions of your contribution must agree across the CV, letter and statements. The documents develop different aspects of the application: the CV records the work, the letter explains how your experience fits the position, and the research statement develops the proposed program. [7].
The examples follow Mira Okafor, a fictional postdoc applying for a research program-manager role involving collaborations between genomic researchers and clinical teams.
Compare the outline she might use for a research post with the one for this program-manager role:








Document and reader
Early sections
Later sections




Academic CV for a research post
Education; research appointments and contributions; publications and preprints with exact status
Teaching and mentoring; awards, service and invited presentations


Resume for the program-manager role
Selected project coordination; collaboration and review experience
Relevant analysis methods; education and concise research background



These are working outlines, not universal templates. If the advertisement emphasizes teaching, regulation or a particular method, the order and space should change accordingly.
For a resume, choose the few experiences that answer the role’s questions. Explain the research in terms the intended reader can understand while retaining the technical detail needed to judge your work. Name the problem or responsibility, the action you personally took, and the output a new reader can assess. Use the vocabulary of the call when it accurately describes your work. [6]; [1].
Use short entries, visible dates and enough white space to separate sections. Quantify the scale or outcome when it helps—for example, the number of people trained or projects coordinated. Keep method names that establish a technical qualification; explain their purpose when the first reader may be a recruiter outside your field. [6].



Example: one factual contribution, two document entries


CV — Research experience

Postdoctoral researcher, Systems Genomics Group, 2024–present
Cross-laboratory perturbation screen

Developed and documented the reproducible analysis workflow.
Coordinated a results review with clinical and computational collaborators.
Trained two junior researchers to run and check the workflow.


Resume — Project coordination


Postdoctoral researcher, Systems Genomics Group, 2024–present


Coordinated a perturbation-screen project across two laboratories, using one documented analysis workflow for the joint review.
Presented the findings and unresolved questions to clinical and computational collaborators, then recorded the checks assigned to each laboratory.
Trained two junior researchers to run and check the workflow.



The resume entry gives more space to coordination and shared analysis because these are central to the target role. For a computational-research position, the analysis itself would need more technical detail.

title: CVs, resumes, letters and references
text:
Writing a cover letter
When a letter is requested, name the role, explain your interest in the organization and develop a few examples of relevant experience. Use each paragraph to address a requirement, with enough context to explain your contribution. Leave the full chronology to the CV or resume. [2].
For this example, the advertised role includes coordinating joint projects and organizing research reviews.



Example: a short letter that connects fit to evidence

Dear Hiring Committee,
I am applying for the Research Program Manager position because your joint-project program brings genomic researchers and clinical teams together around shared studies. Coordinating that kind of work has become the part of my postdoctoral research that I most want to develop.
During my postdoc, I coordinated a perturbation screen across two laboratories. I developed the shared analysis workflow and trained two junior researchers to run and check it. This gave both teams a common set of results to discuss while retaining access to the underlying analysis.
I also organized the project review with clinical and computational colleagues. I presented the findings and unresolved questions, then documented the checks each laboratory would undertake. This combination of technical understanding, a common review process and clear follow-up is what I would bring to the institute’s joint projects.
Thank you for considering my application. I would be pleased to discuss the position with you.
Sincerely,
Mira Okafor


The letter connects Mira’s interest in the institute’s joint projects to her experience coordinating analysis and agreeing follow-up work with collaborators. The resume lists these contributions; the letter explains why she wants to make this work central to her next role.

title: CVs, resumes, letters and references
text:
Asking for references
Choose referees who know your work well enough to describe your contribution. Ask whether they can provide a strong reference, leaving time to approach someone else if necessary. Discuss why you are seeking this role and which parts of your work together are relevant to it. Send the position description, current application materials, those selected examples, and the submission instructions and deadline. For several applications, keep the deadlines and links in one table. [5].
If a referee asks for a draft or notes, provide factual material: the context, your role, the result and relevant examples from your work together. The referee must decide what to endorse and write the final assessment. Check submission confirmations and send a polite reminder when a deadline approaches.
Before submitting, compare the documents with the call. Check dates, role titles and publication status across the packet; ask a reader to identify your strongest qualifications from the first page; and inspect the exported files for layout problems.

title: Finding and applying for positions
text:
Choose the appropriate application route
Begin with the work you want to do and the experience you can offer. Search advertisements and organizations working in that area, and ask colleagues about opportunities. Keep track of promising positions and their deadlines.
The application route depends on whether you are seeking research training, a postdoctoral project or a role with defined responsibilities.
For each serious option, note why it interests you, which requirements you meet and what you still need to find out. Keep the requested materials and contact details with the deadline.
The selection conversation also differs. A PhD interview usually tests preparation for training and gives you evidence about supervision and the programme. A postdoc discussion asks what scientific direction you could develop together, what you already contribute and what the group can support. A non-academic employer is recruiting for defined work: an early screen may test the basic match, while later technical, behavioral or panel interviews may ask how you handled decisions, collaboration and setbacks. Ask for the format rather than assuming that one academic research talk prepares you for every route.

title: Finding and applying for positions
text:
Search
What to establish
Application route




PhD
Relevant projects or supervisors, training arrangements and funding
Check whether you apply to a programme or a specific project, and whether prior supervisor contact is expected. [2]


Academic postdoc
The research direction, training and resources the group can offer
Apply to advertised positions or inquire directly with a relevant group, following any contact instructions. [1]


Non-academic scientific role
The work, required capabilities and team
Use the advertised process; conversations with people in the role can help you understand the requirements.

title: Finding and applying for positions
text:
Finding opportunities
Combine programme and employer sites with job boards, professional networks and conversations. Ask colleagues which organizations work on the questions or problems that interest you. Follow useful leads beyond familiar institutions.
For a postdoc, list groups connected to the questions, methods or research direction you want to develop. Read recent work, then narrow the list through conversations with people in the field, current members and alumni. Include relevant groups without advertised openings: some recruit through direct inquiries. [1].
For a PhD, check how a supervisor is assigned. A programme may offer rotations or several potential supervisors; a project-based position may already have a defined question and supervisor. Confirm availability, entry requirements and the funding arrangement before preparing an application. Ask what support covers and for how long. See Choosing an advisor and research environment for assessing supervision. [2].
For a non-academic role, identify what the person hired will do, which capabilities are essential and who they will work with. Match each requirement to evidence from your experience. Separate requirements you do not yet meet from experience you have but need to explain in the employer’s terms. If the advert leaves a requirement unclear, ask someone familiar with the work before deciding whether you meet it. Use CVs, resumes, letters and references to turn these matches into application material.

title: Finding and applying for positions
text:
Write a specific inquiry
Before contacting someone, read their group’s work and any application instructions. Explain the connection to your experience and ask a question the recipient can answer, such as whether the group anticipates recruiting in your intended period.
For an academic-postdoc inquiry, name the research connection, give one or two examples of relevant work and say when you hope to start. Ask whether the group expects to recruit or would be willing to discuss a possible project. Include or link materials only when requested or when they help the recipient assess the inquiry. [1].
If a direct inquiry receives no reply, send a short follow-up after allowing time for a response, then continue with other opportunities. A conversation does not replace a required formal application: keep track of that deadline separately. [1].



Example: a short, specific postdoc inquiry

Nadia is finishing a cell-biology PhD in September 2027. She has built a live-imaging workflow that segments and tracks epithelial repair fronts. Dr Imani’s fictional group studies immune–epithelial interactions during tissue repair. Nadia has read two recent papers from the group and wants to develop a project that combines imaging with quantitative analysis.

Subject: Postdoctoral inquiry: live imaging of epithelial repair
Dear Dr Imani,
I expect to complete my cell-biology PhD in September 2027. I developed a live-imaging workflow to segment and track epithelial repair fronts, and would now like to study how immune cells influence that repair. Your group’s work on immune–epithelial interactions is closely connected to this question.
Do you expect to recruit a postdoc in autumn 2027? I would welcome a conversation about whether my imaging and analysis experience could contribute to your research. I have attached my CV and a brief research summary.
Best wishes,
Nadia Patel

Questions about supervision and possible projects can follow if Dr Imani is interested in discussing recruitment.

title: Finding and applying for positions
text:
Prepare for the interviews
An interview can include an initial screening call, a research talk, meetings with possible colleagues, an assessment task or several conversations over a visit. Ask for the agenda, who you will meet and any presentation or task instructions. Use this information to prepare: a recruiter may need a concise explanation of how your experience meets the role’s requirements, while a scientific colleague may ask how you chose a method or interpreted a result. Prepare questions about the work and support you would need before accepting.
For a postdoc, prepare to explain your PhD question, your contribution and what the results establish. Read the prospective group’s recent papers and bring ideas to discuss. If a question falls outside your knowledge, explain what you understand and ask for clarification where needed. Ask about supervision, resources, project ownership and support for your next career step. [1].
For a non-academic role, prepare brief examples that connect your experience to the problem described in the advert: a technical decision, a collaboration, a setback or a result that changed a next step. Be ready to distinguish what you did from what the team did. Ask how the team defines a successful first period in the role, what it needs from the person hired and how the work is evaluated. For a PhD, explain the experience that prepares you to learn and investigate the proposed area, then ask about the programme route, available supervisors and training environment.



Example: discussing a possible postdoc project

Asked how she would begin in Dr Imani’s group, Nadia says: “I would first learn how the group currently measures repair and which results are reliable enough to build on. Then I would try my tracking workflow on a small experiment and compare what it shows with the existing analysis. If it adds useful information, we could plan a larger imaging project. I can bring the segmentation and reproducible analysis; I would need help learning the immune-cell assays.”


After each conversation, write down what you learned, what remains uncertain and the promised next action. Send a brief follow-up when it is appropriate to thank the person, correct a material omission or confirm an agreed step. This record will also help you compare an offer with the criteria you set at the start.

title: Finding and applying for positions
section: Review the search and compare offers
text:
Review the search and compare offers
Keep several possibilities active while awaiting decisions. Review where applications stop. If applications to apparently suitable roles rarely reach screening, ask a knowledgeable reader to assess whether your experience meets the requirements and whether the documents make that clear. If interviews repeatedly expose the same gap, distinguish difficulty explaining your experience from experience you still need to gain. The first calls for a clearer example; the second may require training or a different choice of roles. Record promised follow-ups and deadlines [3].
When an offer arrives, compare the actual work and conditions with your priorities. Resolve unanswered questions about the project, supervision, funding or employment period, location and start date. If other decisions are pending, ask when a response is needed and whether more time is possible. Use the research-environment comparison for a PhD or postdoc, and return to your career priorities for other roles. [1].

Checks as the search progresses


I understand the position, application route and requirements.
I can explain why the work interests me and which experience prepares me for it.
I have followed the position’s stated application or contact instructions.
I have prepared research or work examples and questions for the interview.
I have recorded what I learned and kept the rest of the search moving.

title: Finding and applying for positions
text:
References



sabbagh, u. (2021, November 5). How to find, apply for, and choose a postdoc.
Fomina, A. (n.d.). A quick guide to Ph.D. Sci.STEPS.
Jensen, D. G. (2010, August 20). Tooling Up: A Job-Search Plan for the Person Without One (Part One). Science Careers.

title: Finding a group leader position
text:
Define an independent program
Leading a group changes the work as well as the job title. You would set research priorities, support people and obtain resources alongside doing science. Decide whether you want that combination, then look for positions whose research, teaching and mentoring responsibilities fit the group you intend to build. [3].
Build the program around questions you intend to lead. Explain how your previous work prepares you to address them, which projects you would begin, and how their results would guide later work. Independence can come from a distinct question or approach within the same field. Discuss with your current supervisor which questions each group will pursue, what materials or data can be transferred, and where collaboration will continue. Agree who will lead the overlapping work; continued collaboration need not prevent you from developing a distinct program. [2].
Prepare a short program summary before searching widely. Include the people, facilities and funding needed to start; these needs will help you assess calls and later offers. If an essential assay can only be performed in your current lab, agree how that work could continue or develop an alternative before making it central to the proposal.

title: Finding a group leader position
text:
Finding suitable positions
Compare each call with your program summary. A research institute, a university department and a teaching-focused position may offer very different time, facilities and student populations. Check whether your projects can work in that setting, who you could collaborate with and how the group would be staffed. Use recent faculty appointments and conversations with colleagues to understand the local expectations. [2].
For each role, keep the advertised criteria and requested materials alongside the parts of your program that fit and the questions you still need to ask. Confirm facilities, appointment terms and local expectations with the host. A department’s scientific interests may match yours even when its available space or staffing cannot support your first projects. [2].

title: Finding a group leader position
text:
Prepare the faculty application
Adapt the materials to the call, using CVs, resumes, letters and references. The research statement should connect your important contributions to the program you intend to build. Write for scientists outside your specialty: explain why the question matters, how your prior work prepares you to address it, and what you will lead. Give enough experimental detail for them to assess whether the first projects are feasible. The exact balance between past and future work depends on the call. [2]; [4].
Use the letter to explain your interest in the position and the contribution you would make. In a teaching or mentoring statement, connect experience to specific plans for this setting: what you have taught, how you helped someone learn, and how you would develop that work with the students or researchers there. [2].

Test readiness with the research statement
Drafting the statement can help you judge readiness. You need both an account of completed work and credible future projects. Organize the draft around four parts:







Part
What a reader should be able to find




Research trajectory
How your prior contribution prepares you to address the new question, and which work belongs to the former and proposed groups.


Program question
A question broad enough to matter to adjacent scientists, stated without assuming that the proposed answer is already known.


First projects
What each project compares, which possible explanations it can distinguish, how the findings would guide the next experiment, and whether it can run alongside another project.


Feasibility and growth
The people, facilities and access required to begin; how the first projects could be funded and how their answers create the next tractable question.



The following planning sheet uses the hypothetical epithelial-injury program introduced in Chalk talks.



Example: turn a program into a research-statement plan

Opening question and significance
How does resolved inflammation change the next epithelial injury response? Understanding whether cells retain an injury history could explain why the same tissue responds differently to a later insult.
Preparation and independent boundary
Prior work on acute inflammation supplies the biological starting point and culture experience. The former lab continues acute inflammation-signalling studies. The new group leads the epithelial re-injury comparisons and functional assays; any shared protocol or collaboration will be agreed explicitly.
First project and decision — Year 1
After removing the inflammatory cue, compare exposed and control airway organoids. Measure cell composition, expression and accessibility to assess whether a retained difference occurs within the same cell types or reflects a changed mixture of cells. These comparisons guide which explanation to investigate further; the re-injury project tests whether exposure history changes function.
Parallel project and dependency — Months 9–24
Re-injure matched organoids and measure barrier repair and inflammatory output. This can begin alongside the first project. A mechanistic project starts only after a reproducible functional difference is established.
Conditions for starting
Confirm access to primary airway organoid cultures, a cue-clearance assay, sufficient single-cell facility capacity and a first researcher able to run the functional assay. State an alternative analysis or facility route if the preferred access is unavailable.


Give the draft to readers with different roles: one who knows the field, one who can assess a related scientific question, and one who understands the prospective setting. Ask them to mark the first point where they lose the question, cannot distinguish the projects, or cannot see how the work starts. Revise the plan behind the prose when their answer exposes a missing comparison, dependency or boundary.
Share the program summary and application materials with your referees, including the agreed boundary with your current lab. See reference requests for coordinating their submissions.

title: Finding a group leader position
text:
Prepare for the interview
Before a visit or remote interview, ask for the itinerary, audiences and presentation formats. Read recent work by the people you will meet. Prepare concise explanations of your previous contributions, initial projects, independence, possible funding routes and teaching experience. Discuss genuine scientific connections with prospective colleagues, and use meetings with recent hires to ask how the department supports a new group. [2]; [4].
Match questions to the person who can answer them. A facility director can explain capacity, fees and sample preparation; a department chair can clarify teaching, review and space commitments; a recent hire can describe what support was available in practice; trainees can describe supervision and local research life. Record the answer, the person who gave it and what still needs written confirmation. For a resource your first project depends on, ask when you could use it and what would have to be arranged first.
For the job talk, use Explaining research to an audience, Designing a presentation and Delivering a talk and answering questions to develop and rehearse a scientific explanation. For a chalk talk, use the board-map method: show the program overview, a comparison that distinguishes your proposed explanations, and how different findings would change the next experiment. Rehearse interruptions and returning to the map.

title: Finding a group leader position
text:
Comparing and negotiating offers
Once an offer exists, cost the first projects and compare their needs with the proposed support. Include staffing and running costs as well as equipment and space. Check when the resources become available and what restrictions apply: do salary amounts include benefits, for example, and must startup funds be spent by a particular date? Also discuss the teaching and service expected while you establish the group. Use these details to explain each request. [1]; [4].
For the proposed epithelial program, access to an established single-cell facility could reduce the need to purchase equipment. Check its capacity, charges and sample-preparation support before removing those items from the budget. Airway-organoid culture, cue-clearance measurements, staffing and facility access must also be available when each project is due to begin.
Use the same categories to compare offers, including the start date, teaching load, appointment or review timetable and personal constraints. Prioritize the requests that determine whether you can establish the program. Discuss alternatives when an item is unavailable—for example, funded facility access instead of equipment—and ask for the agreed resources and conditions in writing. Seek advice from recent hires and an experienced colleague who understands the local appointment system. [1].
For the hypothetical epithelial program, a request sheet could look like this:










Program need
What to establish from the offer
Acceptable alternative or follow-up




Airway-organoid culture
Suitable space, access date and responsibility for any preparation
Temporary shared space with a written date for the permanent arrangement


Single-cell analysis
Facility capacity, access charges, sample-preparation support and booking lead time
Another facility only if its cost and turnaround fit the first-project schedule


First researcher
Amount, duration, eligible role and whether salary costs include benefits
A different staffing mix that still supplies the required assay expertise


Time to establish the group
First-year teaching and service assignments
A specified lighter schedule or delayed course responsibility, where the setting permits


Startup funds
Included cost categories, purchasing process and any spending deadline
Written extension or staged funds when procurement or hiring will outlast the initial period





The written follow-up should lead with appreciation, then separate essential clarifications from ranked requests. Each request should name the work it enables. Avoid copying another applicant’s list: equipment access, teaching arrangements, appointment terms and negotiable items vary by institution and jurisdiction.
