title: Career transitions
text:
Decide what needs to change
Before making a career move, work out what you want to change. A new position may leave the same workload or funding uncertainty in place. Consider whether a change of project, supervisor or role would address the problem.
Think about what you would want to keep as well as what you want to leave. You may still enjoy research but need more predictable hours or a longer contract. If so, investigate whether another research setting offers those conditions before deciding whether to change the kind of work you do.
Compare the available options against the conditions you want to change and those you want to preserve. Include changing project or supervisor as well as leaving a degree or institution. Note what you still need to find out before deciding [4].
Discuss the options with people who know the work and can help assess its prospects. Working conditions, mentorship and alternatives to an academic career were recurring concerns in a survey of postdoctoral researchers [1]. When a supervisor is part of the problem, seek advice elsewhere before deciding how to raise it.

title: Career transitions
text:
Example: deciding what to change

Amir is a postdoc who still enjoys microscopy and troubleshooting. He no longer wants his next position to depend mainly on building an independent publication programme, and he needs to remain in the same region.
Staying for another year could complete an active paper, but it would not change the type of work or the uncertain funding horizon. A second postdoc would offer more bench research, yet preserve the same features he wants to leave. After visiting a microscopy core and speaking with two staff members, Amir learns that the role would replace much of his own-project time with user training, method development and responsibility for reliable shared workflows.
Amir accepts the core-facility role. The decision is a trade-off: he gives up some control over research questions in return for locally based, collaborative technical work. He agrees to a six-week start date only after identifying what the active paper needs and what can be handed over.

title: Career transitions
text:
Plan the move
Consider applying directly when you have investigated the new role and could start when needed. An intermediate step may help if something specific prevents the move or you still need to try the work before committing. A short placement could help you judge whether the work suits you. A course could teach a required skill; a short contract could provide income before the next position starts. Relocation or caring responsibilities may also affect the route. Decide what the intermediate step needs to accomplish and when you would be ready to move on. Compare it with applying directly before committing to another course or position.
Work backwards from the intended start date. List unfinished work and any materials or access that need to be transferred, then agree who will handle each item and when. Discuss any contribution you expect to continue after departure.
Allow time for delays and agree which unfinished tasks could be handed over if they cannot be completed before departure. Consider the workload during the transition alongside family and caring responsibilities. Agree the limits of any temporary overlap between roles [5].

title: Career transitions
text:
Handing over projects
For each active project, explain the question, what the work has established and what remains to be decided. Record where a colleague can find the data, notebooks, code and samples, with the relevant versions and permissions. Include instructions for regenerating the current result. Label provisional analyses, identify assumptions still to be tested and describe approaches that failed. Flag supplies that may run out or access that will expire, and identify who can decide how to continue.
Ask a colleague to retrieve the material and reproduce a result from these instructions before you leave. Arrange continued institutional storage and access with the group; follow its rules for notebooks, data and samples [3].



Example: a project handover

Amir will start in a microscopy core facility in six weeks. His handover record assigns the remaining work and identifies where to find the material.
Manuscript: the main analysis is complete. The collaborating researcher will check a control by 14 May and discuss its implications with Amir on 16 May. Repository release v1.3 and the figure-to-data table are in the lab project space.
Pilot project: no feasible next experiment remains with the available materials and time. The notebook, raw data and a note explaining the stopping decision are indexed in the project space.
Access check: a colleague will regenerate Figure 2 using the README before Amir leaves. Amir will correct any missing instructions. The lab administrator will confirm which group account retains access.

title: Career transitions
text:
Continuing responsibilities
Tell the people who need to plan around the change once the timing is settled. Explain what you can finish before leaving and agree any continuing responsibilities, such as contributing to manuscript revisions. If you are taking a project to a new group, discuss which questions, materials and collaborations will move with it [2].
Discuss authorship on unfinished papers with the contributors and record the agreement. Ask prospective referees whether they can support your application. Arrange any continuing access to data or systems with the institution.
If a relationship is difficult, reduce unnecessary dependence: keep clear records, obtain advice from more than one mentor and use the appropriate local route for a matter that cannot be resolved directly.

title: Career transitions
text:
Begin the next role
Before starting, discuss your initial responsibilities and who can give feedback. Ask colleagues how decisions and routine communication work, and agree when to review your progress [2].
Agree what to work on before the first review, allowing time to learn unfamiliar procedures. A research scientist might learn a quality-system workflow and complete a defined analysis; an editor might assess a supervised submission while learning the journal’s decision process and audience. Find out whose work depends on yours and what they need from you. Adjust the plan with your supervisor or manager as you learn more about the role.

text:
References

title: Mentoring
text:
Agreeing expectations
Discuss what the researcher wants to learn and what support the mentor can provide. A short mentoring agreement can record those expectations and give both people something to revisit as the work and the researcher’s needs change [6].
Prepare separately before the first substantial conversation or when revisiting the arrangement. The researcher identifies current work, decisions they want help with, capabilities they want to develop and circumstances that affect what they can undertake. The mentor identifies what support they can reliably provide, where another person is better placed to help and which constraints are fixed. Begin with the researcher’s account, then compare it with the mentor’s expectations. Preparing independently gives both people a chance to identify priorities before either adopts the other’s view [7].
Record the decisions in language that both people can use. A concise agreement might cover:
Choose a meeting interval that fits the current work and test whether it produces useful decisions. A weekly meeting that repeatedly ends without a choice, action or feedback is not automatically better than a less frequent meeting with good preparation. Conversely, a new method, a difficult transition or a stalled project may justify temporarily closer contact. Early-career researchers surveyed in a 2026 preprint placed high value on useful regular meetings, open communication, boundaries and participation in decisions; the study does not imply one schedule for every relationship [5].
Do not require disclosure of private circumstances. A researcher can state the work consequence—“I cannot attend before 10:00 for the next six weeks” or “I need to change the travel plan”—without explaining a diagnosis, family matter or other personal detail. The mentor should explain which constraints can be changed, which require another office and how to reach that office.
Keep individual supervision and development in this agreement. Put practices shared across the group in the lab manual, and keep safety, employment, data and programme requirements in their authoritative records.

title: Mentoring
text:
Purpose: Which research decisions and development goals should this relationship support now? What lies outside its scope?
Contact: Which meetings are protected? What belongs in a meeting, a short message or a written draft? What counts as urgent?
Preparation: What should the researcher send or decide before a meeting? What will the mentor read, check or arrange?
Decisions: Which choices can the researcher make independently? Which require discussion because of cost, safety, ethics, shared resources or project commitments?
Feedback: How will each person ask for feedback on work, reasoning and the relationship? How quickly can each realistically respond?
Boundaries: What working-time, privacy and leave expectations apply? Which matters should go to a programme, manager, committee or specialist service?
Development: Which capability or opportunity will be developed next, and how will practice and feedback occur?
Review: When will the agreement be revisited, and what event should trigger an earlier conversation?

title: Mentoring
text:
Use meetings to develop judgment
Bring the material needed for one or two consequential questions. A useful agenda says what has changed, what decision is needed and what the researcher currently recommends. Attach a figure, short rationale or draft when the evidence itself matters; routine status can be brief so the meeting has time for the decision.
Ask the researcher to propose the next experiment and explain what its possible results would tell them. Discuss the reasoning before supplying your own answer. If they cannot choose a next step, find out why. They may need help interpreting a control, training in the method or a decision about access that only you can make. Asking them to be more independent will not resolve a decision they lack the authority to make.
Give a novice a task on which they can practise without putting irreplaceable material or a major project commitment at risk. Demonstrate the technique, explain common failure modes and begin with a task whose expected behavior is already known. As performance becomes reliable, shorten the instructions and move responsibility for planning, execution and interpretation to the researcher [4]. When choosing a research problem together, consider whether it interests the researcher, whether it is feasible with the available expertise and what they would learn by pursuing it [2].



Example: mentor a decision without taking it over

In this fictional example, Aruna is a second-year doctoral researcher studying a signaling reporter in cultured cells. She can run the established assay and controls reproducibly and can plan and document a complete run without supervision. Two later pilot runs after a perturbation show different reporter timing. The second also has lower viability and uses a new reagent lot. There is time for one more run this week: either a limited diagnostic comparison or the first large downstream assay.
Aruna’s mentor begins: “Which run would you do this week?”
“Delay the downstream assay and compare the old and new lots in the same culture batch,” Aruna says. “I’ll use the established controls and record viability.”
“What would that let you conclude?”
“If the timing follows the lot and the controls and viability are acceptable, I’ll replace that lot and start the downstream assay next week. If it does not, or viability still differs, the comparison has not resolved the earlier inconsistency and I’ll bring back the options before the next run.”
The mentor asks what delaying the downstream assay costs. They agree to use this week’s run to check the reagent-lot explanation before committing to the larger assay. The mentor confirms access to the old lot and control material and offers to review Aruna’s one-paragraph rationale before she commits the material. Aruna owns the design, run and first interpretation. Their follow-up will examine the controls and viability before deciding whether to proceed.


If Aruna had never run the assay, the same handover would be premature. The mentor or an experienced colleague should first demonstrate the workflow, observe a practice run and check that Aruna can recognize failed controls. If the choice could irreversibly consume rare material, the mentor should join the decision even after Aruna has mastered the technique. Match support to demonstrated capability for this task and the cost of error.
Peer and specialist mentors can provide day-to-day methods knowledge that the primary mentor lacks. Agree which training they will provide and recognize that contribution. A junior researcher should not become solely responsible for another person’s training. The primary mentor must check that the teacher has time and credit, and that the learner knows who will review their progress and help when the teacher cannot.

title: Mentoring
text:
Feedback
Be clear about what needs to change. “The conclusion exceeds these controls” concerns scientific reasoning. “I need the figure two days before the meeting if you want line-by-line comments” concerns workflow. “I spoke for most of our last three meetings; I want you to present your recommendation first next time” concerns the mentoring relationship. Mixing these can turn a correctable issue into a judgment about the person.
Point to the part of the work or the interaction that needs to change, explain the problem and agree what will happen differently next time. The researcher should also be able to say which support was useful, where advice conflicted or arrived too late and what they need next. Reciprocal feedback does not make the power relationship equal; it gives the senior person information they are responsible for acting on.
When the same problem recurs, compare it with the agreement. Ask whether the expectation was unclear, the promised support was unavailable, the capability was overestimated or circumstances changed. Revise the arrangement and set a review point. Repeated credit-taking, retaliation, blocked access to other advice, coercive disclosure or unsafe practice requires help beyond an ordinary feedback conversation. Use a committee, programme lead, manager, ombud or the institution’s current formal route. Do not require the more vulnerable person to repair the relationship alone.

title: Mentoring
section: Plan development beyond the immediate project
text:
Plan development beyond the immediate project
Hold a broader planning conversation periodically and at transitions. Both people prepare independently; the researcher speaks first. Review recent work and discuss what they want to learn or explore next, including career questions that their current project will not answer. Identify opportunities to do that work, the support needed and any limits on time or access. Agree a small number of actions and dates so that development receives time alongside project tasks.
Look for opportunities to practise the skill in real work. A researcher learning to write could draft part of a paper and discuss the revisions with a coauthor. Someone learning how publication decisions are made could join an editorial conversation or work through a review with an experienced colleague [1]; [8]. Obtain permission before involving a trainee in confidential communication, and agree their role.
A useful plan names one near-term opportunity and what evidence will show learning. “Improve presentations” is difficult to act on. “Give the next 10-minute project update; rehearse once with the postdoc; ask two colleagues whether the decision and uncertainty were clear; review the recording with the mentor on 12 November” creates practice and feedback.
Career development may reveal options that the primary mentor does not know well. Use exploring career options to compare paths, then identify someone who can supply current experience. The mentor’s responsibility is to support an informed choice, including when it differs from their own path.

title: Mentoring
text:
Build a mentoring network
One person rarely provides deep technical guidance, project authority, career knowledge, sponsorship and confidential perspective. List the roles the researcher needs now and where each can come from: primary supervisor, methods expert, collaborator, committee member, peer, career contact or institutional adviser.
The primary mentor should welcome complementary mentors, make introductions where useful and state that seeking other advice is expected. Multiple relationships can reduce dependence and make conflicting advice visible [3]. When advice conflicts, return to the decision: which adviser has relevant knowledge or authority, what assumptions differ and who ultimately owns the choice?

Review a mentoring relationship


Both people can state the current purpose, boundaries and next review date.
Meetings end with a decision, action or clearly named unresolved question.
The researcher explains reasoning before the mentor supplies an answer.
Support matches capability for the particular task and the cost of error.
Feedback can travel in both directions without requiring private disclosure.
The development plan includes real practice, feedback and a date, not only aspirations.
Other mentors cover needs that the primary relationship cannot meet.
Repeated power, safety, credit or conduct problems have a route beyond the direct supervisor.

title: Lab manuals and shared expectations
text:
Decide what needs documenting
A lab manual helps members find the group’s shared practices without having to learn every convention by watching others. Explain who is responsible for routine work and whom to ask when an arrangement does not fit.
The manual need not contain every protocol, personal agreement or university rule. Operational instructions and checklists can sit in the same document when a small group can keep it navigable; a larger group may link separate protocol, safety and data records. Choose the arrangement that lets a member find the current instruction and its owner [5].
List the recurring questions first. Ask current members what they had to learn by watching others, which questions receive different answers and which unstated expectations have delayed work or made them reluctant to ask for help. Review onboarding questions, repeated booking or handover problems and decisions that depend on seniority. Include technicians, managers, students, postdocs and research staff so that the manual covers the responsibilities and support each needs, including the work of maintaining shared resources.
Write down a practice when it recurs across members and knowing it in advance changes what someone does. Common candidates include communication and response times, meetings, shared equipment, routine responsibilities, time away, data and code, mistakes, feedback, joining and leaving. Choose among these topics according to the group’s work: field seasons, clinical data and shared instruments raise different questions from those of a small theoretical group. Published manuals illustrate those choices; they do not establish a universal policy.
Keep shared practices in the lab manual: routine workflow, reciprocal expectations, responsible roles and routes for questions or concerns. Keep an individual’s goals, supervision, feedback and development in a personal mentoring agreement; see mentoring. Keep employment conditions, safety rules, ethics approvals, data-management plans, access controls and collaboration-specific decisions in the responsible institutional or project record. The lab manual can link to those records and explain what members need to do.
Keeping these records separate prevents a local preference from appearing to be an institutional requirement and keeps private matters out of a group document. Mentor–mentee expectations should be tailored and revisited as the relationship changes [4].
Decide which material can be public, which belongs on an internal group site and which should remain in an access-controlled project or institutional system. Prospective members can benefit from seeing genuine expectations. Keep sensitive contact details, restricted data procedures and individual accommodations in the appropriate protected record.

title: Lab manuals and shared expectations
text:
Writing the policies
A value such as “respect people’s time” can introduce a section, but it does not settle a booking clash. State when the policy applies, what people should normally do and who is responsible. Then explain what changes in a foreseeable exception and where someone can take a question or concern. Name who keeps the policy current. These points can fit into a short paragraph; they do not each need a separate heading.
Use reciprocal language where responsibility is reciprocal. If members should flag a delayed analysis, state when and to whom; if the project lead promises a response or decision, state that too. Include a route that does not depend solely on the person whose conduct might be questioned. A manual can name an institutional ombud, graduate programme, staff representative or reporting office using the organization’s current terminology. It should not promise confidentiality, remedies or authority that the group cannot provide.
The SAFE Labs authors similarly turn broad aspirations into actions that can be documented while leaving groups to choose policies suited to their setting [3].



Example: a shared-equipment policy


Northbank Imaging Group manual — shared microscope bookings, version 1.1

Finish at the booked end time whenever possible. If an acquisition is likely to run over, the current user updates the calendar and contacts the next user as soon as they know. The next user decides whether moving their start is workable; silence does not mean agreement. If the users cannot agree, each tells the lab manager how time-critical the session is, what preparation is already committed and whether the work can be repeated. The manager decides, records the reason and arranges a replacement slot when one is needed. If the manager is involved in the clash, the facility director makes the booking decision. Concerns about unfair treatment can also go to the institution’s staff-advice office.
Live-cell acquisitions may need a longer window because the useful endpoint depends on cell behaviour. Label this when booking and include a realistic buffer. This exception does not change institutional access or lone-working rules.
The current user remains responsible for the acquisition log, shutdown or handover and cleaning. The lab manager owns the booking policy. Repeated overruns or an exception that the policy does not handle trigger an earlier review; otherwise the next review is 1 March 2027.


This is one fictional group’s arrangement. Another facility could reserve fixed changeover periods, assign priority by study stage or prohibit overruns.

title: Lab manuals and shared expectations
section: Draft the manual with the people affected
text:
Draft the manual with the people affected
The person accountable for the group should first state the constraints and promises they can actually uphold. Then collect cases from the people affected. A meeting can expose differing interpretations; a short form or private route lets members raise concerns they may not voice in front of a supervisor. Asking members to contribute does not transfer the leader’s responsibility for employment, safety or fair treatment.
Scale the drafting process to the group. A small lab may revise a short draft together. A larger group can assign topic teams, exchange drafts and use several meetings to resolve inconsistent language. The WIN Physics group used volunteer teams, cross-review and advice from departmental and human-resources specialists for its multi-PI group of about 30 people [6].
For each section, compare an ordinary case with an awkward one. Check whether the responsible person has the authority and capacity to act and whether the exception is clear. Ask the appropriate institutional office to review policy-sensitive sections. The responsible leader then confirms what the group can adopt. Record unresolved concerns and keep a route outside the direct supervisor for a member who cannot safely resolve a matter within the group.
Keep the first version short enough to finish. Mehr selected topics around his group’s asynchronous collaborations, left specialist platform detail elsewhere and observed which sections members ignored or could not understand [5].

title: Lab manuals and shared expectations
text:
Introduce, use and revise it
Publish a version, effective date and named owner. Walk through the document with current members, then discuss the relevant sections with a prospective or new member rather than sending a link without context. An acknowledgement can record that the person received the current version and had a chance to ask questions. It should not be presented as blanket consent, a waiver of rights or proof that every expectation is fair.
Refer to the manual when the described situation occurs. If practice differs from the text, either correct the practice or revise the document. Mariam Aly describes using her manual during onboarding, holding herself to its promises and sharing maintenance of a separate practical wiki [1].
Review the manual on a set date, and revise it sooner after a new instrument, changed institutional rule, repeated exception or unclear responsibility. Communicate material changes directly and keep a short change log so that members can tell which expectation applied when. A review of how the group works can reveal when the practice itself needs to change before its description is updated.



Example: adopting and revising the booking policy

The Northbank lab manager begins with two recurring cases: unannounced overruns and unrealistically short bookings made to secure scarce time. Current users discuss both at a lab meeting and can add examples through an anonymous form. The manager drafts two options, checks the facility’s access rules and asks the affected users to test each option against a normal fixed-sample session and a variable live-cell acquisition.
The group leader confirms which arrangement the lab can support. The manager publishes version 1.0, explains it at a meeting and includes the booking section in onboarding. Members are asked to report unclear cases to the manager; a person concerned about unfair treatment can also use the institution’s staff or student route.
During the six-week trial, members interpret “a short shift” differently. Version 1.1 removes that phrase: affected users must agree directly, and the lab manager decides when they cannot. The change log records the reason. The next review is scheduled for six months later, with an earlier review if the same exception recurs.

title: Lab manuals and shared expectations
text:
Data and AI practices
The data section should help a member find an approved place to store and work with their data and the person who can arrange access. Explain which kinds of data each environment can hold and how to record versions or changes during active work. Point to the project record used when someone joins or leaves. Keep dataset-specific retention, consent, transfer and access conditions in the data-management or ethics record that governs the project. Link to that record and explain what members need to do, rather than creating a second copy of rules that may change.
For generative AI, check the current policies that apply to the institution, funder, project partners, data and intended publication. Record the version consulted, approved tools or environments, excluded inputs, uses that require a project record or disclosure, and who verifies the output. A trainee may be able to check generated syntax while still needing to develop the judgment required to choose an analysis or interpret a result. Discuss concrete tasks before writing the rule, and connect permitted use to what the member can explain and verify [2]. Detailed questions about contribution and authorship belong in collaboration, authorship and credit.

title: Lab manuals and shared expectations
text:
Check whether the manual works
Give one section to a member who did not draft it. Ask them what they would do in the ordinary case, what would change in the stated exception and whom they would contact if the responsible person were involved in the concern. If those answers require unwritten knowledge, revise the section.
Check that links open, named roles still exist, public and internal material are separated, and each promised response has an owner with capacity to provide it. Compare the written rule with recent practice. Where they differ, establish whether the practice needs correcting or the manual needs updating before revising the text.

title: Lab manuals and shared expectations
text:
References



Aly, M. (2018). The key to a happy lab life is in the manual. Nature, 561, 7–8.
Blekhman, R. (2026, April 5). You need to make AI guidelines for your lab. Ran’s Substack.
Donà, E., Gahan, J. M., Lau, P., and colleagues. (2025). The SAFE Labs Handbook as a tool for improving lab culture. eLife, 14, e108853.

Mehr, S. A. (2020). How to write a lab handbook. The Biologist, 67(2), 26–29.
Tendler, B. C., Welland, M., Miller, K. L., & the WIN Handbook Team. (2023). Why every lab needs a handbook. eLife, 12, e88853.

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
Priorities and planning
Before taking on new work, consider what the group would need to do it. A promising project may require a method nobody knows yet or more supervision than you can provide. Plan those commitments alongside existing projects and the support already promised to group members.
Translate the group’s longer-term questions into near-term priorities. To understand recovery from stress, for example, you may first need to establish an assay. Decide whether that takes priority this month over completing another analysis or recruiting a specialist, and explain the choice to the group [2, pp. 53–54].
For each priority, agree who will do the work and what support they need. Check it against existing obligations, including thesis completion and the maintenance of shared material. Decide when to review progress before adding further work.
Keep near-term goals concrete while leaving the longer direction open to discovery. Three to six months for immediate priorities and one to three years for scientific growth can be useful starting horizons; shorten them when access or funding is uncertain. Discuss the plan with the group so that people can question the assumptions and explain what their part will require [4].
Scientific goals should specify what can be learned, not demand a preferred result. A milestone can be a working assay with interpretable controls, a complete dataset or a decision about feasibility. If evidence undermines the original idea, completing that decision can be good work even when the project changes direction.
crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
Match resources to the work
Review what is available, what is committed and what is only hoped for. A submitted grant, anticipated fellowship or informal offer of instrument access should remain a separate scenario until it is confirmed. Ask the local finance or research-support team to help translate the plan into costs over time. Include the full appointment cost of people, required student costs where applicable, consumables, facility charges and continuing maintenance. Spending restrictions and end dates can make a nominal balance unavailable for the work you intend [4].
Check what would happen if a grant were unsuccessful, an instrument arrived late or a key person left. Which promised work could no longer be completed? Decide what to reduce or postpone before the group runs out of the time or resources needed for it. Buying facility access may let a project continue while an instrument is unavailable; another project may need to wait.
Equipment decisions also need an operating plan. Compare ownership with facility access using anticipated use, booking constraints, maintenance, technical support and delivery time. A purchase that depends on an unavailable room, missing component or untrained user cannot yet support an incoming researcher. Ask who can help with procurement, installation and access before promising a start date [3, pp. 3–4].
Time is another limited resource. Estimate the training, supervision and coordination that a new commitment requires, including the demands it places on senior researchers. Count the leader’s teaching, writing, administration and existing supervision. A salary can fit the budget while the person’s training cannot fit the week. When the problem concerns how workload or access is distributed, use sustainable and inclusive research workplaces to redesign the arrangement with the people affected.
crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
Hiring
Identify the work that needs someone to do it. A group may need reliable daily culture maintenance, help with a specialist analysis or a researcher to develop a new question. Consider whether a facility service or collaboration could meet the need, or whether the group should reduce its planned work. If hiring is the appropriate choice, describe the responsibilities and required skills. State what the person can learn in the role and who will train and supervise them.
There is no universal first hire. An experienced technician may establish continuity and support training but cost more. A novice may be an excellent choice when the leader has time to teach and the work can wait for that learning. A postdoc needs scope for scientific judgment and development as well as funded time. Compare the role’s contribution with the support it needs, rather than treating one career stage as a cheaper substitute for another [1, pp. 8–17].
Check the appointment route with the relevant programme, department or human-resources team before advertising. Student placements, fellowships and staff appointments can have different procedures and obligations. Follow the current local process for classification, pay, recruitment and offers.

Evaluate evidence for the role
Choose the criteria before reviewing applicants. Separate what someone must already be able to do from what you can teach. Use the same core questions and a comparable opportunity to demonstrate the required work. A short, relevant scenario might ask how a candidate would investigate an inconsistent control or document a handover. Explain what it assesses and avoid asking applicants to perform an unpaid piece of the group’s research.
Ask about the candidate’s actual contribution, how they handled uncertainty and how they worked with others. For someone without research experience, examples from coursework or other work can demonstrate careful records, learning and coordination. Evaluate those examples against the role rather than requiring an experience the position is meant to provide [5, pp. 16–20].
Record evidence against the criteria and ask other interviewers to do the same. “The candidate described checking and correcting a sample-label error” is useful evidence; “they seemed like one of us” is difficult to inspect. Collaboration matters, but similarity, confidence, eye contact or enthusiasm are poor substitutes for what the work requires. Give candidates time to think and opportunities to ask questions. Follow the agreed reference-check process, including permission before contacting a current supervisor [2, pp. 83–89].
The candidate is also choosing an environment. Explain the available funding, current limitations, supervision, responsibilities and scope for development. Arrange a conversation with current members in which the leader is absent. Answer what you can honestly provide; separate an intention from an authorized commitment.



Example: choose a hire and revise the operating plan

Nadia leads a fictional cell-biology group with two doctoral researchers. One is completing a thesis; the other recently joined. The technician who maintains cultures and reagent records will leave in eight weeks. Nadia wants to replace that role and begin a second assay, but she can currently provide six hours a week of direct training. The new doctoral researcher needs four of those hours.
Nadia and the department’s finance adviser cost two appointments over their full proposed duration, including the associated running costs. Both are affordable from committed funds. A novice appointment would leave enough money for the second assay; an experienced appointment would require postponing it. They do not include a pending grant in either budget.
Work required: Maintain cultures and stocks, identify routine quality problems, keep complete records and provide a usable handover. Developing the second assay is a separate aim.
Support needed: Nadia estimates that a novice would initially need four hours of direct training each week, in addition to the doctoral researcher’s four. An experienced hire would still need local training, estimated at two hours. These are assumptions for this group, to be checked after appointment. The finishing researcher has no unallocated training capacity.
Decision: Recruit for the experienced role and postpone the second assay. Six hours of planned training fits the six available; eight does not. The group retains an important existing activity and protects the student’s training. The trade-off is a slower expansion of the programme. Core-facility imaging already meets the present study’s needs, so Nadia also defers a proposed instrument purchase.
Continuity: Nadia checks the hiring timetable with the department. If the appointment starts after the technician leaves, she will pause new experimental runs and maintain only essential cultures herself. The expansion will remain deferred during that gap.
Selection: Candidates receive the same culture-record scenario and explain what they would check before declaring a batch usable. Interviewers assess the required technical judgment, documentation and communication. The selected candidate supplies concrete examples of these capabilities and asks for training on the group’s local system. Nadia and the candidate agree that this training will precede independent responsibility.
Start and review: The outgoing technician prepares the inventory and handover. Nadia arranges access and required training, protects the two weekly training hours and reviews the first complete work records with the new member. Independence requires reliable execution and recognition of failed controls, rather than a desired experimental result. If local training takes longer than estimated, Nadia revises the work allocation before adding tasks.
Reconsideration: At the next resource review, Nadia will revisit the second assay if funding and supervision capacity are both available. A grant award alone will not establish that the group can support another trainee.


The experienced appointment is justified by this group’s bottleneck and capacity. With sufficient teaching time and a less urgent continuity need, the novice route could be preferable. Experience also does not remove the need to check readiness for the particular task.
crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
Onboarding
Arrange access, workspace and training before the new member arrives. Name who can answer everyday questions and who is responsible for supervision. Discuss the relevant shared expectations, then make a separate mentoring agreement for the person’s support and development.
Choose an early task that teaches the local workflow and has an interpretable outcome. Supply the protocol or starting material, expected controls, record location and a person to consult when something differs. Observe enough of the work to check that the new member recognizes errors and knows when to pause. Include technical training and the practical work of finding records, sharing progress and making a handover [5, p. 20].
Set a review point around that first task. Ask what remained unclear, which promised support was available and what the person can now do independently. Adjust the next assignment accordingly. If a senior researcher provides training, agree the time and its effect on their own project; do not quietly add responsibility because they happen to be approachable.
crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
Delegating responsibility
When delegating work, agree what the person is expected to accomplish and which decisions they can make. Specify the available resources and the changes they must discuss with you first. Check that they understand and can accept the responsibility, and agree when to review progress. Tell others whose cooperation is needed, and support the person’s decisions within the agreed scope [2, pp. 55–57].
Match independence to capability for the task and the consequence of error. Someone can independently maintain an established workflow while needing close discussion for a new method. Review at meaningful points without reclaiming every choice because you prefer a different style. Retain decisions involving commitments or authority that cannot be delegated by the group itself.



Example: a bounded handover of booking decisions

For an experienced researcher coordinating a fictional imaging pilot, a written handover could say:

You will coordinate imaging for the current pilot within the approved facility allocation. You can arrange slots with the users, change the order of runs within the agreed design and ask the facility to resolve an access problem. Keep the schedule and reasons for changes in the project record. Bring any change to sampling, extra expenditure or a clash with another project’s agreed time to me before committing it. We will review the schedule after the first acquisition cycle. I will tell the team that these booking decisions are yours and remain responsible for resolving a resource conflict you cannot settle.

If the coordinator has never used the facility’s booking system, first provide training and supervised practice.


Detailed agreements between collaborating groups belong in collaboration, authorship and credit.
crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
Meetings and review
Use different conversations for different decisions. An individual meeting can examine a researcher’s reasoning and support needs. A project meeting can resolve a shared dependency. A group meeting can compare interpretations and discuss scientific direction. Give each a purpose, useful preparation and a record of decisions, owners and next checks; choose frequency around the work rather than filling the calendar [2, pp. 58–60].
When work stalls, first establish what happened. A valid negative result, a failed procedure, a blocked resource and a missed agreed action need different responses. Compare the expectation with training, access, workload and supervision before deciding that the person lacks motivation. Discuss the specific observation privately, hear their account and agree the support, action and review needed. The leader may need to change a promise or priority as well as asking the member to change their work [5, pp. 33–36, 54–57].
Keep enough contact with methods, controls and original records to understand the science being produced. Invite concerns before results are polished, give people room to disagree and recognize work that enables others: maintenance, curation, training and coordination. A recurring problem should produce a decision about support or responsibility, not an indefinitely repeated expression of disappointment. Detailed feedback and difficult conversations are treated in feedback and conflict. A safety or integrity concern needs the appropriate institutional route promptly; it should not wait for the next routine project review.
Give your own leadership work time and support. Protect thinking, writing and supervision in the calendar; tell the group how to reach someone when you are unavailable. Seek advice from experienced leaders, peers and administrative specialists. To improve a particular practice, examine where it causes difficulty. For example, record which decisions wait for your approval for a fortnight, then delegate a suitable recurring class of decision and check whether the team can act within its scope [2, pp. 51–53].
crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
Preparing the review
Choose a period that allows you to compare the last agreed priorities with what actually happened. An annual discussion can provide a broad view, with shorter reviews after a substantial change in staffing, funding or workload. Do not wait for that meeting to address an urgent concern. [7, pp. 115–121]; [8, pp. 719–720].
Prepare a brief account of what the group has learned and can now do. Include progress that has not yet led to a paper, such as establishing a method or completing an analysis. Recognize training and maintenance that allow others to work. Then identify commitments that have changed and obstacles that recur. If a paper is delayed, explain what is holding it up: an unresolved scientific question may require a different response from work that repeatedly loses its allotted time. [8, pp. 719–720].
Bring enough information to discuss resources honestly. Which work is already promised? Which skills, facilities and supervision does it require? Where will a departure, a funding end date or a new responsibility change what is feasible? Distinguish confirmed support from an application or an informal offer. Share the constraints needed for the decision without circulating individual salary, health or personnel information. Beltrao (2022) [6] offers one example of considering people, research and funding together; its particular costs and group size are not benchmarks for other laboratories.
Invite members to prepare their own observations before seeing the leader’s conclusions. Ask which arrangements help them do good work, where work repeatedly gets stuck and what change would make a meaningful difference. A specific example gives the discussion something to examine. People should also have a way to raise concerns outside the group meeting, especially when they involve a supervisor or colleague on whom they depend. [8, pp. 718–720]; [7, pp. 112–113].
Agree who will read written responses, what will be retained and how concerns requiring another route will be handled. In a small group, a supposedly anonymous comment can identify its author through its details. Do not promise anonymity that the collection method cannot provide. The feedback and conflict chapter explains how to distinguish a discussion of shared practice from a concern that needs individual or institutional attention.
crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
Discussing recurring problems
Begin with what is working well enough to preserve. A new procedure can unintentionally remove something valuable, such as informal technical help or time to explore a surprising observation. Then examine the concerns, allowing members to describe what they see before the leader offers an explanation. Differences between accounts are useful information: someone who receives quick help may not see how much work it creates for the person providing it. [7, pp. 112–117].
Follow a concern far enough to distinguish plausible explanations. If analyses are late, ask whether the data are ready, the method is established, the necessary expertise is available and the assigned researcher has the time the plan assumed. A problem shared by several projects may require changing how the group allocates work. A difficulty specific to one person’s training may be better addressed in a mentoring conversation. Neither conclusion follows simply from the missed date. [8, p. 720].
Include the effects of routine work on access and development. Who repeatedly trains newcomers, maintains equipment or resolves urgent requests? Who has opportunities to learn, present and take responsibility? Use the workplace review to examine these patterns in more detail. The purpose is to understand how the arrangements operate, not to ask individuals to justify private circumstances in front of colleagues.
Keep the discussion specific when views differ. Record the observation, the competing explanations and what would help distinguish them. A vote cannot determine why an assay is failing, and a majority’s comfortable experience does not settle another member’s report of poor treatment. Address concerns about conduct through the appropriate route; do not use a group review as an improvised investigation.
crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
Choosing changes
Compare a proposed change with the work it would displace. Training a backup, improving documentation or changing a meeting format takes effort now, even when it will save effort later. State where that time will come from. Asking everyone to fit it around existing commitments leaves the capacity problem unresolved. [8, pp. 719–720].
Members can help compare alternatives without being made responsible for securing a budget they do not control. Explain which changes the group can agree itself and which require a decision elsewhere. Do not promise additional funding or support until the person with that authority has agreed.
Choose a small enough change that the group can support it and tell whether it helped. The following example postpones an attractive collaboration because the existing work already depends on support that is spread too thinly.



Worked example: protect an existing project before adding another

This fictional microscopy group has a PI, two postdocs, two doctoral researchers and a technician. Two projects use the same imaging assay and analysis workflow. A collaborator has proposed a third pilot. One postdoc will leave in four months, and the technician handles most troubleshooting.
The PI initially thinks more frequent progress meetings would help a delayed analysis. Preparing for the group review changes the picture: sample processing is on schedule, but the researcher doing the analysis is repeatedly interrupted to help resolve assay problems. The technician also lacks a trained backup. Another meeting would reveal the delay without supplying the missing time.

Decision record — 2 October

Priority. Bring the existing analysis to its agreed checkpoint and establish a second person who can troubleshoot the assay before the postdoc leaves.
Change. Defer the collaborator’s pilot. Protect two analysis sessions each week by routing routine assay questions through the technician during agreed support periods. Urgent problems that could lose samples still receive immediate attention; repeated urgent requests trigger a review of the arrangement.
Training and resources. One doctoral researcher will complete a supervised troubleshooting run with the technician. The PI will remove a planned exploratory experiment from that researcher’s schedule and postpone a nonessential imaging batch assigned to the technician. Those changes provide time for both people. The PI will also ask the core facility whether it can provide continuing support.
Responsibility. The PI will explain the delay to the collaborator this week. The technician and doctoral researcher will agree the training run. The analyst will bring the completed analysis, or a specific remaining obstacle, to the next review.
Review — six weeks later. Check whether the analysis reached its checkpoint, the backup can complete the troubleshooting run and interruptions have become manageable. Reconsider the pilot only with an explicit estimate of its workload and available support.
At the six-week review, the analysis has reached its checkpoint and the trainee has completed the supervised run. Independent troubleshooting still needs to be demonstrated. The core facility cannot offer continuing support. The group retains the protected analysis time and keeps the pilot deferred while the PI and collaborator reduce its scope. Progress on the existing work has improved, but the extra capacity needed for a third project has not yet been established.


The collaborator could reasonably be disappointed: postponement may cost a scientific opportunity. Accepting the pilot would also have a cost, borne partly by the people whose current work would slow down. The decision therefore depends on the value and timing of both projects, not on a general rule against new work. Here, the unresolved support problem favors postponement. Check that the new arrangement has not quietly transferred every interruption to the technician.
crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
Following up
Distribute a concise account of the agreed decisions and invite corrections. Keep personal disclosures and sensitive case details out of the shared record. If a change affects a standing practice, update the relevant lab-manual section. If it changes a collaborator’s responsibilities or delivery date, revise the collaboration agreement.
At the next review, distinguish an action completed from a problem resolved. A training session may have happened without making the trainee ready to work independently. A revised schedule may meet a deadline while shifting the same workload into evenings. Ask the people affected whether the arrangement works, using an appropriate private conversation when a public answer would be difficult. Compare that account with the agreed evidence of improvement. [7, pp. 115–121]; [8, p. 720].
When a change has not helped, revisit the explanation and the resources before repeating the instruction more firmly. Keep the reason for changing or retaining the arrangement with the decision, so a later review can build on what the group learned.
crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Leading and reviewing a research group
text:
References

Burroughs Wellcome Fund and Howard Hughes Medical Institute. (2006). Making the Right Moves: A Practical Guide to Scientific Management for Postdocs and New Faculty (2nd ed.).
Goldstein, B., & Avasthi, P. (2021). A guide to setting up and managing a lab at a research-intensive institution. BMC Proceedings, 15(Suppl 2), 8.

crumbs: Leading and reviewing a research group

title: Collaboration, authorship and credit
text:
Start from the shared question
Discuss the shared question and what each collaborator hopes to gain from the work. Agree the contributions and resources needed to begin, then revisit responsibilities and credit as the project develops.
Describe the question and how combining your expertise or resources will help answer it. Ask what each participant contributes and hopes to learn. Decide whether the work calls for a consultation, a standard service or continuing scientific collaboration. A specialist invited only after data collection may be unable to repair the design. When their judgment can change the question, measurements or interpretation, involve them during design [6].
Check capacity as well as interest. Estimate each contribution and identify the time, staff, computing, samples or access that support it. Routine analysis, data curation and software maintenance still require skilled labor. If one group must absorb unfunded work, say so and decide whether the project remains mutually workable [6].
The starting conversation should leave room for different aims. One collaborator may want a biological finding; another may need a method that advances their own research. Agree whether developing that method is part of the project and whether the available time and resources support it. Otherwise, one person may expect a finished analysis while the other expects time to develop and test a new approach.

title: Collaboration, authorship and credit
Collaboration, authorship and credit
text:
Coordinate across expertise
Ask collaborators which choices make their part of the work trustworthy and which limitations affect the shared claim. Before handing data over for analysis, discuss how measurements were acquired, which observations were excluded or missing, and what transformations and model assumptions the analysis requires. The analyst needs to understand how the measurements arose, and the experimentalist needs to understand what the analysis can distinguish.
Before a meeting, circulate the protocol change, diagnostic plot, discrepant result or draft claim that needs discussion. Record what the group decides, why, who will act and what they will check next. Invite disagreement while the group can still change its interpretation or planned work. If a collaborator cannot raise concerns about the design or interpretation, their expertise has little opportunity to shape the result [2, pp. 45, 50–51].
Review the plan when the evidence changes the work. A new analysis may become a central intellectual contribution; a planned method may become routine; a contributor may leave or join. Revise responsibilities, resources and credit expectations together.

title: Collaboration, authorship and credit
text:
Contributions, authorship and order
First describe each person’s contribution. Then apply the relevant authorship criteria, agree author order and decide how to acknowledge other work. A contribution record informs these decisions but does not automatically determine them.
Describe contributions. Record what each person actually did. CRediT offers 14 roles, including conceptualization, investigation, methodology, data curation, software, formal analysis, visualization, supervision and two writing roles. Use the vocabulary when it fits the work; do not turn the roles into points or assume that every role has equal weight [5].
Decide authorship eligibility and responsibility. Check the target journal and relevant disciplinary or institutional guidance. CRediT is descriptive and is not designed to determine authorship. For journals that follow ICMJE, authors must meet four requirements. In summary, each author must:

Have contributed substantially to developing the study’s ideas, planning it, or obtaining, analyzing or interpreting its data.
Have helped write the manuscript or critically assessed its intellectual content.
Have approved the version being published.
Accept responsibility for helping resolve concerns about the work, including parts carried out by others. [4, section 2].

If someone questions the work’s reliability, authors must help ensure that the concern is investigated and any problem addressed. They should know who carried out the other parts of the study and have confidence in those contributions. This does not mean personally repeating every specialist check. Consult the full ICMJE criteria when deciding eligibility, and confirm that every author has reviewed and approved the version being submitted. [4, section 2].
Corresponding authorship involves managing communication with the journal and ensuring that submission requirements are met; it does not by itself establish a larger scientific contribution. [4, section 2].
Decide order collectively. Name the convention being used and the rationale. Order conventions differ across fields and journals. Shared-first or shared-senior designations also depend on journal policy. A contribution statement can clarify the work, but displayed order may still affect evaluation [6].
Recognize other work. Name non-author contributions as the journal permits, specify the contribution and obtain any required consent. Recognition can also include named presentations, software or data citations and a contribution record for evaluation when those outputs reflect the work.
For an ICMJE-following journal, do not exclude a person who made the substantial contribution in the first criterion by withholding the chance to review or draft the manuscript and approve it. Offer a real opportunity with access and time to participate. Authorship follows only if the person then meets all four criteria [4].



Example: a completed contribution and credit decision

At the final dataset review, the hypoxia project no longer matches its opening expectations. Leo’s diagnostics reveal a batch effect; he redesigns the model and works with Aisha on an additional balanced collection. The change alters the claim. Leo also drafts the analysis and findings and creates the main quantitative figures. Aisha continues to lead the biological work and writes the first complete manuscript. Their central intellectual and practical leadership is now comparable in scope and duration, although the work differs.
Mei’s acquisition design and interpretation are also substantial. Because the selected journal follows ICMJE recommendations, the team gives her the opportunity to complete its manuscript responsibilities. She revises the imaging methods and interpretation, critically reviews the complete paper, approves the submitted version and accepts the journal’s accountability requirement. Rao’s documented conception, interpretation and substantive manuscript review qualify him under the selected policy; funding and supervision alone would not.
Target rule: The journal permits a shared-first statement and follows ICMJE authorship recommendations. All four authors have critically reviewed or drafted the paper, approved this version and accepted the stated accountability obligation.

Contribution record: Aisha—conceptualization, investigation, validation and writing the original draft. Leo—methodology, software, formal analysis, visualization and writing the analysis and findings. Mei—methodology, investigation, validation and critical review and editing. Rao—conceptualization, supervision, interpretation and critical review and editing.

Byline decision: Aisha and Leo are shared first authors. Aisha is displayed first because the group agrees that her integrated study leadership and complete first draft justify that sequence. Leo’s comparable quantitative leadership is stated in the equal-contribution note and contribution statement. Mei follows them. Rao is last under the group’s field convention and his documented contribution.
Trade-off: The shared-first note represents the team’s judgment, but displayed order may still influence evaluation.
Other credit: The technician performed routine stock maintenance and trained Aisha in an established assay, without contributing to the study’s conception, design, data acquisition, analysis or interpretation. The team records the actual work and acknowledges it by name with permission. Aisha and Leo are assigned the biological and quantitative portions of two planned presentations, and each contributor receives this record for evaluation.


If the journal did not allow a shared-first designation, the contribution and eligibility decisions would remain the same. The group would need to choose one displayed order, document its rationale and record the unchosen alternative and trade-off. CRediT roles would still describe the work; they would not calculate the answer.

title: Collaboration, authorship and credit
section: Address a credit disagreement with evidence
text:
Address a credit disagreement with evidence
Start with the disputed decision. “My analysis is missing from the contribution statement,” “I meet the journal’s authorship criteria,” and “I should be listed first” are different claims. Reconstruct the agreed plan and actual work, including changes in scope, drafts, decisions and approvals. Then apply the current target policy and ask what proposed outcome follows from that evidence.
Discuss the record with everyone whose credit would change and write down the revised decision. Early discussion and written updates reduce surprises, but the first agreement is not conclusive when contributions change [1]. Avoid bargaining with unrelated resources or future favors. When a power difference makes direct discussion difficult, use the neutral route named in the agreement or seek confidential procedural advice from the institution.
Journal editors usually lack the evidence and authority to adjudicate who qualifies. Under current ICMJE recommendations, unresolved authorship-eligibility questions should be investigated by the institution or institutions where the work was performed, while author order is decided collectively by the author group [4]. Other journals and disciplines may use different procedures. Broader relationship conflict, retaliation concerns or formal allegations need their appropriate local route and more support than an authorship worksheet can provide; see feedback and conflict.

title: Collaboration, authorship and credit
text:
End or transform the collaboration
A project can end while a collaboration continues, and a person can leave while papers, software or datasets remain active. Name which event is happening. Review the outputs still expected, stewardship of shared records and materials, permitted access, remaining consultation, credit review and the date when obligations end. Follow the applicable institutional agreements for data, confidentiality, intellectual property and employment; a collaboration plan does not decide those rights.
State what was learned, what remains unresolved and who can answer questions about each part. If the team begins a new question, write a new scope and contribution record [2, pp. 46, 132–134].

title: Sustainable and inclusive research workplaces
text:
Workload and availability
A research group can offer flexible hours and still make them difficult to use. Someone who leaves at the agreed time may miss decisions made over evening drinks; someone who works remotely may spend their day waiting for access to a shared computer. A colleague who reliably trains newcomers may have less time for the research on which their progress is judged.
Start with a recurring difficulty and discuss what would help with the people affected. If someone has too much assigned work, the person assigning it needs to help decide what can wait. Advice about personal planning will have little effect while the same commitments remain [3].
Before adding a deadline or responsibility, look at the work already committed. Include preparation, documentation, analysis, meetings, teaching, training and shared duties as well as experiments. Ask which tasks have a fixed window and which can move. An afternoon sampling endpoint may be biologically constrained; a meeting scheduled after it may simply be convenient for one person.
Compare the plan with the time, equipment and qualified help actually available. When it does not fit, choose what changes: reduce the scope, move a deadline, stop a lower-priority task or arrange suitable cover. Members can identify which commitments compete for their time, but the person who assigns the work must help decide what gives way. Review planned and actual work after a representative period, including unexpected duties, rather than treating a missed target as evidence of poor motivation [3, Rules 4–5].
Separate tasks that require presence from those that allow choice of time or location. An operator must attend an acquisition they have agreed to run; an analyst may be able to work elsewhere. Agree when people need to overlap, how handovers happen and when a response can be expected. Flexibility still needs supervision, access to information and a way to resolve a blocked task [5, Rule 2].
Make communication match that agreement. If a leader sends messages at unusual hours, state when a reply is expected and use scheduled delivery where useful. Establish a separate route for genuinely time-sensitive operational problems, with a named person responsible during the relevant window. Routine questions should not turn every group member into permanent backup. Someone’s preference for late work does not set everyone else’s availability.
Occasional field campaigns, sampling windows or submission deadlines may need a temporary arrangement. Before committing, agree what it must accomplish, when it ends, who can provide qualified cover and what other work will be reduced or deferred. Check applicable working-time and safety arrangements with the responsible people. Plan the return to ordinary work as part of the decision. If the same demand keeps recurring, change the project, staffing or deadline to account for it in the regular workload [6]; [5, Rule 7].

title: Sustainable and inclusive research workplaces
text:
Access and participation
Look at what someone must be able to do to contribute. Can they obtain the necessary equipment without paying personally? Reach the meeting space, use the online platform and read the material? Attend when decisions are made? Understand enough of the discussion to ask a question? Ask about practical needs privately and offer a route for raising them with the appropriate institutional service. Do not expect one member to represent an entire identity group or teach colleagues about every barrier [4, Rules 1–2 and 6].
Give people more than one way to contribute to important decisions. Circulate the question and essential material in advance, allow written input, and record the decision where everyone involved can find it. During discussion, make room for questions and contributions from people who have not spoken. A quiet person may have useful evidence; fluent or rapid speech is not the only sign of understanding. Low-stakes opportunities to ask about a method or work through a coding problem can help people learn without turning every uncertainty into a performance assessment [4, Rules 5 and 9].
Keep optional social gatherings optional in practice. Offer different ways to meet colleagues, including some during ordinary working hours. If a conversation over dinner produces a research decision, bring that decision back to the relevant work discussion before relying on it. People who cannot attend should retain access to opportunities and information. Ask whether the arrangements work for the people affected; attendance alone cannot tell you whether they feel included.
Make the work of maintaining the group visible. Training, organizing visitors, taking notes and arranging celebrations all take time. Check who repeatedly does them, how much capacity they consume and whether that person is also getting development opportunities. Distribute duties with attention to role, competence and workload; identical rotations may be unsuitable for specialist tasks. Acknowledge contributions and include them when discussing workload and progress. Raffington describes tracking and discussing this often overlooked work so that it can be shared more fairly [6].
Document the shared arrangement in the lab manual. Keep personal circumstances and individual support agreements in the appropriate private record. A written expectation is useful only when the group follows it and the responsible person can act on it.

title: Sustainable and inclusive research workplaces
text:
Assessing contributions
Explain what good work looks like for the person’s role and stage. A developing researcher may need to show sound experimental decisions and explain uncertainty. A technician may contribute reliable operation, troubleshooting and training. An analyst may deliver a checked, documented analysis that others can use. Discuss the work itself, the evidence that will demonstrate progress and the support needed to produce it [6]; [5, Rules 3 and 6].
Use concrete evidence rather than impressions of commitment. Long presence in the lab, quick replies and confident language do not establish that a result is trustworthy. A journal’s average citation count also cannot establish the quality of a particular paper or its author’s contribution; the underlying papers vary substantially [1, pp. 9–12]. Read the work and identify what the person actually did.
Distinguish what the researcher can influence from what remains uncertain. They can choose appropriate controls, keep records, check an analysis and respond to feedback; they cannot promise a desired biological result or journal acceptance. A result that challenges the hypothesis differs from a failed procedure or a measurement that cannot answer the question. Assess what the work permits the researcher to conclude and how they followed it up. When progress differs from the plan, also examine the support: was required training available, did a shared duty expand, or was an instrument unavailable? Agree the next action and record why the target or support changed. Recognizing careful work does not require continuing a project when no feasible next experiment can answer its question.
Use the mentoring agreement for individual development and the collaboration plan for project contributions and credit. Shared support work deserves recognition, while authorship still requires an appropriate contribution to the particular publication.

title: Sustainable and inclusive research workplaces
text:
Practical support
If someone says an arrangement is becoming difficult, offer a private conversation about what would help. They might need a changed task, a clearer priority, time away, equipment access or advice from another person. Listen before choosing the remedy. An ordinary conversation about workload need not begin with a diagnosis or an account of family circumstances. Formal support or accommodation processes may have their own information requirements; help the person find the responsible service rather than collecting that information in a group meeting [2, pp. 10, 19–21].
A supervisor can change work within their authority and help someone reach suitable support. That role does not make them a therapist or medical assessor. Keep current staff and student support routes easy to find, including an option outside the direct supervisor. Check who a service covers, how to contact it and what its privacy terms actually say. Do not promise confidentiality or an institutional outcome on behalf of another office.
Peer groups, personal interests and optional wellbeing activities may be useful resources. They cannot settle an impossible deadline, inaccessible workplace or unresolved mistreatment. Ayres’s discussion of university programmes pairs support for individuals with changes to the conditions creating difficulty [2, chapter 5]. If a problem lies beyond the group leader’s authority, identify the institutional decision needed and who will pursue it. Avoid leaving the person who raised the problem responsible for obtaining every remedy. For concerns about treatment or retaliation, use the support and power considerations before choosing a conversation or disclosure route.

title: Sustainable and inclusive research workplaces
text:
Planning a change
Choose a change the group can carry out with the people and resources available. State what will continue, what will change and what work will be displaced. Give each action an owner who has the authority and time to carry it out. Agree how you will check whether it addressed the problem, when to review it and what would require an earlier decision. Discuss individual needs privately; record the availability and work arrangements needed for coordination in the shared plan.



Example: a four-week sampling and analysis plan
This fictional group has six afternoon sampling endpoints over four weeks. Two people are trained and authorized to operate the assay. One cannot stay into the evening; the other already maintains stocks and trains a new member. The analyst lacks a suitable workstation. Some research decisions have been made at optional evening gatherings.

The group considers training a third operator immediately, which would delay this assay, or keeping the two qualified operators while postponing a new pilot and reducing their other duties. The established assay can finish within the operators’ agreed hours if preparation begins earlier. The group chooses the second option for this run and writes the following plan.
Purpose and period. Complete the six established sampling sessions and a documented initial analysis over the next four weeks. This plan applies to those sessions; it does not create an expectation of evening availability.
Sampling and other duties. Before the first session, the two operators and group leader confirm the six dates, preparation times and handovers. The leader postpones the new pilot until after this run. A third colleague, already trained in stock care, covers that duty for the four weeks; the leader reduces that colleague’s other assigned work accordingly. New-member assay training resumes after the run. During the pause, the leader agrees a suitable starter task and a named supervisor with available time; the new member is not assigned unsupervised assay work. The sampling operators retain responsibility for the assay records.
Access and decisions. The analyst and computing support agree a suitable shared-workstation booking before the first dataset is ready. If access cannot be provided, the leader revises the analysis date rather than expecting the analyst to buy equipment. Project decisions take place at the scheduled daytime meeting, with material circulated beforehand and a written-input route for anyone who cannot attend. The meeting chair records decisions. Evening social conversations may suggest ideas, but do not commit absent colleagues to work.
Progress and support. The leader and each member agree their relevant contribution: complete assay records, checked analysis with unresolved issues identified, stock-care coverage or defined training progress after the run. Each assay run is reviewed against the protocol, controls and observations. A result that does not support the hypothesis is not itself an assay failure. Individual support arrangements are discussed separately; the shared plan records only the availability needed for coordination.
Review and exceptions. At the end of week two, the leader checks with the members whether the workload and access arrangements are working. An absent qualified operator, repeated overrun or missing workstation access triggers an earlier decision. The leader reschedules a session or changes scope if safe, authorized cover is unavailable. Nobody is treated as automatic evening backup. At the end of week four, the group confirms which duties return and whether the pilot can start; it does not assume that deferred work now fits.


Check whether cover has merely moved an overload to another colleague. Another group may need to delay the experiment, arrange different resources or abandon a lower-priority aim. When similar difficulties recur across projects, include them in a review of how the group works.
